beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Java is a programming language: a precise way to describe data and the steps a computer should perform.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can write programs, reason about their behavior, and explain why one implementation is safer or faster than another. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Java like a written language for a very literal teammate: grammar matters, every instruction has a meaning, and missing details become bugs. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: check the runtime using `java --version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Values, references, identity, and equality
theorySections.explanation: Java always passes arguments by value. For an object variable, the copied value is a reference, so two callers can observe mutations to the same object even though the reference itself was copied. Identity asks whether references designate the same object; logical equality is a type-defined relation implemented by equals and must remain consistent with hashCode when values enter hash-based collections.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A Java variable never contains an object itself: it contains either a primitive value or a reference value that can point to an object.
theorySections.analogy: A reference is like a house address written on two cards. Copying the card does not copy the house; both cards still lead to the same house.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Unlike a postal address, a Java reference is opaque, garbage-collected, and cannot be arithmetically changed into another valid reference.
theorySections.concreteExample: If two variables reference one ArrayList, adding through either variable changes the shared list, but reassigning one variable leaves the other unchanged.
keyPoints: Primitives contain values; reference variables contain reference values, not objects inline.
Reassigning a parameter never reassigns the caller's variable.
Mutable keys can become unreachable inside HashMap when equality-relevant state changes.
Prefer immutable value objects and define equality from stable domain identity or value semantics.

theorySections.title: Generics, variance, and erasure
theorySections.explanation: Java generics are invariant: List<Integer> is not a subtype of List<Number>. Wildcards express use-site variance, where ? extends T is a producer you read as T and ? super T is a consumer you may write T into. Most generic type arguments are erased from runtime representation, which explains bridge methods, heap-pollution hazards, and why new T(), T.class, and generic arrays are unavailable.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Generics let the compiler protect relationships between types, while wildcards state whether a container will mainly produce or consume values.
theorySections.analogy: A sealed crate labelled Apples can be treated as a producer of Fruit, but allowing arbitrary Fruit into it could put an orange in an apple-only crate.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Real crates retain their labels; most Java generic labels are erased at runtime, so reflection and array creation follow different rules.
theorySections.concreteExample: A List<? extends Number> can safely yield a Number but cannot accept an Integer because the actual list might be List<Double>.
keyPoints: PECS is a usage rule, not a replacement for understanding variance.
Erasure preserves older JVM compatibility but limits runtime reification.
Raw types disable useful checks and can move a failure far from its cause.
A generic method can capture a wildcard even when callers cannot name its type.

theorySections.title: Collections and stream semantics
theorySections.explanation: Collection interfaces specify contracts rather than one universal performance profile. ArrayList favors indexed reads and append, HashMap relies on stable equality and distribution, TreeMap maintains comparator order, and concurrent collections make different consistency promises. Streams describe a lazy pipeline; terminal operations trigger traversal, and parallel execution is safe only when functions are non-interfering, associative where required, and worth the coordination cost.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collections store data under different access guarantees, while a stream is a one-use recipe that performs work only when a terminal operation asks for a result.
theorySections.analogy: Choose a collection like choosing storage: a numbered shelf suits indexed access, a labelled locker suits key lookup, and a conveyor belt suits a processing pipeline.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Hardware locality, hashing, resizing, and concurrency make real performance more nuanced than a storage-room comparison.
theorySections.concreteExample: Filtering and mapping a stream builds a lazy pipeline; collect or count triggers traversal, and trying to reuse the consumed stream fails.
keyPoints: Choose by access pattern, ordering, mutation, cardinality, and concurrency requirements.
HashMap expected O(1) depends on hashing quality and resizing; it is not a worst-case guarantee.
A stream is not a collection and cannot generally be reused after a terminal operation.
Parallel streams use shared pool resources and are rarely a free latency improvement.

theorySections.title: Class lifecycle and JVM execution
theorySections.explanation: A class is loaded, verified, prepared, resolved as needed, and initialized before first active use. Bytecode begins in an interpreter or lower compilation tier while runtime profiles identify hot methods and branches. The JIT may inline, eliminate allocations, and specialize code using assumptions; invalid assumptions cause deoptimization back to safer code, so warm-up behavior can differ sharply from steady state.
theorySections.plainEnglish: The JVM verifies portable bytecode, begins executing it conservatively, watches real behavior, and optimizes frequently used paths into machine code.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre rehearses from the script, notices the scenes performed most often, and builds faster stage arrangements for those hot scenes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: JIT optimization is based on guarded runtime assumptions and can be undone through deoptimization, unlike a permanently rebuilt theatre set.
theorySections.concreteExample: A call site that repeatedly sees one implementation may be inlined; loading a new implementation can invalidate that assumption and deoptimize it.
keyPoints: Loading and initialization are distinct; static initialization is synchronized per class.
JIT optimization uses observed profiles and may later be revoked.
Microbenchmarks need a harness such as JMH to control warm-up and dead-code elimination.
Bytecode portability does not imply identical performance across JVMs or collectors.

theorySections.title: Memory management and garbage collection
theorySections.explanation: Objects become collectible when they are unreachable from GC roots, not when a scope visually ends. Most JVMs allocate quickly in thread-local buffers and collect young objects frequently because most die young. Collector choice trades throughput, pause behavior, CPU, memory overhead, and operational predictability; a memory leak in managed code is usually unintended reachability rather than missing free calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: The collector reclaims objects only after no path from a live root can reach them; leaving a scope does not by itself guarantee collection.
theorySections.analogy: A warehouse removes boxes that are no longer listed from any active inventory chain, not boxes that merely have not been opened recently.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Collectors move, scan, and reclaim objects according to implementation strategies; the analogy does not predict pause time or physical placement.
theorySections.concreteExample: A cache that keeps every request object reachable from a static map leaks memory even though no business code uses the old entries.
keyPoints: Stack versus heap is an implementation-oriented explanation; escape analysis can change allocation.
finalize is unsafe and obsolete; use ownership protocols such as try-with-resources.
A larger heap can reduce collection frequency while increasing worst-case recovery or scan costs.
Heap pressure, allocation rate, retained size, and pause time are different measurements.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and the Java Memory Model
theorySections.explanation: The Java Memory Model defines when writes by one thread become visible to another and which reorderings are legal. Happens-before edges arise from program order, monitor release/acquire, volatile write/read, thread start/join, and library synchronization. volatile provides visibility and ordering for a variable but does not make compound read-modify-write operations atomic; correctness begins with an invariant and a synchronization policy that covers every participating field.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Threads need specified ordering edges so that one thread's writes become visible to another; elapsed time or debugger observation is not such a guarantee.
theorySections.analogy: Two offices use a signed handover log: the signature establishes which update must be visible before the next worker begins.
theorySections.analogyLimit: CPU caches and compiler reorderings follow formal memory-model rules, so everyday notions of 'happened earlier' are not sufficient.
theorySections.concreteExample: Writing data and then a volatile ready flag lets a reader that observes ready also observe the earlier data writes, but ready++ is still not atomic.
keyPoints: A data race is not merely two threads executing at once; it is conflicting unsynchronized access.
volatile is appropriate for independent state publication, flags, and some carefully designed algorithms.
Locking protects invariants, not individual lines of code.
ConcurrentHashMap makes its own operations safe but cannot atomically protect arbitrary multi-step workflows.

misconceptions.claim: Java passes objects by reference.
misconceptions.correction: Java passes every argument by value; for objects the value copied is a reference.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Mutation through the copied reference is visible to both callers, which is confused with pass-by-reference parameters.

misconceptions.claim: volatile makes a counter increment thread-safe.
misconceptions.correction: volatile gives visibility and ordering, while count++ is still a read-modify-write race.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Atomic visibility of one read or write is mistaken for atomicity of the whole expression.

misconceptions.claim: The garbage collector prevents memory leaks.
misconceptions.correction: GC reclaims unreachable objects; unintended strong references can retain an unbounded graph forever.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Leak is incorrectly defined as forgotten free rather than memory that remains reachable without being useful.

misconceptions.claim: LinkedList is generally faster for insertions.
misconceptions.correction: Insertion is cheap only after locating a node; traversal, allocation, and poor locality often dominate.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Big-O for the mutation step is quoted while the search and hardware costs are omitted.

misconceptions.claim: Streams are always more efficient and parallel streams use all cores safely.
misconceptions.correction: Streams improve composition; performance depends on pipeline shape, allocation, data size, splitting, and shared-pool contention.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Declarative syntax and the word parallel are treated as performance guarantees.

misconceptions.claim: String is immutable, so a String reference cannot change.
misconceptions.correction: The String object cannot change, but a variable may be assigned a different String reference.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Object immutability is confused with variable finality.

revisionChecklist: Explain Java pass-by-value with a mutation and reassignment example.
State the equals/hashCode contract and the mutable-key failure mode.
Choose among ArrayList, HashMap, TreeMap, HashSet, and concurrent collections with complexity and locality trade-offs.
Derive PECS and explain erasure, raw types, bridge methods, and heap pollution.
Trace class loading through initialization, then interpreter/JIT/deoptimization behavior.
Explain reachability, GC roots, generational collection, allocation rate, and leak diagnosis.
Construct happens-before edges and distinguish visibility, atomicity, ordering, liveness, and thread safety.
Compare synchronized, Lock, atomics, immutability, confinement, executors, and virtual threads.
Read a thread dump, heap summary, JFR capture, and dependency tree at interview depth.
Explain Spring proxy/transaction boundaries and JPA persistence-context plus N+1 traps.
setup: Install a supported JDK rather than only a JRE, then verify java and javac resolve to the same distribution.
Select the project language/release level explicitly so local syntax does not silently exceed the deployment runtime.
Use Maven Wrapper or Gradle Wrapper and commit the wrapper metadata for a reproducible build entry point.
Pin direct dependencies, inspect the resolved transitive graph, and keep test/runtime scopes intentional.
Compile, run unit tests, package, and start the artifact once before changing code.
runtime: Source is compiled to class-file bytecode, then loaded, verified, linked, and initialized by a class loader.
Bytecode begins in interpreted or lower-tier execution while profiling identifies hot methods, branches, and types.
The JIT compiles and speculatively optimizes hot paths; invalid assumptions trigger deoptimization.
Objects are allocated in managed memory and reclaimed by reachability-based collectors; external resources still require explicit ownership.
Threads follow the Java Memory Model, so cross-thread correctness depends on happens-before edges rather than observed timing.
testing: Use plain unit tests for value objects and deterministic policy, without booting a framework container.
Use integration tests for serialization, persistence mappings, transaction boundaries, and external contracts.
Test concurrency with invariants, controlled coordination, repeated schedules, and specialized tools rather than sleep-based timing.
Use JMH for microbenchmarks so warm-up, dead-code elimination, constant folding, and measurement overhead are controlled.
debugging: Read the first application exception and its cause chain; do not begin at the final wrapper message.
Capture a thread dump for deadlock, blocked pools, or request stalls and correlate thread state with locks and queues.
Use JFR or async-profiler for CPU, allocation, lock, and wall-clock evidence before optimizing.
Compare heap histograms and retained paths to GC roots when the post-GC live set grows.
Inspect bytecode or generated proxy classes when language/framework behavior disagrees with the source-level intuition.
performance: Separate startup/warm-up behavior from steady-state throughput and tail latency.
Measure allocation rate, retained size, GC CPU/pause time, contention, queueing, and downstream waits as distinct signals.
Prefer better algorithms, batching, locality, and bounded concurrency before collector flags or unsafe micro-optimizations.
Treat connection pools, executor pools, caches, and parallel streams as capacity controls with saturation points.
security: Treat deserialization, expression languages, reflection, file paths, SQL, templates, and process execution as input boundaries.
Use modern TLS and credential providers; never place secrets in source, logs, exception messages, or command history.
Run with least-privilege identities and minimize exposed management/JMX/actuator endpoints.
Track dependency provenance and advisories, but validate exploitability and upgrade compatibility rather than blindly suppressing findings.
failureModes: equals/hashCode changes or mutable keys corrupt collection lookup assumptions.
Unbounded executors, queues, caches, or thread-per-request designs exhaust memory or downstream capacity.
Missing happens-before edges create races that disappear under a debugger.
Long-lived roots, listeners, ThreadLocals, or caches retain otherwise dead object graphs.
Framework proxy boundaries are bypassed by self-invocation, final/private methods, or thread changes.
ORM defaults hide N+1 queries, oversized persistence contexts, accidental cascades, or transactions that are too wide.

workedExamples.title: Immutable value key with a valid equality contract
workedExamples.explanation: A record derives value-based equals and hashCode from immutable components. Validation prevents an invalid key, and a separately constructed equal key retrieves the same bucket entry.

workedExamples.title: Visibility is not compound atomicity
workedExamples.explanation: AtomicLong supplies one linearizable read-modify-write operation. volatile would make individual accesses visible but could not protect the compound increment.

workedExamples.title: Bounded asynchronous work with failure propagation
workedExamples.explanation: The fixed pool bounds active work and try-with-resources owns shutdown on supported JDKs. A production version must also define timeouts, cancellation, queue capacity, partial-failure policy, and whether blocking work should use virtual threads.

questions.prompt: Is Java pass-by-reference? Prove your answer with alias mutation and parameter reassignment.
questions.answer: Java is pass-by-value. A method receives a copy of the caller's reference value. Mutating the referenced object is observed through every alias, but assigning the parameter to a new object changes only the local copied reference.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates often use pass-by-reference to describe shared mutation, even though true pass-by-reference would allow reassignment of the caller's variable.
rubric: Separates object mutation from reference reassignment.

questions.prompt: Why must equal objects have equal hash codes, and what breaks when a key mutates inside HashMap?
questions.answer: HashMap selects a bucket from the hash and then checks equality. Equal objects with different hashes may be searched in different buckets. If equality-relevant state mutates after insertion, lookup uses the new hash while the entry remains under the old bucket, so retrieval or removal can fail.
questions.whyTricky: The contract is memorized but rarely connected to the actual lookup path and stable-key requirement.
rubric: States both directions of the contract correctly.
Connects hash to bucket selection and equals to collision resolution.

questions.prompt: Explain List<? extends Number> versus List<? super Integer>. What can be read and written?
questions.answer: The extends list produces values safely readable as Number, but no non-null concrete Number subtype can be inserted because its captured type is unknown. The super list consumes Integer values safely, while reads have only the guaranteed type Object.
questions.whyTricky: Many answers repeat PECS without demonstrating what the compiler can prove for each operation.
rubric: Gets allowed reads and writes right for both forms.
Mentions the null exception only if useful.

questions.prompt: Does volatile make an object thread-safe? Explain using a stop flag and a counter.
questions.answer: volatile applies to reads and writes of the field and creates ordering/visibility edges. It works for a one-writer stop flag whose state is independent. A volatile counter increment is still multiple operations and loses updates; use an atomic, lock, confinement, or redesigned invariant.
questions.whyTricky: Visibility, atomicity, and compound object invariants are collapsed into one vague idea of thread safety.
rubric: Contrasts a valid flag with invalid increment.
Names a correct alternative and invariant scope.

questions.prompt: What happens from java Main to optimized machine code?
questions.answer: The launcher creates a JVM, loads and verifies classes, links and initializes them, then executes bytecode initially through interpretation or lower tiers. Runtime profiles identify hot paths; tiered JIT compilers inline and specialize into machine code. Guard failure or class loading can invalidate assumptions and trigger deoptimization.
questions.whyTricky: Bytecode execution is often simplified to either pure interpretation or one-time compilation, omitting profiling and reversible optimization.
rubric: Covers class lifecycle and bytecode verification.

questions.prompt: A Java service's memory grows although GC runs. How do you distinguish healthy growth, pressure, and a leak?
questions.answer: Observe post-GC live-set trend, allocation rate, pause/CPU behavior, and workload. Healthy warm-up plateaus; pressure has high churn or insufficient headroom; a leak shows retained live data growing across comparable full collections. Compare heap histograms and dominator/retained paths to GC roots, then verify the owning lifecycle.
questions.whyTricky: Heap size, allocation, and retention are different signals, while dashboards often show only total used memory.
rubric: Uses post-GC live set rather than one snapshot.
Explains retained-path investigation and lifecycle ownership.

questions.prompt: When can parallel streams be slower or incorrect?
questions.answer: They can be slower for small inputs, cheap operations, poor spliterators, ordered pipelines, boxing, blocking work, or a contended common pool. They become incorrect when operations interfere with the source, mutate shared state, or use non-associative reductions whose grouping changes the result.
questions.whyTricky: The API makes parallelism syntactically trivial while its cost model and algebraic requirements remain hidden.

questions.prompt: Why might @Transactional appear to do nothing in Spring?
questions.answer: Spring commonly applies transactions through a proxy. Self-invocation bypasses that proxy; private/final methods or unsupported proxy arrangements may not be intercepted; checked-exception rollback differs by policy; and crossing threads loses thread-bound transaction context. Verify proxy entry, propagation, exception policy, and database boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: The annotation is mistaken for a language feature rather than metadata interpreted at a runtime interception boundary.
rubric: Connects transaction context to thread and database work.

flashcards.back: Always pass-by-value; object arguments copy a reference value.
If a.equals(b), then a and b must return the same hash code while used as keys.
Producer extends, consumer super; derive permitted reads/writes from the captured unknown type.
A specified ordering that makes earlier actions visible to later actions; it is stronger than wall-clock timing.
volatile orders individual field access; it does not make a compound read-modify-write atomic.
Useful lifetime ended but a path from a GC root still retains the object graph.
Optimized code returns to a safer tier when a speculative runtime assumption becomes false.
A method call through this bypasses an external proxy, so proxy advice such as transactions may not execute.

technologies.title: OOP, SOLID, UML, and LLD
technologies.summary: Object modeling, composition, SOLID trade-offs, UML notation, design patterns, and interview-sized low-level designs.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: OOP, SOLID, UML, and LLD is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of OOP, SOLID, UML, and LLD like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: run focused tests using `./gradlew test --tests '*ParkingLot*'`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: a simpler interface that hides lower-level details
the point where responsibility moves between parts
a rule that must remain true while the system changes

technologies.mentalModel: An object owns an invariant and offers behavior that preserves it; a good design keeps reasons to change narrow and dependencies explicit.

theorySections.title: Objects preserve invariants
theorySections.explanation: An object is useful when it owns a coherent rule and exposes operations that cannot leave it invalid. Encapsulation is therefore not private fields plus getters; it is the placement of decisions beside the state they protect. Value objects model interchangeable values, while entities retain identity through changing attributes.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Give each business rule one owner and expose operations that keep that owner's state valid instead of exposing raw setters.
theorySections.analogy: A bank vault does not hand out its combination and ask callers to update balances; a teller performs approved operations while enforcing the rules.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software objects may be copied, persisted, or accessed concurrently, so ownership still needs explicit transaction and lifecycle boundaries.
theorySections.concreteExample: Order.pay(receipt) checks the current state and amount before changing DRAFT to PAID, making an invalid transition impossible through the public API.
keyPoints: Begin with invariants and use cases, not class nouns.
Expose behavior that expresses domain intent rather than raw mutation.
Choose entity identity and value equality deliberately.
Make invalid states hard or impossible to construct.

theorySections.title: Composition, inheritance, and polymorphism
theorySections.explanation: Inheritance couples a subtype to the promises and extension behavior of its base. It is appropriate for a genuine substitutable relationship, not merely code reuse. Composition assembles behavior through explicit collaborators and usually localizes change; interfaces let clients depend on a needed capability without inheriting state or implementation.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Inheritance promises substitutability, whereas composition connects smaller collaborators and lets their behavior vary without sharing an implementation hierarchy.
theorySections.analogy: A car has an engine by composition; an electric car is a kind of car only if every client expecting a car can use it without broken promises.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Natural-language 'is-a' and 'has-a' labels do not prove behavioral substitutability or appropriate software ownership.
theorySections.concreteExample: Inject a PaymentPort into CheckoutService so Stripe and a test fake can be substituted without making CheckoutService inherit vendor behavior.
keyPoints: Apply Liskov substitution to observable behavior, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.
Prefer composition when behavior varies independently or ownership matters.
A wide interface increases accidental coupling; design around client needs.
Delegation is explicit reuse and can preserve encapsulation better than subclassing.

theorySections.title: SOLID as diagnostic questions
theorySections.explanation: SOLID names common change and substitution pressures, but each principle has a cost. SRP asks whether unrelated actors force one module to change. OCP asks whether expected variation has a stable seam. ISP prevents clients from depending on irrelevant operations. DIP moves policy away from volatile details; it does not require an interface for every class.
theorySections.plainEnglish: SOLID helps locate change pressure, oversized contracts, and reversed dependencies; it is a set of questions rather than five mandatory shapes.
theorySections.analogy: A toolbox separates tools by jobs that change for different reasons, but it does not put every screw into its own box.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Module boundaries are driven by actors, volatility, and coupling; the mnemonic alone cannot select the right number of abstractions.
theorySections.concreteExample: Extract a TaxPolicy when jurisdictions vary, but keep a one-line immutable Money value concrete instead of creating an IMoney interface.
keyPoints: Principles guide trade-offs; they are not a scorecard.
Abstract around demonstrated variation or boundary risk.
Dependency direction is about policy ownership, not package count.
Too many indirections can make behavior harder to trace and change.

theorySections.title: Patterns and their forces
theorySections.explanation: A pattern is a named response to recurring forces, not a template to insert. Strategy varies an algorithm, State varies behavior with lifecycle, Adapter translates an existing interface, Decorator composes responsibilities, Observer distributes notification, and Command represents an action for queuing, logging, or undo. Their liabilities—indirection, ordering, lifecycle, and debugging—belong in the decision.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A design pattern earns its place only when a recurring variation, integration, lifecycle, or communication problem is actually present.
theorySections.analogy: Patterns are like proven building details: a fire door solves a specific safety force, but installing one in every interior opening adds cost without benefit.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software forces change faster than construction constraints, and the same class diagram can hide very different runtime behavior.
theorySections.concreteExample: Use Strategy when pricing policy varies by tenant; use State when the same order changes allowed behavior as it moves through its lifecycle.
keyPoints: State and Strategy may look alike structurally but solve different forces.
Observer needs subscription lifecycle and delivery semantics.
Singleton hides global coupling and is not the same as one domain instance.
Factory value appears when construction policy or families vary.

theorySections.title: From requirements to an LLD
theorySections.explanation: A strong LLD interview begins with actors, use cases, constraints, and out-of-scope choices. Convert rules into invariants and important lifecycles into state machines. Assign one owner to each mutable invariant, sketch public operations, walk a success and failure sequence, then add extension points only where requirements indicate variation.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Start from actors, use cases, rules, and failure paths; then assign state and behavior to owners and test the design by walking sequences.
theorySections.analogy: Planning a transit station begins with passenger journeys and safety constraints, not with drawing rooms and naming doors.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Unlike a physical station, software boundaries can be refactored, but persisted data and public APIs still make some changes expensive.
theorySections.concreteExample: For a parking lot, define entry, spot assignment, payment, and exit invariants before introducing Vehicle, Ticket, Gate, and PricingPolicy classes.
keyPoints: Clarify before naming classes.
State transitions expose missing rules and invalid operations.
Sequence diagrams test whether responsibilities actually collaborate.
Include concurrency, idempotency, persistence, and error semantics when relevant.

theorySections.title: Design for tests and operations
theorySections.explanation: Testability emerges from explicit boundaries, deterministic policy, and controllable time, randomness, I/O, and external services. Operational design adds structured events, correlation, safe retries, and diagnosable state. A design that is elegant on a class diagram but cannot explain failure ownership, observability, or migration is incomplete.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Make decisions deterministic and external effects explicit so behavior can be tested, failures can be observed, and recovery ownership is clear.
theorySections.analogy: An aircraft cockpit exposes instruments and controlled inputs so crews can test systems and diagnose faults without dismantling the plane.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Instrumentation can itself fail or add cost, and a mock cannot reproduce every property of a real database, clock, or network.
theorySections.concreteExample: Inject a Clock into expiry policy, test boundary instants without sleeping, and emit a correlated event when the real scheduler performs expiry.
keyPoints: Inject volatile effects, not every trivial object.
Test public behavior and invariants before implementation structure.
Define retry and idempotency together.
Treat logging, metrics, and audit needs as design inputs.

misconceptions.claim: Encapsulation means making fields private and adding getters/setters.
misconceptions.correction: Encapsulation hides decisions and preserves invariants; indiscriminate setters expose the representation again.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Language access modifiers are taught as the goal instead of one enforcement mechanism.

misconceptions.claim: Inheritance is required for polymorphism.
misconceptions.correction: Interface implementation, function values, protocols, and composition all provide polymorphic behavior.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Introductory examples combine subtype polymorphism with class inheritance.

misconceptions.claim: Every dependency needs an interface to satisfy DIP.
misconceptions.correction: DIP concerns stable policy depending on abstractions at meaningful volatile boundaries, not interface count.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Mechanics of mocking and DI frameworks replace analysis of dependency direction.

misconceptions.claim: A design pattern is automatically good design.
misconceptions.correction: A pattern is justified only when its forces exist and its added indirection costs less than the problem.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Pattern names are rewarded in interviews even when their consequences are not discussed.

misconceptions.claim: Composition is always better than inheritance.
misconceptions.correction: Composition is often more flexible, while inheritance is valid for stable substitutable taxonomies and framework extension contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: A useful preference is misremembered as an absolute law.

misconceptions.claim: LLD ends when the class diagram is complete.
misconceptions.correction: The design must survive sequence walks, invalid transitions, concurrency, persistence, tests, and operational failure.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Static diagrams are easier to present than runtime behavior.

revisionChecklist: State the invariant owned by every important object.
Distinguish entity identity, value equality, and service behavior.
Explain association, aggregation, composition, and inheritance without relying only on UML diamonds.
Apply Liskov using behavior, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants.
Explain each SOLID principle with a benefit, counterexample, and overuse cost.
Match Strategy, State, Adapter, Decorator, Observer, Command, and Factory to their forces.
Turn a use case into a state machine and success/failure sequence.
Name ownership for concurrency, transactions, idempotency, and retry.
Identify god objects, anemic models, feature envy, temporal coupling, and speculative abstractions.
Describe tests, observability, versioning, and migration for the design.
setup: Write the actors, top use cases, constraints, and out-of-scope behavior before drawing classes.
Extract domain vocabulary and replace ambiguous nouns or verbs with definitions shared by the interviewer.
List invariants and lifecycle states, then assign exactly one owner to every mutable rule.
Select a small executable language/project with a focused unit-test command and a text diagram format.
Prepare one success sequence and one failure/concurrency sequence to drive the design review.
runtime: Objects collaborate through calls or messages; runtime behavior is the sequence of responsibilities, not the class diagram alone.
Entities preserve identity, value objects preserve value semantics, and services host behavior with no natural object owner.
Composition gives an owner explicit lifecycle control; shared references require a separate ownership policy.
Polymorphic dispatch selects behavior through a contract, while construction and wiring decide which implementation participates.
Persistence, network, clock, randomness, and concurrency are effects that cross explicit boundaries.
testing: Test invariant-preserving public behavior and rejected transitions before private implementation details.
Use fakes for owned ports when deterministic behavior matters; reserve mocks for verifying important interaction contracts.
Walk state-machine transitions, including invalid, repeated, and concurrent commands.
Add integration tests where serialization, database transactions, framework proxies, or third-party adapters define behavior.
debugging: Reproduce the failing use case as a sequence of domain operations rather than inspecting classes in isolation.
Find the first object whose invariant becomes false and the caller that was allowed to violate it.
Trace dependency wiring when the wrong strategy, adapter, or decorator executes.
Inspect lifecycle ownership for leaked observers, duplicated handlers, stale state, or missing cleanup.
performance: Count remote calls, database queries, allocations, copies, and lock acquisitions hidden behind object methods.
Avoid object graphs that require loading an entire aggregate for a narrow operation.
Use immutable values and coarse, explicit operations to reduce coordination and defensive copying.
Optimize a measured collaboration path without moving domain invariants into infrastructure code.
security: Place authorization checks beside the operation and resource they protect, not only in presentation code.
Prevent mass assignment by exposing intention-revealing commands rather than binding untrusted data directly to entities.
Keep secrets and privileged vendor APIs behind narrow ports with auditable adapters.
Model replay, idempotency, audit, and sensitive-data lifetime as domain requirements when relevant.
failureModes: A god object accumulates unrelated actor-driven changes and becomes a concurrency bottleneck.
An anemic model exposes setters while services duplicate or contradict invariants.
Inheritance is used for code reuse even though subtype behavior violates the base contract.
Pattern layers add indirection without a real variation or integration force.
Observer subscriptions leak, reenter unexpectedly, or deliver failures without isolation.
A memorized class diagram ignores state transitions, errors, concurrency, persistence, and operational diagnosis.

workedExamples.title: Put a state transition beside its invariant
workedExamples.explanation: The Order owns the transition and rejects invalid states. A generic setStatus method would move the lifecycle rule into every caller and make invalid transitions easy.

workedExamples.title: Strategy varies policy without subclass conditionals
workedExamples.explanation: Checkout depends on the behavior it needs. Pricing policies can vary independently, but an interface is justified here only because pricing is a real extension axis.

workedExamples.title: Adapter keeps a vendor contract at the boundary
workedExamples.explanation: The application owns PaymentPort and its domain vocabulary. The adapter translates vendor details once, giving tests a stable seam and containing a future provider migration.

questions.prompt: What does encapsulation protect beyond field visibility?
questions.answer: It protects representation choices and invariants by keeping decisions inside a stable behavioral boundary. Callers request domain operations instead of coordinating raw state through getters and setters.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates often define a language mechanism rather than the design property it supports.

questions.prompt: When is inheritance preferable to composition, and how do you test substitutability?
questions.answer: Use inheritance when the subtype genuinely honors the base contract and the taxonomy/extension point is stable. Test that client-observable preconditions are not strengthened, postconditions are not weakened, invariants hold, and exceptional behavior remains compatible. Use composition when behaviors vary independently or ownership/lifecycle should remain explicit.
questions.whyTricky: Answers often repeat 'favor composition' without identifying a valid inheritance case or Liskov criteria.

questions.prompt: Differentiate Strategy and State even when their class diagrams look identical.
questions.answer: Strategy represents a policy chosen by a client or configuration and is usually interchangeable without implying lifecycle. State represents behavior governed by an internal lifecycle; transitions are domain events and the current state constrains valid operations.
questions.whyTricky: Structural pattern memorization hides the different intent and ownership of transitions.

questions.prompt: Design a parking lot without starting from classes. What do you ask and derive first?
questions.answer: Clarify vehicle/spot types, allocation policy, entrances, tickets, pricing, payment, capacity, concurrency, persistence, and out-of-scope features. Derive invariants such as one active ticket per parked vehicle and one occupant per spot, then model ticket/spot lifecycles and operations before choosing collaborators and extension seams.
questions.whyTricky: The familiar problem tempts candidates to dump memorized classes before requirements and invariants.

questions.prompt: Does dependency injection automatically satisfy dependency inversion?
questions.answer: No. A container can inject concrete low-level details into high-level policy while the source dependency still points the wrong way. DIP is achieved when policy owns or depends on a stable abstraction and volatile details implement it; DI is one wiring technique.
questions.whyTricky: Framework mechanics, inversion of control, dependency injection, and the SOLID principle are often conflated.
rubric: Separates DIP from DI and IoC.

questions.prompt: How would you make an Observer-based notification design reliable?
questions.answer: Define subscription ownership, delivery ordering, sync versus async behavior, failure isolation, backpressure, retry/idempotency, duplicate handling, and unsubscribe lifecycle. For durable cross-process events, use a log or broker with explicit delivery semantics rather than an in-memory observer alone.
questions.whyTricky: Textbook Observer omits lifecycle and distributed delivery failure.

questions.prompt: Why can an anemic domain model be either a smell or a reasonable design?
questions.answer: It is a smell when domain invariants are scattered across services that manipulate public state, creating low cohesion and invalid transitions. It can be reasonable for simple CRUD/data-transfer boundaries or functional architectures where immutable data and pure policy functions preserve rules clearly.
questions.whyTricky: The term is often treated as a universal verdict independent of complexity and programming style.
rubric: Names a legitimate simple or functional case.
Uses invariant ownership as the deciding criterion.

questions.prompt: How do you evaluate whether an abstraction is premature?
questions.answer: Identify the concrete variation it isolates, current duplication in knowledge rather than syntax, expected change evidence, client simplification, and cost of indirection. Prefer the simplest stable boundary now; refactor when a second or third case reveals the true axis of variation.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates either abstract every similarity or reject abstraction until duplication is severe.
rubric: Distinguishes knowledge duplication from textual repetition.

flashcards.back: Hide representation decisions and expose behavior that preserves invariants.
Entity continuity comes from identity; value objects are interchangeable by their attributes.
Do not strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or violate base invariants and expected behavior.
High-level policy and low-level details depend on an abstraction owned around the policy boundary.
Strategy selects policy; State models lifecycle-dependent behavior and transitions.
Subscription lifecycle, ordering, reentrancy, failure isolation, delivery semantics, and backpressure.
Actors → use cases → constraints → invariants → state transitions → operations → collaborators.
The abstraction predicts variation without evidence and costs more to understand than the duplication.

technologies.title: Database Management Systems
technologies.summary: Relational theory, SQL, normalization, indexes, query plans, ACID, isolation, MVCC, locks, WAL, replication, partitioning, and NoSQL trade-offs.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Database Management Systems is a database system: software that stores data, finds it again, and protects correctness when many operations happen together.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can design reliable data models, write efficient queries, and keep important information correct through failures and concurrent updates. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Database Management Systems like a carefully run library: data has an address, indexes speed up discovery, and borrowing rules prevent conflicting changes. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: connect safely using `psql "$DATABASE_URL"`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: a request to read or change stored data
an extra structure that makes selected lookups faster
a group of changes treated as one logical operation

technologies.mentalModel: A DBMS turns logical relations into durable pages while coordinating concurrent histories that must still satisfy declared invariants.

learningPath.title: Relational foundations
learningPath.objective: Model data and query it without violating meaning.
topics: relations, tuples, attributes, domains, keys, and constraints
relational algebra and SQL's bag/null semantics
SELECT, joins, grouping, subqueries, CTEs, and window functions
functional dependencies and normalization through BCNF

learningPath.title: Storage and execution
learningPath.objective: Connect logical SQL to physical work.
topics: pages, records, buffer pools, and storage layout
B+ trees, hash indexes, composite keys, covering and partial indexes
statistics, cardinality estimation, join algorithms, sorting, and query plans
write-ahead logging, checkpoints, crash recovery, and durability

learningPath.title: Transactions and scale
learningPath.objective: Reason about concurrent histories and data distribution.
topics: ACID, serializability, anomalies, and isolation levels
locks, deadlocks, MVCC, snapshots, vacuum, and optimistic control
replication, consensus boundaries, failover, and consistency
partitioning, sharding, rebalancing, secondary indexes, and distributed transactions

learningPath.title: Production database engineering
learningPath.objective: Diagnose plans, contention, growth, and failure while preserving invariants.
topics: schema evolution and zero-downtime migration
connection pools, admission control, hot rows, and queueing
backup, restore, point-in-time recovery, RPO, and RTO
NoSQL models, CAP/PACELC, workload fit, and polyglot costs

theorySections.title: Relational meaning and SQL reality
theorySections.explanation: The relational model describes sets of tuples constrained by predicates, while practical SQL uses bags by default and introduces NULL with three-valued logic. Keys and constraints are executable domain rules, not documentation. A query states the desired result; the optimizer is free to choose an equivalent physical plan under the engine's semantics.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Tables represent facts under constraints, but SQL keeps duplicate rows by default and treats missing information with three-valued logic.
theorySections.analogy: A table is a ledger whose column and key rules reject impossible entries; a query asks for a view without prescribing the clerk's retrieval route.
theorySections.analogyLimit: SQL bags, NULL, optimizer rewrites, and concurrent transactions have no exact paper-ledger equivalent.
theorySections.concreteExample: WHERE middle_name <> 'Lee' excludes NULL middle names because the comparison is UNKNOWN, not TRUE; use an explicit NULL policy.
keyPoints: SQL duplicates persist unless DISTINCT or a uniqueness property removes them.
NULL means missing/unknown/not-applicable by design choice and comparisons may yield UNKNOWN.
Primary, unique, foreign-key, and check constraints protect invariants under every writer.
Logical query order differs from textual and physical execution order.

theorySections.title: Normalization and denormalization
theorySections.explanation: Normalization uses functional dependencies to separate facts so each is represented once and update anomalies disappear. Third normal form preserves dependencies under common conditions; BCNF enforces a stronger determinant rule. Denormalization can be a measured read optimization, but it creates synchronization work and requires one explicit source of truth.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Store each independent fact once so one update cannot leave contradictory copies; duplicate only when a measured read need justifies synchronization work.
theorySections.analogy: Keep one authoritative address book and reference a contact ID instead of handwriting the same address into every appointment entry.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Distributed caches and analytics copies may intentionally lag, so software must define source-of-truth and repair behavior beyond the analogy.
theorySections.concreteExample: Move customer address out of every order row when orders should reference the customer, but snapshot the shipping address when historical truth must not change.
keyPoints: A functional dependency is about valid states, not a coincidence in sample data.
Normalization does not mean one table per concept or universally more joins.
Surrogate keys do not remove natural uniqueness constraints.
Denormalized copies need ownership, repair, and consistency policy.

theorySections.title: Indexes and access paths
theorySections.explanation: A B+ tree keeps ordered keys in shallow pages and supports equality, ranges, ordering, and prefix scans. An index helps only when its access plus heap/table work costs less than alternatives. Composite index order, selectivity, clustering, covering columns, predicate implication, write amplification, and cache behavior determine real value.
theorySections.plainEnglish: An index is an additional ordered or hashed structure that can reduce reads for certain predicates while adding storage and write maintenance.
theorySections.analogy: A book index jumps to pages for selected terms, but adding an index for every possible phrase would make the book enormous and updates expensive.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Database indexes interact with page layout, caches, statistics, visibility, and join algorithms beyond a printed index.
theorySections.concreteExample: An index on (tenant_id, created_at DESC) supports one tenant's newest rows, while reversing the columns may scan many tenants.
keyPoints: The leftmost-prefix guideline describes usable ordered prefixes, not an absolute ban on other plans.
Low-selectivity indexes can still help covering, ordering, partition pruning, or combined predicates.
Every index adds storage, write, vacuum/maintenance, and planning cost.
EXPLAIN estimates must be compared with actual rows, loops, buffers, and time.

theorySections.title: Transactions, isolation, and anomalies
theorySections.explanation: A transaction is a unit whose committed effects must satisfy database guarantees, but ACID does not automatically make application logic correct. Isolation constrains observable interleavings. Read phenomena such as dirty reads are only part of the story; write skew and predicate anomalies require reasoning about the invariant and whether the schedule is serializable.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A transaction groups changes, while isolation determines which interleavings other transactions may observe; application invariants still need deliberate protection.
theorySections.analogy: Two ticket agents need a reservation rule, not just separate notebooks, or both can see one remaining seat and sell it.
theorySections.analogyLimit: MVCC snapshots and serialization graphs are formal mechanisms; a human queue analogy does not describe every allowed anomaly.
theorySections.concreteExample: Two doctors both observe another doctor on call and independently go off duty; snapshot isolation can allow the write-skew invariant violation.
keyPoints: Isolation level names differ in exact behavior across engines.
Lost update can be prevented through locks, atomic predicates, version checks, or serializable execution.
Snapshot isolation prevents many anomalies but can permit write skew.
The transaction boundary must include the reads and writes that jointly protect an invariant.

theorySections.title: MVCC, locks, and recovery
theorySections.explanation: MVCC stores multiple row versions so readers can see a snapshot without blocking every writer. It does not eliminate locking: writers still coordinate and predicates or metadata may lock. WAL records changes before dirty pages reach durable storage, enabling redo and sometimes undo during recovery; checkpoints bound recovery work but are not backups.
theorySections.plainEnglish: MVCC keeps row versions for consistent snapshots, locks coordinate conflicting work, and WAL records changes before data pages so crashes can be recovered.
theorySections.analogy: Editors read dated document editions while writers reserve specific sections; a change journal lets the office reconstruct accepted edits after a power loss.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Version visibility, lock granularity, redo/undo, and durability guarantees vary by database engine and storage stack.
theorySections.concreteExample: A long-running report holds an old snapshot, forcing the database to retain dead row versions and delaying vacuum cleanup.
keyPoints: Long transactions retain old versions and can delay cleanup.
Deadlock is a cycle of waits; engines detect or prevent it and abort a participant.
WAL ordering is the durability mechanism, while data pages may flush later.
Backup plus WAL/archive enables point-in-time recovery; replication alone is not backup.

theorySections.title: Replication, partitioning, and distributed trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Replication creates copies for availability and read scale but introduces lag, failover, and consistency decisions. Partitioning divides data and can reduce scanned work when predicates align with the partition key. Sharding moves partitions across nodes, making cross-shard transactions, joins, uniqueness, rebalancing, and secondary indexes operationally expensive.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Copies improve availability and read capacity but may lag; partitions divide ownership, making cross-partition guarantees and movement more expensive.
theorySections.analogy: Several branch libraries can serve readers locally, but catalogue updates travel, and moving a collection changes where cross-branch requests must go.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Network partitions, quorum rules, consensus, and machine-speed failover create behaviors unlike ordinary library coordination.
theorySections.concreteExample: After a write to the primary, an immediate read from a lagging replica may miss it unless the system provides session stickiness or a consistency token.
keyPoints: A replica can faithfully reproduce accidental deletion or corruption.
Synchronous replication changes latency and availability trade-offs; it does not remove every loss window automatically.
Choose partition keys from access patterns, growth, skew, and lifecycle.
CAP applies during partitions; PACELC highlights latency/consistency trade-offs even otherwise.

misconceptions.claim: ACID means every concurrent transaction behaves correctly.
misconceptions.correction: ACID properties and the chosen isolation level still require an application transaction boundary that protects the actual invariant.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: The acronym is treated as a blanket correctness certificate.

misconceptions.claim: An index always makes reads faster.
misconceptions.correction: The optimizer may prefer a scan when index traversal, random fetches, low selectivity, or stale estimates cost more.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Index lookup complexity is considered without page I/O, result cardinality, and maintenance cost.

misconceptions.claim: MVCC means readers and writers never block.
misconceptions.correction: Row versions reduce conflicts, but writers, schema changes, unique checks, predicates, and resource limits can still block.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: The common reader/writer benefit is promoted as a universal lock-free guarantee.

misconceptions.claim: Read committed prevents lost updates and write skew.
misconceptions.correction: It prevents dirty reads in common engines but application read-modify-write sequences can still race.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Named isolation levels are memorized only through a short anomaly table.

misconceptions.claim: Replication is a backup.
misconceptions.correction: Replication improves availability; destructive or corrupt changes can propagate, so independent tested backups are still required.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Both features create extra copies but serve different failure models.

misconceptions.claim: NoSQL databases do not have schemas or transactions.
misconceptions.correction: They enforce data shapes and transactional scopes differently; the schema may live in application code and evolution still exists.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Flexible-schema marketing is confused with absence of contracts.

revisionChecklist: Explain relations, keys, constraints, bags, NULL, and logical SQL order.
Derive 1NF through BCNF from functional dependencies and identify update anomalies.
Compare B+ tree and hash indexes; reason about composite, covering, partial, and clustered access.
Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE using estimates, actual rows, loops, buffers, join algorithms, and spill signals.
Define ACID without using circular slogans and tie atomicity/durability to recovery.
Recognize lost update, write skew, phantom/predicate anomalies, and choose a protection mechanism.
Explain MVCC snapshots, version retention, vacuum/cleanup, locks, and deadlock handling.
Trace WAL, checkpoint, crash recovery, backup, restore, RPO, and RTO.
Compare replication consistency/failover modes and explain why replicas are not backups.
Choose partition/shard keys and account for skew, rebalancing, global constraints, and cross-shard work.
setup: Run a local engine version close to production and record its isolation, collation, extension, and durability settings.
Create a disposable database through migrations rather than a hand-edited schema.
Load representative cardinalities and skew; tiny uniform fixtures cannot validate plans or contention.
Enable safe query timing/statistics and learn the engine's EXPLAIN ANALYZE output before tuning.
Prove backup and restore to a separate target before treating the environment as recoverable.
runtime: The parser and binder resolve SQL names and types; the optimizer transforms the logical request into a costed physical plan.
Executors scan indexes or tables, apply joins/sorts/aggregates, and move pages through the buffer pool under memory limits.
Transaction control creates snapshots or locks according to the engine and isolation level.
WAL is forced in the required order before dirty data pages, allowing recovery after a crash.
Background workers checkpoint, clean old versions, update statistics, replicate logs, and maintain storage structures.
testing: Test constraints and transaction invariants against the real engine, not only a mocked repository.
Use fixtures that include NULLs, duplicates, skew, boundary dates, concurrent conflicts, and large cardinalities.
Assert migration forward/backward compatibility and mixed-version application behavior during rolling changes.
Exercise backup restore, failover, retry/idempotency, and isolation anomalies as operational tests.
debugging: Start with the actual plan and compare estimated versus actual rows, loops, buffers, spills, and time.
Inspect active sessions, waits, blockers, lock graphs, and transaction age before blaming query text.
Check statistics freshness, data distribution, parameter values, index health, bloat, and cache state.
For correctness, reconstruct the transaction interleaving and the invariant each statement assumed.
performance: Optimize the complete access path: result cardinality, index traversal, base-row fetches, joins, sorts, network, and client work.
Keep connection pools and query concurrency below the point where database queueing and contention dominate.
Index for demonstrated predicates/order/coverage while budgeting write amplification, storage, and maintenance.
Partition for pruning and lifecycle, then verify skew and planning overhead; do not use it as a substitute for indexes.
security: Use parameter binding and allow-listed identifiers; placeholders do not substitute table or column names.
Grant separate least-privilege migration, application, read-only, and administrative identities.
Encrypt connections and managed storage, protect backups, rotate credentials, and audit privileged access.
Use row-level security or tenant predicates only with explicit tests that prevent cross-tenant bypass.
failureModes: Missing constraints allow concurrent writers to create states application validation claimed were impossible.
Cardinality misestimates select a join order or algorithm that collapses after data distribution changes.
Long transactions retain MVCC versions, block cleanup, expand storage, and delay replicas.
Retrying an ambiguous commit without idempotency duplicates business effects.
Replica lag serves stale data into a workflow that assumed read-your-writes consistency.
A shard or partition key hotspots one node and turns global uniqueness, joins, and rebalancing into outages.

workedExamples.title: Prevent aggregate inflation before joining
workedExamples.code:
WITH paid AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS paid_cents
  FROM payments
  WHERE status = 'captured'
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(o.total_cents) AS ordered_cents,
       SUM(COALESCE(p.paid_cents, 0)) AS paid_cents
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN paid p USING (order_id)
GROUP BY o.customer_id;
workedExamples.explanation: Payments are reduced to one row per order before the join. Aggregating after a one-to-many join without controlling cardinality can multiply order totals.

workedExamples.title: Build an index from the access path
workedExamples.code:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_tenant_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (status, total_cents);

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT created_at, status, total_cents
FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
workedExamples.explanation: The equality prefix and ordered suffix support the filter plus order/limit. Included columns may avoid base-row fetches, but actual rows, buffers, visibility, and write cost must still be measured.

workedExamples.title: Make a read-modify-write explicit
workedExamples.code:
UPDATE accounts
SET balance_cents = balance_cents - 500,
    version = version + 1
WHERE id = 7
  AND version = 12
  AND balance_cents >= 500;

-- Require exactly one affected row; otherwise reload or reject the conflict.
workedExamples.explanation: One conditional statement makes the balance check and update atomic for the row while the version detects concurrent change. The application must treat zero updated rows as a business or concurrency outcome, not success.

questions.prompt: Why can SELECT COUNT(*) FROM A JOIN B return more rows than either table?
questions.answer: A join emits one result for every matching tuple pair. One-to-many or many-to-many relationships multiply rows, and SQL retains duplicates unless semantics or DISTINCT remove them. Validate join keys and intended cardinality before aggregating.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates think of joins as attaching columns rather than producing matching pairs.

questions.prompt: Normalize an order containing customer, product, and quantity facts. What dependencies matter?
questions.answer: Identify determinants such as customer_id → customer attributes, product_id → product attributes, order_id → customer/date, and (order_id, product_id or line_id) → quantity/price-at-sale. Separate entities and line facts while retaining historical values whose meaning belongs to the order, then enforce natural uniqueness explicitly.
questions.whyTricky: Mechanical normal-form recipes can incorrectly move historical transaction facts back to mutable master data.

questions.prompt: Why might an index on status not be used, and when could it still help?
questions.answer: If most rows share the selected status, index traversal plus many heap fetches may exceed a sequential scan. It may still help as a partial index for rare states, as a covering index, with ordering/limit, combined with another selective column, or when clustering/cache conditions favor it.
questions.whyTricky: Low cardinality is repeated as an absolute rule without considering the complete access path.
rubric: Gives at least two valid helpful cases.
Mentions measurement with a real plan.

questions.prompt: Show write skew under snapshot isolation and fix it.
questions.answer: Two transactions read a snapshot showing two doctors on call. Each updates a different row to go off call; row-level write conflicts do not overlap, so both commit and violate the at-least-one invariant. Fix with serializable isolation, an explicit lock covering the predicate/aggregate owner, or a redesigned constraint with one contended invariant row.
questions.whyTricky: Snapshot isolation sounds serializable and each row update is individually conflict-free.
rubric: Provides a mechanism that protects the predicate.

questions.prompt: How does WAL make commit durable when data pages are not yet flushed?
questions.answer: The engine records redo information in an append-oriented log and ensures the relevant log record reaches durable storage before acknowledging commit. Dirty data pages may flush later. After a crash, recovery starts from a checkpoint and replays committed logged changes, applying engine-specific undo/visibility rules as needed.
questions.whyTricky: Durability is often incorrectly equated with synchronously rewriting every affected table page.
rubric: Separates log flush from page flush.

questions.prompt: A query became slow after data growth although SQL is unchanged. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: Capture the actual plan and compare estimated versus actual rows, loops, buffers, time, sort/hash spill, and chosen join order. Check statistics freshness/correlation, parameter sensitivity, index/data distribution, cache, bloat, locks, and resource pressure. Change one cause, rerun with comparable inputs, and guard the plan or model where appropriate.
questions.whyTricky: The unchanged query text distracts from changing distributions, statistics, cache, and resource contention.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing a database connection pool reduce throughput?
questions.answer: Beyond the database's useful parallelism, more active sessions contend for CPU, memory, locks, cache, and I/O, increasing queueing and context switches. Keep the pool bounded near measured service capacity, apply admission control/timeouts, and use application queues rather than moving an unbounded queue into the database.
questions.whyTricky: A connection is confused with additional database capacity.
rubric: Proposes bounded pools and admission control.

questions.prompt: Choose a shard key for a multi-tenant event store.
questions.answer: Start from dominant reads/writes, tenant size skew, locality, retention, and cross-tenant queries. tenant_id gives locality but hot/huge tenants need subpartitioning; time-only keys hotspot recent writes. A composite or hashed tenant bucket plus time range may balance load, but secondary access, rebalancing, global ordering, and tenant migration must be designed explicitly.
questions.whyTricky: Even distribution and query locality pull in different directions, and real tenants are rarely uniform.

flashcards.back: Rows may repeat by default; relational set intuition does not imply automatic deduplication.
X → Y means every valid database state gives equal Y values whenever X values are equal.
An index contains all columns needed by a query, potentially avoiding base-row fetches subject to visibility rules.
Transactions read the same predicate, update disjoint rows, and jointly violate a cross-row invariant.
Old versions consume space and cleanup work; long snapshots can delay reclamation.
The log describing a change becomes durable before the changed data page is written.
RPO is acceptable data loss window; RTO is acceptable restoration time.
Replica serves availability/read scale; an independent backup recovers from propagated destruction and historical loss.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Operating Systems like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect processes using `ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,pcpu,pmem,comm`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

the point where responsibility moves between parts
a rule that must remain true while the system changes

technologies.mentalModel: The kernel multiplexes processors, memory, and devices while presenting isolated processes with stable abstractions and enforceable protection boundaries.

files, directories, inodes, devices, and pipes

topics: context switching, scheduler goals, queues, priorities, and fairness
races, critical sections, atomic operations, mutexes, semaphores, and condition variables
