theorySections.title: Protection and the system-call boundary
theorySections.explanation: Applications execute in user mode with restricted privilege. A syscall, exception, or interrupt transfers control through a defined kernel entry path, switches execution context, validates untrusted arguments, and may block or schedule other work. A mode switch is not necessarily a process context switch; the same thread may enter and return from the kernel.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Applications run with limited privilege and must ask the kernel through validated system calls to access protected hardware and shared resources.
theorySections.analogy: A hotel guest requests the locked maintenance room through reception; the receptionist checks identity and performs or authorizes the operation.
theorySections.analogyLimit: A syscall can block, resume, or interact with interrupts at machine speed, and entering kernel mode does not necessarily switch processes.
theorySections.concreteExample: read(fd, buffer, n) crosses into the kernel, validates the descriptor and user buffer, and may sleep until data arrives.
keyPoints: Privilege separates policy enforcement from application code.
Syscall arguments and user pointers must be validated by the kernel.
Mode switch and thread/process switch are different events.
Interrupts are asynchronous; exceptions and traps arise from current execution.

theorySections.title: Processes, threads, and descriptors
theorySections.explanation: A process is a protected resource container with an address space, descriptors, credentials, and at least one thread. Threads are schedulable execution contexts sharing the process's memory and many resources. File descriptors are per-process references to kernel open-file descriptions, which is why duplicated descriptors can share offsets and status while retaining separate descriptor flags.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A process contains protected resources and an address space; threads are scheduled instruction streams sharing most of that process state.
theorySections.analogy: A process is an office with shared files and permissions; threads are workers with their own desks and task position inside the same office.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Threads share memory with formal synchronization requirements, while real workers do not expose CPU registers, stacks, or descriptor tables.
theorySections.concreteExample: After fork, parent and child see copy-on-write memory and inherited descriptors; exec replaces the child's program while selected descriptors remain open.
keyPoints: A thread owns registers and a stack but shares the process address space.
fork creates a new process using copy-on-write rather than eagerly copying every page.
exec replaces the process image while preserving selected process attributes.
A descriptor number is not the underlying file object.

theorySections.title: Scheduling and synchronization
theorySections.explanation: A scheduler chooses runnable threads under goals such as fairness, latency, throughput, priority, and energy. Synchronization creates ordering around shared invariants: atomics provide indivisible operations and memory order, mutexes provide exclusion, semaphores count permits, and condition variables wait for predicates while releasing a lock. Correct waiting always rechecks the predicate because wakeups and competing consumers exist.
theorySections.plainEnglish: The scheduler allocates CPU time, while synchronization establishes safe ordering for operations that jointly protect shared state.
theorySections.analogy: A kitchen scheduler assigns chefs to stations, and a single claim ticket prevents two chefs from serving the same order.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Preemption, memory ordering, priority inversion, and spurious wakeups follow OS and hardware rules beyond human work allocation.
theorySections.concreteExample: A consumer waits on a condition variable inside a while loop because it may wake spuriously or another consumer may take the item first.
keyPoints: Concurrency means overlapping lifetimes; parallelism means simultaneous execution.
A critical section is defined by a shared invariant, not merely shared code.
Condition-variable waits belong in a loop around a predicate.
Priority inversion needs protocols such as priority inheritance when relevant.

theorySections.title: Virtual memory and page faults
theorySections.explanation: Each process sees a virtual address space translated through page tables and cached in the TLB. A fault may signal an invalid access, demand-load a file page, allocate a zero page, or copy a shared page on write. Paging provides protection and flexible mapping; it does not imply that every address currently occupies physical RAM.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Each process uses virtual addresses that the hardware and kernel translate to protected physical frames, creating or loading mappings on demand.
theorySections.analogy: A hotel room number is a guest-facing address; management maps it to physical space and can move storage without changing the number guests use.
theorySections.analogyLimit: TLBs, page sizes, copy-on-write, memory mapping, and fault types do not correspond cleanly to hotel operations.
theorySections.concreteExample: Writing a forked page triggers a copy-on-write fault, allocates a private frame, copies data, and updates that process's page table.
keyPoints: TLB misses and page faults are different events.
Minor faults avoid storage I/O; major faults require slower backing work.
Copy-on-write defers copying until a writer needs a private page.
Memory-mapped files use the page cache but still need durability semantics.

theorySections.title: Filesystems, caching, and durability
theorySections.explanation: The VFS presents common file operations while concrete filesystems map names to metadata and data blocks. Reads and writes commonly interact with a page cache, so write completion to memory is not the same as durable persistence. Journaling orders metadata or data updates for crash recovery, while fsync-like operations request durability within hardware and filesystem guarantees.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Successful writes often reach memory caches before durable storage, so crash-safe replacement requires deliberate ordering and synchronization.
theorySections.analogy: Writing an order on a whiteboard is fast but not durable; recording it in the bound ledger and updating the index survives the office closing.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Controllers, drive caches, journaling modes, and filesystem guarantees determine what fsync actually protects.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a temporary file, fsync it, rename it atomically, then sync the directory when the name itself must survive a crash.
keyPoints: Rename can be atomic for namespace visibility without making file contents durable by itself.
Buffered writes can succeed before storage persists them.
Directories may need syncing for durable name creation or rename.
A journal is recovery metadata, not a user-data backup.

theorySections.title: Containers and virtual machines
theorySections.explanation: A container is a process tree isolated and limited through kernel mechanisms such as namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, and seccomp; it shares the host kernel. A virtual machine exposes virtual hardware and runs a guest kernel through a hypervisor. These boundaries have different startup, density, compatibility, and attack-surface trade-offs.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Containers isolate process views while sharing the host kernel; virtual machines emulate hardware and run a separate guest kernel.
theorySections.analogy: Containers are apartments sharing one building's structure; VMs are separate houses on managed plots with their own internal utilities.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Namespaces and hypervisors create technical boundaries whose strength depends on configuration and vulnerabilities, not physical walls.
theorySections.concreteExample: A container may have its own PID namespace and CPU limit but still invokes the host kernel, whereas a VM boots its own kernel.
keyPoints: Images package files; namespaces isolate views; cgroups account and limit resources.
Root inside a container is not automatically equivalent to host root, but configuration can erase the boundary.
VMs provide a separate guest kernel and generally a stronger isolation boundary.
Neither container nor VM eliminates the need for resource and security policy.

misconceptions.claim: A process is a program running on the CPU.
misconceptions.correction: A process is a resource/protection container; one or more threads are the schedulable execution contexts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Introductory diagrams collapse program image, process resources, and executing thread.

misconceptions.claim: A system call always causes a context switch to another process.
misconceptions.correction: It switches privilege mode and enters the kernel; the same thread may return without the scheduler choosing another thread.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Mode transition and scheduler context switch both involve saving machine state.

misconceptions.claim: Virtual memory is disk used as extra RAM.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual memory is the address-translation/protection abstraction; swap or mapped files are possible backing stores.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Paging under memory pressure is the most visible symptom taught to users.

misconceptions.claim: A mutex and semaphore are interchangeable locks.
misconceptions.correction: A mutex has ownership and protects an invariant; a semaphore counts permits/events and need not be released by the acquiring thread.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: A binary semaphore can superficially mimic exclusion.

misconceptions.claim: write() means data is safely on disk.
misconceptions.correction: It usually means data reached kernel buffers; durability requires the relevant flush/fsync and filesystem/hardware guarantees.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Successful API completion is confused with persistence across power loss.

misconceptions.claim: Containers are lightweight virtual machines.
misconceptions.correction: Containers isolate processes that share a kernel; VMs virtualize hardware for a separate guest kernel.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Both package isolated user environments and are managed with similar operational tools.

revisionChecklist: Differentiate program, process, thread, address space, and kernel object.
Trace syscall entry and separate privilege switch from scheduler context switch.
Explain fork, copy-on-write, exec, exit, wait, zombies, orphans, and signals.
Choose mutex, semaphore, condition variable, atomic, spinlock, or message passing from the invariant and wait cost.
Prove the four deadlock conditions and compare prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery.
Translate a virtual address through page tables/TLB and classify page faults.
Explain page cache, buffered I/O, mmap, writeback, journaling, fsync, and crash consistency.
Compare pipes, sockets, shared memory, and message queues by copying, coordination, and failure.
Distinguish namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, seccomp, containers, and VMs.
Use ps, /proc, strace, vmstat, iostat, ss, lsof, and pressure signals without guessing.
setup: Use a Linux environment where /proc, strace, process tools, and compiler diagnostics are available.
Compile small C/POSIX experiments with warnings, debug symbols, and sanitizers enabled.
Record kernel, architecture, container/VM, CPU-count, page-size, and resource-limit context before comparing behavior.
Create disposable programs for fork/exec, signals, threads, mmap, files, and sockets instead of experimenting on production processes.
Learn how to collect process, thread, memory, I/O, and network evidence without requiring unsafe privileges.
runtime: The kernel schedules threads, handles traps/interrupts, manages virtual memory, and mediates access to devices and objects.
A process groups an address space, descriptors, credentials, limits, and namespaces around one or more threads.
System calls cross a validated privilege boundary and may complete immediately, block, or awaken other waiters.
Virtual addresses translate through page tables/TLBs to physical frames or trigger faults that the kernel resolves.
Filesystem and device I/O commonly passes through page caches, request queues, drivers, DMA, and asynchronous completion.
testing: Use deterministic synchronization in concurrency tests; never treat sleep duration as proof of ordering.
Inject syscall failures, short reads/writes, EINTR, disk-full, permission, process-death, and partial-I/O cases.
Run sanitizers and race detectors while remembering that absence of a report is not a proof of correctness.
Test crash consistency by terminating at controlled write stages and checking the recovered on-disk invariant.
debugging: Begin with process/thread state, parentage, exit status, descriptors, limits, and current waits.
Use strace to locate blocking or failing syscalls, then narrow to the subsystem rather than tracing indefinitely.
Use vmstat, /proc, smaps, pressure stalls, and fault counters to distinguish allocation, retention, paging, and contention.
Use iostat/per-device latency and queue evidence for storage, and perf/eBPF tools when syscall-level evidence is insufficient.
performance: Separate runnable-queue pressure, user CPU, kernel CPU, I/O wait, lock wait, and memory pressure.
Budget context switches, cache/TLB locality, NUMA placement, copying, and syscall frequency.
Use batching, asynchronous I/O, zero-copy paths, or affinity only after proving the bottleneck and correctness impact.
Bound worker counts and queues so overload becomes controlled backpressure rather than global thrashing.
security: Assume every user pointer, length, file path, descriptor, and ioctl input crossing the kernel boundary is hostile.
Drop privileges, capabilities, writable mounts, device access, and syscalls that the workload does not need.
Treat container namespaces as one layer; combine user namespaces, capabilities, seccomp, LSM policy, and patched kernels.
Avoid unsafe temporary-file patterns, inherited descriptors, shell interpolation, and world-writable permission assumptions.
failureModes: A child is not reaped and accumulates as a zombie, or inherited descriptors keep pipes/sockets unexpectedly open.
A missed wakeup, data race, lock-order cycle, starvation, or priority inversion prevents progress.
Unbounded threads or memory mappings exhaust limits long before physical memory appears full.
Long dirty-write queues or incorrect fsync assumptions lose acknowledged data after a crash.
Memory pressure causes reclaim, major faults, swap, or OOM selection that is misdiagnosed as CPU slowness.
A privileged container, broad capability set, host mount, or kernel vulnerability collapses the intended isolation boundary.

workedExamples.title: Wait on a predicate, not a notification
workedExamples.explanation: pthread_cond_wait atomically releases the mutex while sleeping and reacquires it before returning. The loop handles spurious wakeups and another consumer winning the race.

workedExamples.title: Create a child, replace its image, and reap it
workedExamples.explanation: fork creates a child process with copy-on-write memory; exec replaces only the child image. The parent handles interrupted waits and reaps the child so it does not remain a zombie.

workedExamples.title: Durable same-filesystem replacement
workedExamples.explanation: The temporary file is made durable before an atomic same-filesystem rename, then the directory entry is synced. Exact guarantees remain filesystem- and hardware-dependent, so errors must be checked in real code.

questions.prompt: Process versus thread: what is owned, shared, and scheduled?
questions.answer: A process owns a protected address space and resource context such as descriptors and credentials. A thread owns an execution context—registers, stack, scheduling state—and is scheduled. Threads in a process share memory and many resources, making communication cheap and races possible.
questions.whyTricky: Definitions often say 'lightweight process' without identifying the actual ownership boundary.

questions.prompt: What exactly happens on a page fault?
questions.answer: The CPU cannot complete a translation/access and traps into the kernel with fault information. The kernel validates the mapping and permissions. It may reject the access, allocate/map a zero page, perform copy-on-write, or load backing data, update page tables/TLB state, and restart the instruction; blocking I/O may let another thread run.
questions.whyTricky: Page fault is commonly equated only with swapping from disk.

questions.prompt: Why must condition-variable waiting use a while loop?
questions.answer: The condition variable is a notification mechanism, not the predicate. Wakeups can be spurious, several waiters can race for one state change, or another thread can consume the condition before this waiter reacquires the lock. Recheck the protected predicate while holding the mutex.
questions.whyTricky: A signal is mistaken for a durable transfer of the condition itself.

questions.prompt: Construct a deadlock and distinguish it from starvation and livelock.
questions.answer: Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other's lock, satisfying mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Starvation means a runnable participant is repeatedly denied progress; livelock means participants keep changing state in response to each other but no useful work completes.
questions.whyTricky: All three appear as 'the program is stuck' from the outside.

questions.prompt: Why can load average be high while CPU utilization is modest?
questions.answer: On Linux, load includes runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep, commonly waiting on I/O. Many blocked storage/NFS tasks can raise load without consuming CPU. Inspect runnable queues, task states, pressure stalls, iostat, and per-task wait evidence before adding CPU.
questions.whyTricky: Load average is widely misread as CPU percentage.

questions.prompt: Does fsync(file) make an atomic replace durable?
questions.answer: A robust pattern writes a temporary file, fsyncs it, renames it over the target, then fsyncs the containing directory where required. Rename provides atomic namespace replacement on the same filesystem, but durability of file data and the directory entry requires the relevant flushes and depends on filesystem guarantees.
questions.whyTricky: Atomic visibility and crash durability are separate properties.

questions.prompt: Why can adding threads reduce throughput?
questions.answer: Past useful parallelism, threads add scheduling/context-switch cost, cache/TLB disruption, lock contention, memory/stack pressure, and downstream queueing. For CPU-bound work size near available cores; for blocking work use measured wait/service ratios, bounded queues, and backpressure rather than unbounded threads.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is confused with free parallel capacity.

questions.prompt: Are containers secure isolation? Compare them with VMs.
questions.answer: Containers provide meaningful process isolation through namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, LSMs, and seccomp, but share the host kernel, so kernel bugs and privileged/misconfigured containers threaten the host. VMs add a guest-kernel and virtual-hardware boundary, usually stronger but heavier. Choose and harden based on threat model.
questions.whyTricky: The debate is framed as secure versus insecure instead of layered controls and failure boundaries.
rubric: Uses threat model and hardening controls.

flashcards.back: Protected resource container: address space, descriptors, credentials, and one or more threads.
Schedulable execution context with registers, stack, and state; shares process resources.
Mode switch changes privilege; context switch changes the scheduled execution context.
Wait atomically releases a mutex; wakeups require rechecking the protected predicate in a loop.
Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
Share pages read-only after fork; copy a page only when a writer needs a private version.
Requests persistence of relevant file state; namespace durability may also require syncing the directory.
Namespaces isolate views, cgroups account/limit, capabilities/seccomp restrict; host kernel is shared.

technologies.title: Computer Networks
technologies.summary: TCP/IP, subnetting, routing, ARP, NAT, ICMP, UDP, TCP, DNS, TLS, HTTP/1–3, sockets, proxies, load balancers, CDNs, WebSockets, gRPC, security, and debugging.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Computer Networks is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Computer Networks like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect addresses using `ip address`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: a simpler interface that hides lower-level details
the point where responsibility moves between parts
a rule that must remain true while the system changes

technologies.mentalModel: Networks move best-effort packets across independently managed hops; reliability, naming, security, and application semantics are layered on top.

topics: bits, frames, packets, segments, encapsulation, and MTU
MAC addresses, Ethernet switching, ARP/neighbor discovery, and VLANs

ports, sockets, UDP, TCP, and client/server lifecycles

learningPath.objective: Explain how a hostname becomes an authenticated application exchange.
topics: DNS hierarchy, recursion, caching, records, TTL, and failure
TLS handshake, certificates, PKI, key agreement, SNI, ALPN, and session resumption
HTTP semantics, caching, cookies, compression, and HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
proxies, reverse proxies, load balancers, CDNs, WebSockets, and gRPC

learningPath.title: Transport and distributed behavior
learningPath.objective: Reason about loss, latency, congestion, retries, and partial failure.
topics: TCP handshake, sequence space, acknowledgements, flow control, congestion control, and teardown
QUIC streams, UDP substrate, migration, and head-of-line behavior
timeouts, retry budgets, idempotency, circuit breaking, and backpressure

latency budgets, bandwidth-delay product, queueing, bufferbloat, and capacity

multi-region routing, anycast, service discovery, meshes, and failure domains

theorySections.title: Layering, forwarding, and MTU
theorySections.explanation: Each hop forwards a network-layer packet using a routing decision while link-layer frames are rebuilt for the next local medium. Encapsulation adds headers and reduces payload space. If a path cannot carry a packet, IPv4 may fragment under limited conditions, while robust endpoints use path-MTU discovery and avoid black holes caused by blocked ICMP feedback.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Applications wrap data in protocol headers; every router forwards the IP packet while replacing the local link-layer envelope for the next hop.
theorySections.analogy: A parcel keeps its destination address while each regional courier replaces the local transport label used for the next depot.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Packets may be dropped, reordered, encrypted, fragmented, or encapsulated, and routers do not provide the end-to-end guarantees of a courier contract.
theorySections.concreteExample: A remote server's IP stays in the packet, but the first Ethernet frame uses the default gateway's MAC address, not the server's MAC.
keyPoints: MAC addresses are local-link identifiers; IP addresses support routed delivery.
Switches learn source MAC locations; routers choose next hops by longest-prefix match.
TTL/hop limit prevents indefinite routing loops.
MTU, MSS, tunneling overhead, and ICMP handling affect seemingly random large-request failures.

theorySections.title: IP addressing, subnetting, routing, and NAT
theorySections.explanation: CIDR represents an address prefix whose length determines network and host portions. Routers select the most specific matching route, then resolve the next-hop link address. NAT rewrites address/port mappings and creates state that affects inbound reachability, failover, and observability; it conserves or translates addressing but is not a security model by itself.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A prefix describes an address region, routers choose the most specific matching route, and NAT rewrites endpoint identity while keeping translation state.
theorySections.analogy: A postal sorter chooses the most detailed matching region code, while a company mailroom replaces internal desk numbers with one public return address.
theorySections.analogyLimit: NAT also rewrites ports and expires state, and Internet routing policy is more complex than hierarchical postal sorting.
theorySections.concreteExample: For 10.0.4.18, a /24 route beats a /16 route; outbound NAT may map its private source and port to a public tuple.
keyPoints: Subnet size follows 2^(address bits − prefix length), subject to protocol/reservation context.
Default gateway is simply the next hop for routes not more specifically matched.
Longest-prefix match beats route listing order.
Stateful NAT can expire idle mappings and complicate protocols carrying addresses.

theorySections.title: TCP reliability, flow, and congestion
theorySections.explanation: TCP provides an ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgements, retransmission, and connection state. Receiver windows protect the receiver; congestion control protects the network by adapting the sending rate to loss and delay signals. TCP preserves order, so loss can delay later bytes even when they arrived, and application message boundaries must be framed separately.
theorySections.plainEnglish: TCP numbers a byte stream, retransmits missing data, preserves order, and limits sending according to both receiver capacity and network conditions.
theorySections.analogy: Numbered pages are mailed in batches; the receiver reports missing pages and available shelf space while the sender slows when the route becomes crowded.
theorySections.analogyLimit: TCP acknowledgements, windows, timers, and congestion algorithms are cumulative and adaptive rather than literal page-by-page messages.
theorySections.concreteExample: One send of 1,000 bytes may arrive through several recv calls, so an application must add a length prefix or delimiter for message boundaries.
keyPoints: The three-way handshake synchronizes sequence state and confirms bidirectional reachability.
Flow control and congestion control solve different bottlenecks.
One send does not correspond to one receive; TCP is a byte stream.
TIME_WAIT protects old segments and permits reliable close; it is not automatically a leak.

theorySections.title: DNS resolution and caching
theorySections.explanation: A stub resolver typically asks a recursive resolver, which follows cached or authoritative referrals through the DNS hierarchy. Records carry TTLs, and negative answers may also be cached. DNS can succeed differently across clients due to cache state, split-horizon views, search paths, record families, load-balancing policy, and DNSSEC validation.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A resolver follows delegated authority from the DNS hierarchy and caches answers—including failures—for their allowed lifetime.
theorySections.analogy: A directory assistant asks regional offices until reaching the office authoritative for a name, then keeps the answer until its expiry time.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Split-horizon views, DNSSEC, multiple address families, load balancing, and negative caching make DNS more than one global phone book.
theorySections.concreteExample: Changing an A record does not update clients that still hold the old answer until its TTL expires or their cache is cleared.
keyPoints: Recursive and authoritative servers have different responsibilities.
CNAME aliases names; it does not redirect HTTP or preserve a URL path.
Changing a record does not instantly purge existing caches.
A/AAAA reachability, resolver choice, and Happy Eyeballs can change observed behavior.

theorySections.title: TLS identity and key establishment
theorySections.explanation: TLS negotiates protocol parameters, authenticates the server through a certificate chain and hostname verification, establishes fresh session keys through key agreement, and protects later records for confidentiality and integrity. Encryption without correct certificate validation can still connect securely to the wrong peer; TLS does not validate application authorization or sanitize content.
theorySections.plainEnglish: TLS authenticates the intended peer, negotiates keys, and protects later bytes from reading or modification in transit.
theorySections.analogy: A courier verifies a signed identity chain, agrees on a fresh locked case, and then transports tamper-evident messages inside it.
theorySections.analogyLimit: A valid certificate authenticates a name and key, not application authorization, honesty, or safety of the transmitted content.
theorySections.concreteExample: A client checks certificate chain, validity, and hostname; accepting any certificate would encrypt traffic to a possible attacker.
keyPoints: The certificate binds identities to a public key through a trusted chain and policy.
SNI selects a virtual host; ALPN negotiates an application protocol such as h2.
Forward secrecy limits retrospective decryption when long-term keys later leak.
mTLS authenticates clients at the transport layer but still needs authorization policy.

theorySections.title: HTTP versions, intermediaries, and caching
theorySections.explanation: HTTP defines methods, status codes, headers, representation metadata, and cache semantics independent of a specific transport mapping. HTTP/1.1 commonly pipelines poorly across connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection but still shares transport loss, and HTTP/3 maps streams over QUIC to reduce cross-stream head-of-line blocking. Proxies and CDNs can transform, cache, retry, and route requests, so end-to-end behavior must include them.
theorySections.plainEnglish: HTTP defines request and response meaning, while versions choose transport mappings and intermediaries may route, retry, transform, or cache traffic.
theorySections.analogy: The order form defines what a customer asks for; phone, multiplexed desk, or courier describes transport, and a regional warehouse may answer from stock.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Intermediaries can parse ambiguously, share connection state, and apply cache rules that have no exact retail equivalent.
theorySections.concreteExample: A POST retried by a proxy after a lost response can duplicate payment unless the application stores and replays results by idempotency key.
keyPoints: Safe and idempotent are semantic properties, not synonyms.
Cache-Control, validators, Vary, and shared/private scope jointly determine caching.
A 502/503/504 often identifies an intermediary failure class, not the root cause by itself.
Retrying non-idempotent work requires an application idempotency design.

misconceptions.claim: A switch uses IP addresses and a router uses MAC addresses.
misconceptions.correction: A switch primarily forwards local frames by MAC; a router selects an IP next hop and then uses the local link mechanism, often MAC, for that hop.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Layer responsibilities are taught as mutually exclusive device labels instead of one packet path.

misconceptions.claim: TCP guarantees that one send becomes one receive.
misconceptions.correction: TCP preserves an ordered byte stream and can split or coalesce writes arbitrarily; applications need framing.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Small local tests often happen to preserve apparent message boundaries.

misconceptions.claim: UDP is always faster than TCP.
misconceptions.correction: UDP has less built-in machinery, but an application needing reliability, congestion control, ordering, or handshake security must implement comparable work.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Header size is compared while complete application requirements are omitted.

misconceptions.claim: HTTPS means the website is trustworthy and safe.
misconceptions.correction: TLS authenticates a hostname/key relationship and protects transport; the endpoint may still be malicious or vulnerable.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Browser lock indicators are interpreted as content endorsement.

misconceptions.claim: DNS propagation has a fixed global duration.
misconceptions.correction: Caches expire according to TTL and resolver behavior; authoritative changes are visible as individual cached entries refresh.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Distributed cache expiry is simplified into a single propagation event.

misconceptions.claim: HTTP 502, 503, and 504 are equivalent server errors.
misconceptions.correction: They distinguish bad upstream response, temporary unavailability, and upstream timeout in an intermediary context, guiding different checks.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: All are grouped as retryable 5xx without tracing the proxy path.

revisionChecklist: Trace encapsulation from application bytes to frames and back at each hop.
Calculate IPv4 CIDR ranges and apply longest-prefix routing.
Explain ARP/neighbor discovery, NAT state, ICMP, MTU, MSS, and path-MTU discovery.
Compare UDP and TCP by required semantics rather than speed slogans.
Trace TCP handshake, byte stream, retransmission, flow control, congestion control, teardown, and TIME_WAIT.
Resolve a hostname through stub, recursive, root/TLD/authoritative servers, caches, TTL, CNAME, A/AAAA, and DNSSEC context.
Trace TLS 1.3 identity, certificate verification, key agreement, SNI, ALPN, resumption, and mTLS.
Compare HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 plus caching and idempotency semantics.
Explain L4/L7 proxies, load balancing, CDNs, WebSockets, gRPC, retries, draining, and health checks.
Debug with ip/route/ss/dig/curl/openssl/tcpdump using hypotheses by layer.
setup: Record interface addresses, prefixes, routes, resolver configuration, proxy variables, and active VPN/container namespaces.
Install or identify ip/ifconfig, route, ss/netstat, dig/nslookup, curl, openssl, traceroute, and a packet-capture tool.
Use a disposable client/server pair so connection states, partial reads, timeouts, and retries can be reproduced safely.
Capture clocks and correlation identifiers across client, proxy, load balancer, and server before diagnosing latency.
Know where TLS keys, trust stores, firewall policy, load-balancer health, DNS zones, and CDN cache rules are managed.
runtime: An application resolves a name, selects an address, opens a socket, and asks the OS transport stack to exchange bytes or datagrams.
The host chooses a route, resolves the local next-hop link address, encapsulates a packet in a frame, and hands it to an interface.
Routers decrement hop limit, apply forwarding/policy/NAT as configured, and rebuild link framing for the next hop.
TCP or QUIC manages connection state, loss, flow, congestion, and cryptographic/application negotiation as applicable.
Proxies, load balancers, CDNs, service meshes, and origins each add independent timeout, retry, cache, and failure behavior.
testing: Test protocol framing with split/coalesced reads, truncation, duplicate delivery, reordering where allowed, and malformed lengths.
Test DNS changes under cache, multiple A/AAAA results, failure, and resolver differences.
Test TLS expiry, hostname mismatch, missing intermediates, client-certificate policy, and rotation overlap.
Use fault injection for latency, loss, resets, partial responses, proxy retries, backend draining, and regional failure.
debugging: Localize the failure by layer: name resolution, route/neighbor, transport socket, TLS identity/negotiation, HTTP semantics, intermediary, or application.
Compare client timestamps with server and intermediary traces; a client timeout alone does not reveal where time was spent.
Inspect socket states and retransmission/zero-window signals before assuming application CPU is slow.
Capture the narrowest safe packet sample and account for offload, encryption, NAT, and asymmetric paths when interpreting it.
performance: Decompose latency into DNS, connect, TLS, request queue, server, first byte, transfer, and client processing.
Relate throughput to bandwidth-delay product, congestion window, receiver window, loss, and number of independent connections/streams.
Reuse connections and sessions where safe, but bound pools and respect backend capacity and load-balancer draining.
Control retry amplification with budgets, jitter, deadlines, idempotency, and backpressure across every intermediary.
security: Verify certificate chains and hostnames; encryption without intended-peer authentication is insufficient.
Restrict ingress and egress by identity and destination, protect metadata/internal endpoints from SSRF, and validate proxy headers at trusted boundaries.
Harden HTTP parsing across intermediaries to prevent request smuggling and normalize ambiguous framing.
Use DDoS rate/connection controls, mTLS where appropriate, short-lived credentials, and observable policy decisions.
failureModes: A wrong route, prefix, neighbor entry, or MTU black hole makes only some destinations or payload sizes fail.
DNS caches, split-horizon views, stale negative answers, or IPv6/IPv4 differences produce client-specific behavior.
TCP retransmission, zero windows, connection-pool exhaustion, or TIME_WAIT port pressure is mistaken for an application bug.
Certificate hostname/chain/time problems or SNI/ALPN mismatch breaks TLS despite IP reachability.
Independent proxy/backend timeouts and retries amplify load or duplicate non-idempotent work.
Load-balancer health checks pass while the real dependency path, tenant data, or expensive endpoint is unavailable.

workedExamples.title: Frame messages over a TCP byte stream
workedExamples.explanation: A four-byte network-order length frames one message. recv loops because TCP may return fewer bytes than requested, and EOF before the declared length is an incomplete frame.

workedExamples.title: Inspect DNS, TCP/TLS, and HTTP separately
workedExamples.code:
dig api.example.com A AAAA
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2
curl --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 -v --http2 https://api.example.com/health
workedExamples.explanation: The commands isolate naming, certificate/protocol negotiation, and an HTTP request to a chosen address. --resolve preserves the hostname for SNI and certificate verification while bypassing ordinary DNS selection.

workedExamples.title: Retry an ambiguous request with an idempotency key
workedExamples.code:
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 6f1d...stable-per-business-attempt

transaction {
  existing = idempotency_results.find_for_update(key)
  if (existing) return existing.response
  payment = ledger.capture(command)
  idempotency_results.insert(key, hash(command), payment.response)
  return payment.response
}
workedExamples.explanation: The key is stable across retries and stored atomically with the business result. Concurrent duplicates return the recorded response, while reuse with a different request hash is rejected.

questions.prompt: A laptop sends to an IP outside its subnet. Whose MAC address goes in the Ethernet frame?
questions.answer: The destination IP remains the remote host, but the local Ethernet destination is the next-hop default gateway's MAC, learned through ARP or neighbor discovery. Each router removes and rebuilds the link-layer frame for its next hop.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates assume the remote server's MAC travels end to end.

questions.prompt: Why is TCP a byte stream rather than a message protocol?
questions.answer: TCP numbers and delivers ordered bytes; send calls only place bytes into the stream, and segmentation, buffering, retransmission, and receive sizes are independent. Applications must frame messages using lengths, delimiters with escaping, or a structured protocol.
questions.whyTricky: Local send/receive tests frequently align buffers and create a false message-boundary guarantee.

questions.prompt: Differentiate flow control from congestion control.
questions.answer: Flow control uses receiver-advertised capacity to avoid overrunning the endpoint. Congestion control estimates safe load for the network path and adjusts the congestion window based on acknowledgements, loss, and delay. Effective in-flight data is constrained by both.
questions.whyTricky: Both reduce sender rate and use window-like values.

questions.prompt: Trace opening https://example.com from an empty cache.
questions.answer: Resolve DNS through configured recursive infrastructure, choose an address, route/neighbor-resolve the first hop, establish TCP or QUIC, perform TLS with SNI, certificate/hostname verification and ALPN, send an HTTP request, traverse proxies/CDNs/origin as configured, receive/cache the response, then fetch dependent resources under connection and cache policies.
questions.whyTricky: Answers usually omit one of naming, local forwarding, identity verification, protocol negotiation, or intermediaries.

questions.prompt: Why can ping succeed while HTTPS fails?
questions.answer: ICMP reachability tests a different protocol and policy. TCP/443 may be filtered, no listener may exist, routing may be asymmetric, DNS may choose another address, TLS may fail identity/protocol negotiation, or an HTTP proxy/backend may fail. Test layer by layer with route, socket, TLS, and HTTP evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Reachability is treated as proof that every higher-layer dependency works.

questions.prompt: Explain TIME_WAIT and when many TIME_WAIT sockets are a problem.
questions.answer: The active closer retains state long enough to absorb delayed duplicate segments and retransmit the final acknowledgement, protecting a later connection with the same tuple. Many entries can be normal at high connection churn; they matter when ephemeral ports or state capacity exhaust. Prefer pooling/keepalive and correct ownership before unsafe timeout tuning.
questions.whyTricky: The visible socket count is mistaken for leaked live connections.
rubric: Identifies active closer and tuple reuse.
Diagnoses actual resource exhaustion before tuning.

questions.prompt: HTTP request timed out after a retry and created two payments. Which layer is responsible?
questions.answer: A timeout is ambiguous: the first request may have committed while its response was lost. Transport or proxy retries cannot infer application outcome. The payment API needs a stable idempotency key, atomic key-to-result storage with the business transaction, duplicate/concurrent request handling, and safe replay of the recorded result.
questions.whyTricky: At-least-once delivery and lost responses are mistaken for failed execution.
rubric: Places idempotency at the application/business boundary.
Requires atomic persistence and replay semantics.

questions.prompt: Compare HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 head-of-line blocking.
questions.answer: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams but uses one ordered TCP byte stream, so a lost TCP segment delays delivery of later bytes across all streams. HTTP/3 uses QUIC stream-level ordering over UDP; loss in one stream does not block delivery of data in another, though congestion control and connection-level limits are still shared.
questions.whyTricky: Both protocols advertise multiplexing, which is confused with identical loss behavior.

flashcards.back: Choose the routing entry with the most specific matching network prefix.
Resolve a local IPv4 next-hop address to its link-layer address; it does not find remote-host MACs across routers.
Reliable ordered byte stream; applications define message framing.
Receiver capacity versus network-path capacity.
Aliases one DNS name to another; it is not an HTTP redirect.
Validate chain, time/policy, and hostname; encryption alone does not authenticate the intended peer.
Repeating the same intended request has the same intended effect, though responses and incidental logging may differ.
QUIC gives independent ordered streams, reducing cross-stream transport head-of-line blocking.

technologies.title: Computer Architecture
technologies.summary: CPU pipelines, caches, memory hierarchy, instruction sets, branch prediction, SIMD, and performance reasoning.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Computer Architecture is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Computer Architecture like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: locate the build entry using `rg "main|build|test" .`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: a simpler interface that hides lower-level details
the point where responsibility moves between parts
a rule that must remain true while the system changes

technologies.mentalModel: Computer Architecture turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Computer Architecture turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. A rigorous model identifies formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior, the invariant each unit owns, and the abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with instruction sets and machine code and pipelining and hazards; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Computer Architecture operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through instruction sets and machine code, across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: instruction sets and machine code
pipelining and hazards
Define invariants for the formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Computer Architecture distributes state across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to branch prediction; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow branch prediction from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: branch prediction
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Computer Architecture lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. cache hierarchy and locality is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for cache hierarchy and locality that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: cache hierarchy and locality
define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Computer Architecture involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. virtual and physical memory must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around virtual and physical memory. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: virtual and physical memory
independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Computer Architecture should mirror worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For SIMD and vectorization, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for SIMD and vectorization: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: SIMD and vectorization
worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. For multicore coherence, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving multicore coherence with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: multicore coherence
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Computer Architecture decomposes asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. performance counters and roofline limits should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for performance counters and roofline limits showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: performance counters and roofline limits
asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Computer Architecture combines undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Computer Architecture deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap
formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Computer Architecture is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Computer Architecture build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Computer Architecture code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Computer Architecture faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Computer Architecture defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Computer Architecture deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Computer Architecture mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.

Trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain instruction sets and machine code, pipelining and hazards, branch prediction, and cache hierarchy and locality with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around virtual and physical memory.
Design tests across worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose multicore coherence from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Computer Architecture from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Computer Architecture turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. The principal execution vocabulary is formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.

Trace state explicitly across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Computer Architecture; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.
Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around branch prediction creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Computer Architecture version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For cache hierarchy and locality, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Computer Architecture.

Decompose asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Computer Architecture behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around instruction sets and machine code creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to multicore coherence breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior; trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions; identify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; cross abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: compare instruction sets and machine code with pipelining and hazards.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Computer Architecture, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: build a test strategy for SIMD and vectorization.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around branch prediction, one saturation failure around asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, and one integration or compatibility failure at abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: optimize performance counters and roofline limits without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Computer Architecture only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Computer Architecture: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Compilers is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Compilers like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: locate the build entry using `rg "main|build|test" .`, observe the result, and explain what changed.
