theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Compilers turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. A rigorous model identifies formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior, the invariant each unit owns, and the abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with lexing and token streams and parsing and grammars; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Compilers operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through lexing and token streams, across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: lexing and token streams
parsing and grammars
Define invariants for the formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Compilers distributes state across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to semantic analysis and symbol tables; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow semantic analysis and symbol tables from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: semantic analysis and symbol tables
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Compilers lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. intermediate representations is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for intermediate representations that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: intermediate representations
define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Compilers involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. data-flow analysis must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around data-flow analysis. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: data-flow analysis
independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Compilers should mirror worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For optimization correctness, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for optimization correctness: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: optimization correctness
worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. For instruction selection and register allocation, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving instruction selection and register allocation with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: instruction selection and register allocation
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Compilers decomposes asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. linking loading and runtime interfaces should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for linking loading and runtime interfaces showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: linking loading and runtime interfaces
asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Compilers combines undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Compilers deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap
formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Compilers build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Compilers code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Compilers faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Compilers defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Compilers deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Compilers mental model without product slogans or API lists.

Trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain lexing and token streams, parsing and grammars, semantic analysis and symbol tables, and intermediate representations with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around data-flow analysis.
Design tests across worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose instruction selection and register allocation from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Compilers from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Compilers turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. The principal execution vocabulary is formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.

Trace state explicitly across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Compilers; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around semantic analysis and symbol tables creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Compilers version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For intermediate representations, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Compilers.

Decompose asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Compilers behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around lexing and token streams creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to instruction selection and register allocation breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis

reproduce smallest-failing-case

questions.prompt: Compilers: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior; trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions; identify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; cross abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Compilers: compare lexing and token streams with parsing and grammars.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Compilers, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Compilers: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Compilers: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Compilers: build a test strategy for optimization correctness.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Compilers: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Compilers: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around semantic analysis and symbol tables, one saturation failure around asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, and one integration or compatibility failure at abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Compilers: optimize linking loading and runtime interfaces without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Compilers: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Compilers: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Compilers: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Compilers only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Compilers: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

technologies.title: Theory of Computation

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Theory of Computation is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Theory of Computation like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: locate the build entry using `rg "main|build|test" .`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Theory of Computation turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. A rigorous model identifies formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior, the invariant each unit owns, and the abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with finite automata and regular languages and context-free grammars and pushdown automata; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Theory of Computation operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through finite automata and regular languages, across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: finite automata and regular languages
context-free grammars and pushdown automata
Define invariants for the formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Theory of Computation distributes state across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to pumping lemmas; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow pumping lemmas from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: pumping lemmas
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Theory of Computation lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. Turing machines and decidability is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for Turing machines and decidability that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: Turing machines and decidability
define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Theory of Computation involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. reductions and recognizability must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around reductions and recognizability. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: reductions and recognizability
independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Theory of Computation should mirror worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For time and space complexity, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for time and space complexity: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: time and space complexity
worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. For P NP and NP-completeness, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving P NP and NP-completeness with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: P NP and NP-completeness
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Theory of Computation decomposes asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. randomized and approximation reasoning should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for randomized and approximation reasoning showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: randomized and approximation reasoning
asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Theory of Computation combines undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Theory of Computation deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap
formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Theory of Computation is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Theory of Computation build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Theory of Computation code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Theory of Computation faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Theory of Computation defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Theory of Computation deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Theory of Computation mental model without product slogans or API lists.

Trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain finite automata and regular languages, context-free grammars and pushdown automata, pumping lemmas, and Turing machines and decidability with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around reductions and recognizability.
Design tests across worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose P NP and NP-completeness from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Theory of Computation from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Theory of Computation turns informal behavior into explicit models whose assumptions, invariants, and costs can be tested. The principal execution vocabulary is formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior.

Trace state explicitly across symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Theory of Computation; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.
Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around pumping lemmas creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Theory of Computation version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For Turing machines and decidability, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Theory of Computation.

Decompose asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Theory of Computation behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around finite automata and regular languages creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with formal object, representation, transformation, invariant, cost model, proof obligation, and observable machine behavior; trace define the model, encode an input, apply transformations, preserve invariants, produce an output, measure cost, and validate assumptions; identify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; cross abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: compare finite automata and regular languages with context-free grammars and pushdown automata.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Theory of Computation, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify symbols or instructions, graphs and tables, machine or memory state, intermediate forms, assumptions, and measured evidence; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from independent operations, shared resources, ordering constraints, parallel work, synchronization cost, and memory visibility where applicable; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: build a test strategy for time and space complexity.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for worked derivation, counterexample, property or invariant, reference implementation, measured experiment, and cross-layer validation, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around pumping lemmas, one saturation failure around asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, and one integration or compatibility failure at abstraction layer, representation change, compiler or machine interface, mathematical model, experiment, and implementation. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: optimize randomized and approximation reasoning without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile asymptotic work, critical path, memory hierarchy, representation size, data movement, branching, and synchronization, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around undefined assumptions, unsafe representation, untrusted input, privilege boundary, side channel, generated artifact, and verification gap; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, formal model, diagram, source or intermediate representation, proof sketch, executable artifact, measurement, and revision sheet, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.

rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Theory of Computation: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Theory of Computation only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: locate the build entry using `rg "main|build|test" .`, observe the result, and explain what changed.
