theorySections.title: Values, objects, references, and lifetimes
theorySections.explanation: C++ distinguishes storage, object lifetime, value, and expressions used to identify objects. A reference is an alias and a pointer is an address-like value; neither inherently owns the target. Storage can exist before an object's lifetime begins or after it ends, so a non-null pointer can still dangle. Value categories guide overload resolution and moves but do not themselves promise that a move occurs.
theorySections.plainEnglish: C++ objects have storage, type, value, and lifetime; pointers and references provide access but do not automatically express or extend ownership.
theorySections.analogy: An object is a rented workshop bay, while a pointer is a note containing its bay number; destroying the bay does not erase every copied note.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Compilers may optimize storage away, references are language aliases rather than nullable handles, and object lifetime follows precise abstract-machine rules.
theorySections.concreteExample: Returning a reference to a local std::string leaves a dangling alias because the string's lifetime ends when the function returns.
keyPoints: Trace object lifetime separately from storage duration.
References alias; raw pointers own only by documented convention.
A moved-from object remains valid under its specified but often unspecified state.
string_view and span are non-owning views whose backing storage must outlive them.

theorySections.title: RAII and deterministic resource management
theorySections.explanation: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization binds successful acquisition to an object whose destructor releases the resource. Stack unwinding composes cleanup across early returns and exceptions. The rule of zero delegates ownership to members that already implement correct copy, move, and destruction. unique_ptr expresses exclusive dynamic ownership, shared_ptr counts shared ownership, and weak_ptr observes without extending lifetime.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Bind a resource to an object's lifetime so construction establishes ownership and destruction releases it on every normal or exceptional path.
theorySections.analogy: A hotel key card is issued at check-in and automatically deactivated at checkout, even when the guest leaves earlier than planned.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Shared ownership, cycles, asynchronous work, and process termination require policies beyond one lexical object's destructor.
theorySections.concreteExample: std::lock_guard acquires a mutex in its constructor and unlocks in its destructor when the scope exits after success or exception.
keyPoints: Prefer value members and the rule of zero.
Use unique ownership unless shared lifetime is genuine.
shared_ptr controls lifetime, not every invariant inside the object.
Destructors should not emit failures that escape during unwinding.

theorySections.title: Templates, concepts, and compile-time polymorphism
theorySections.explanation: Templates are instantiated for concrete arguments after name lookup and deduction select a candidate. Substitution failure can remove candidates, while concepts state required operations with clearer constraints. Compile-time polymorphism can inline and specialize behavior without virtual dispatch, but it increases generated code, build work, and coupling to implementation headers.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Templates generate type-specific code from one definition, and concepts state which operations a type must support before instantiation.
theorySections.analogy: A manufacturing jig produces parts in several materials, while the specification rejects materials that cannot tolerate the required operations.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Template instantiation can change overload resolution, code size, diagnostics, and compile time in ways a physical jig does not.
theorySections.concreteExample: A sortable concept can reject a type without an ordering relation at the call site instead of producing a deep substitution error.
keyPoints: Template definitions generally must be visible at instantiation.
Concepts constrain interfaces but cannot prove every semantic law.
Perfect forwarding preserves value categories only through its specific pattern.
Use runtime polymorphism when hiding implementation or runtime substitution matters.

theorySections.title: Containers, iterators, and algorithmic cost
theorySections.explanation: Standard containers expose different complexity, layout, ordering, ownership, and invalidation guarantees. vector stores elements contiguously and usually gives excellent locality; node-based containers preserve selected references but add allocation and indirection. Iterators express traversal capabilities, while algorithms separate operations from storage. Big-O must be combined with data size and hardware behavior.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Standard containers make different guarantees about layout, lookup, insertion, iterator validity, and ownership; algorithms rely on iterator capabilities.
theorySections.analogy: A vector is a row of adjacent lockers, a list is a chain of lockers, and an iterator is a route card whose validity depends on renovations.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Cache lines, allocator behavior, branch prediction, and invalidation rules make actual performance more complex than locker placement.
theorySections.concreteExample: vector::push_back may reallocate, moving all elements and invalidating every pointer and iterator into the old storage.
keyPoints: Know invalidation rules for every mutation used.
reserve changes capacity, not logical size.
Unordered containers provide expected rather than universal constant-time lookup.
Prefer algorithms that make boundaries and intent explicit without hiding complexity.

theorySections.title: Undefined behavior and the abstract machine
theorySections.explanation: Undefined behavior is not a recoverable runtime category: the standard imposes no requirements on an execution that contains it, and optimizers may reason that such paths cannot occur. Unspecified behavior chooses among allowed alternatives, while implementation-defined behavior must be documented. Sanitizers detect many violations but cannot prove the absence of undefined behavior.
theorySections.plainEnglish: The standard defines a portable abstract machine; once a program performs undefined behavior, the compiler owes no meaningful continuation semantics.
theorySections.analogy: Traffic rules guarantee outcomes only while drivers stay on the mapped road; leaving it means the map no longer predicts where the vehicle goes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Undefined behavior can affect code before the apparent bad line because optimization reasons about impossible executions globally.
theorySections.concreteExample: Signed integer overflow may let an optimizer remove a bounds check because the standard says the overflowing execution cannot occur.
keyPoints: The crash site may be far from the original violation.
Signed overflow is undefined; unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range.
Strict aliasing and alignment constrain how stored bytes are accessed as objects.
Compiler success and stable output do not make undefined behavior safe.

theorySections.title: Concurrency and the memory model
theorySections.explanation: The C++ memory model defines sequenced-before within a thread and inter-thread happens-before through synchronization. Atomics prevent data races for their objects and offer ordering from relaxed through sequential consistency. Mutex release/acquire also creates ordering. A condition variable is a notification mechanism; the protected predicate remains the truth and must be checked in a loop.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Concurrent accesses need synchronization that orders memory effects; a data race on ordinary memory makes the program undefined.
theorySections.analogy: Workers update a shared log through numbered, locked handoff points so everyone agrees which entries are visible before the next step.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Atomic memory orders and compiler/CPU reordering are formal relationships, not simply wall-clock order or physical locks.
theorySections.concreteExample: A release store to an atomic ready flag and an acquire load that observes it can publish earlier non-atomic data safely.
keyPoints: A data race on ordinary memory is undefined behavior.
Atomicity of one variable does not protect a multi-field invariant.
Relaxed atomics add no cross-object synchronization.
Deadlock, starvation, livelock, and false sharing are distinct failures.

misconceptions.claim: C++ passes objects by reference by default.
misconceptions.correction: Value parameters copy or move; only reference or pointer parameters alias caller-visible state.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Optimized copies and class syntax hide the selected copy/move operations.

misconceptions.claim: std::move moves an object.
misconceptions.correction: std::move is a cast that permits move-aware overload selection; the selected operation decides what transfers.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: The helper's name describes intended use rather than its literal operation.

misconceptions.claim: Smart pointers make ownership automatically correct.
misconceptions.correction: They encode selected lifetime policies, but shared cycles, wrong ownership, aliases, and concurrent invariants still require design.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Automatic destruction is confused with correct ownership architecture.

misconceptions.claim: A list is faster than a vector for insertion.
misconceptions.correction: Only insertion after a known node is constant time; traversal, allocation, and poor locality often make vector faster.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: One asymptotic mutation step is quoted while lookup and hardware costs are omitted.

misconceptions.claim: Undefined behavior means a throw or crash at that line.
misconceptions.correction: No behavior is required, and optimization may change code far before or after the apparent violation.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Debug builds appear deterministic and make UB look like a normal runtime error.

misconceptions.claim: An atomic member makes the containing object thread-safe.
misconceptions.correction: Atomics protect their own operations; compound relationships across fields still need one synchronization policy.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Atomic access is confused with preservation of a larger invariant.

revisionChecklist: Trace automatic, static, thread, and dynamic storage duration against actual object lifetime.
Explain value categories, copy elision, move construction, and the valid moved-from rule.
Choose raw reference/pointer, unique_ptr, shared_ptr, weak_ptr, span, or value ownership deliberately.
State vector, deque, list, map, and unordered_map complexity plus invalidation and locality trade-offs.
Explain compilation, linking, name mangling, ODR, header templates, and ABI risk.
Distinguish undefined, unspecified, and implementation-defined behavior with examples.
Construct happens-before through mutexes or atomics and identify a data race.
Use compiler diagnostics, debugger, sanitizers, profiler, and benchmark harness for distinct evidence.
Give basic, strong, and no-throw exception guarantees and design RAII cleanup.
Explain when zero-cost abstraction claims hold and how measurement can disprove an assumption.
setup: Install a current Clang or GCC toolchain and verify the compiler, linker, standard library, debugger, and CMake are compatible.
Compile interview code as C++17 with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic and explain every warning.
Maintain separate debug/sanitized and optimized builds because instrumentation and optimization expose different failures.
Use an out-of-source CMake build and compile_commands.json so editors, analysis, and CI share flags.
Run one unit test, one AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer check, and one debugger session before relying on the environment.
runtime: Each translation unit is preprocessed and compiled to object code; the linker resolves definitions, symbols, templates, libraries, and startup.
Automatic objects normally end at scope exit, static objects span program or thread lifetime, and dynamic storage ends when its owner releases it.
The abstract machine defines observable behavior while compilers may transform any implementation that preserves defined behavior.
Value semantics copy or move state; references and pointers create aliases whose validity depends on the target lifetime.
Threads share an address space, and conflicting unsynchronized accesses to ordinary memory create a data race and undefined behavior.
testing: Test public behavior, ownership transfer, boundaries, invalid inputs, and exception guarantees rather than private helper shape.
Run ASan/UBSan for memory and undefined behavior, TSan for races in a compatible build, and static analysis for missed paths.
Use property tests and fuzzers for parsers, serializers, containers, and state machines with strong invariants.
Use a benchmark harness and prevent dead-code elimination, warm-up bias, and unrealistic data layout.
debugging: Start with the first compiler diagnostic; later template errors are often consequences of the earliest failed requirement.
Use a debugger for stacks, values, memory, threads, and watchpoints, then core dumps for non-interactive failures.
Enable sanitizers before manually tracing corruption because the visible crash may occur far after the invalid access.
Inspect assembly or optimization remarks only after a profiler identifies the hot path.
For hangs, collect every thread stack, lock owner, wait predicate, queue depth, and shutdown state.
performance: Choose algorithms and data layout before micro-optimizing syntax; contiguous storage often wins through locality.
Measure wall time, CPU, allocation, cache misses, branch misses, context switches, and tail latency separately.
Prefer value types and reserve predictable capacity, but do not trade correctness for speculative allocation removal.
Treat copies, moves, virtual calls, exceptions, bounds checks, and abstractions as costs to measure rather than slogans to eliminate.
security: Parse untrusted lengths, indexes, integer conversions, encodings, paths, and binary formats with bounds and overflow checks.
Use RAII containers and spans instead of raw owning pointers and unchecked pointer-length pairs at interfaces.
Compile production targets with applicable hardening, sanitizers in testing, dependency scanning, and strong warnings.
Avoid shell construction, unsafe format strings, lifetime escapes, uninitialized data, and serialization of raw object layout.
failureModes: A pointer, reference, iterator, or string_view outlives its object or is invalidated by container mutation.
Double ownership, shared_ptr cycles, manual new/delete, or mismatched allocation APIs leak or corrupt memory.
Signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, invalid shifts, uninitialized reads, or data races invoke undefined behavior.
An exception crosses a destructor, C ABI, thread entry, or noexcept boundary without an intentional policy.
Header definitions violate the One Definition Rule or library changes break ABI despite source compatibility.
A micro-optimization worsens locality, prediction, compile time, or maintainability without improving the measured workload.

workedExamples.title: Exclusive ownership with automatic cleanup
workedExamples.explanation: Construction either produces a valid owner or throws. Destruction closes the file on every scope exit, and copying is forbidden because two owners would double-close one handle.

workedExamples.title: Avoid iterator invalidation during growth
workedExamples.explanation: A vector reallocation moves elements and invalidates every reference, pointer, and iterator. reserve protects only the known capacity window; validity still follows documented mutations.

workedExamples.title: Publish immutable data with release/acquire
workedExamples.explanation: When the acquire load observes the release store, the earlier message write happens-before the read. This is a publication pattern, not a general replacement for protecting mutable state.

questions.prompt: What does std::move do, and what state is the source left in?
questions.answer: std::move casts to an xvalue so overload resolution can select a move operation; it moves nothing itself. A standard-library moved-from object is valid but generally has an unspecified value unless documented otherwise.
questions.whyTricky: The name suggests a transfer and candidates often say the source becomes empty or invalid.
rubric: Makes the selected operation responsible for transfer.
States valid but usually unspecified source state.

questions.prompt: Differentiate pointer validity, object lifetime, and storage duration.
questions.answer: Storage is memory with a duration; an object's lifetime begins and ends within suitable storage; a pointer may retain the same address after lifetime ends but dereferencing it as the former object is invalid. Placement construction makes the distinction explicit.
questions.whyTricky: An address is treated as proof that a live object exists there.
rubric: Uses a local-return or placement example.

questions.prompt: When does vector invalidate iterators and why can reserve help?
questions.answer: Reallocation invalidates all iterators, references, and pointers. Insertion without reallocation has position-specific invalidation. reserve guarantees a capacity floor but never changes size or gives permanent stability.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates memorize that push_back invalidates without conditioning it on capacity.

questions.prompt: Why is returning string_view to a local string wrong?
questions.answer: string_view is a non-owning pointer-length view. The local string destroys its backing characters at return, so the view dangles. Return an owning string or view caller-owned/static storage with an explicit lifetime.
questions.whyTricky: Value-like syntax and cheap copying hide the borrowed lifetime.

questions.prompt: Explain the strong exception guarantee and copy-and-swap.
questions.answer: The strong guarantee leaves observable state unchanged on failure. Prepare new state in temporary RAII owners, then commit with non-throwing swap. It may cost extra allocation or lose storage reuse, so it is not universal.
questions.whyTricky: Exception safety is confused with catching exceptions.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
questions.answer: A data race is conflicting unsynchronized access to one memory location with at least one write; in C++ it is undefined behavior. A race condition is broader timing-dependent incorrectness and can occur with atomics, such as check-then-act.
questions.whyTricky: The terms are used interchangeably in casual discussion.

questions.prompt: When would you choose virtual dispatch over templates?
questions.answer: Use virtual dispatch for runtime substitution, stable interfaces, implementation hiding, or bounded code size. Use templates for compile-time customization and value-type specialization. Include ABI, build time, diagnostics, ownership, and known type-set trade-offs.
questions.whyTricky: The choice is reduced to one indirect call versus inlining.

questions.prompt: Why can signed overflow break a bounds check?
questions.answer: Signed overflow is undefined, so an optimizer may assume it never occurs when proving relationships and remove or reorder checks. Validate before arithmetic or use checked operations; use unsigned only for intentional modular semantics.
questions.whyTricky: Two's-complement hardware is mistaken for the portable language rule.

flashcards.back: Own a resource in an object; construction establishes it and destruction releases it on every scope exit.
A cast to an xvalue that enables move-aware overload selection; it performs no move itself.
Compose ownership from members whose copy, move, and destruction already express the policy.
A non-owning pointer/reference/span/string_view whose backing object lifetime ended.
Moves storage and invalidates every pointer, reference, and iterator into the old allocation.
An execution for which the standard imposes no requirements; not a defined crash mode.
Conflicting unsynchronized accesses to one location, at least one a write; undefined behavior.
When acquire observes release, prior producer actions happen-before later consumer actions.

technologies.title: Python
technologies.summary: Python setup, syntax, runtime and memory model, concurrency, idioms, debugging, performance, security, packaging, testing, and interview questions.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Python is a programming language: a precise way to describe data and the steps a computer should perform.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can write programs, reason about their behavior, and explain why one implementation is safer or faster than another. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Python like a written language for a very literal teammate: grammar matters, every instruction has a meaning, and missing details become bugs. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: check python using `python --version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: the grammar used to write valid code
the system that executes the program
reusable code that your program can call

technologies.mentalModel: Python executes a dynamic object model through an implementation runtime; names reference objects, protocols define behavior, and the event loop coordinates cooperative I/O.

theorySections.title: Names, objects, identity, and mutability
theorySections.explanation: Python assignment binds a name to an object; it does not declare a storage slot containing an object value. Multiple names can reference one mutable object, so mutation is visible through every alias. Rebinding changes only one namespace entry. Identity asks whether two references designate the same object, while equality invokes value-defined behavior. Function arguments use call-by-sharing: an object reference is passed by value.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Python variables are names bound to objects; assignment rebinds a name, while mutation changes an object that several names may share.
theorySections.analogy: Names are sticky labels placed on boxes. Moving a label does not move the box, and two labels on one box both observe changes inside it.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Python manages references and object lifetimes automatically, and some immutable objects may be interned, so labels are not memory addresses.
theorySections.concreteExample: Appending through alias = items changes the shared list, but alias = [] only rebinds alias and leaves items pointing to the old list.
keyPoints: Use is for identity and singleton sentinels such as None; use == for value equality.
Immutable objects cannot change, but names can be rebound.
Shallow copies preserve nested aliases; deep copying follows a configurable graph.
Default argument objects are created once when the function is defined.

theorySections.title: Protocols, data model, and duck typing
theorySections.explanation: Python maps syntax to protocols such as iteration, containment, context management, numeric operations, hashing, calling, and attribute access. Duck typing depends on supported behavior rather than declared ancestry. Abstract base classes and typing.Protocol can document or statically check expectations, but semantic correctness still depends on laws such as stable hashing and iterator behavior.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Python code often depends on supported behavior—iteration, context management, hashing, calling—rather than a declared inheritance tree.
theorySections.analogy: An electrical socket accepts any appliance that follows its plug and voltage protocol, regardless of the appliance's brand or ancestry.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Python protocols can be discovered only at runtime unless static typing is added, and semantic expectations extend beyond method names.
theorySections.concreteExample: for x in value relies on the iteration protocol, so a custom object can participate by implementing __iter__ without inheriting list.
keyPoints: Special methods are usually looked up on the type, not as ordinary instance attributes.
Descriptors power methods, properties, slots, and framework behavior.
Equality without a compatible stable hash makes objects unsafe or unhashable.
Composition and small protocols reduce coupling to wide hierarchies.

theorySections.title: Iteration, generators, and lazy evaluation
theorySections.explanation: An iterable can create an iterator; an iterator returns successive values and raises StopIteration when exhausted. A generator function creates an iterator whose frame is suspended at yield, retaining locals and control position. Laziness reduces peak memory and supports infinite streams, but it defers work and failure, ties resources to consumption, and can repeat expensive computation when recreated.
theorySections.plainEnglish: An iterator yields one value at a time and remembers its position; a generator packages that suspended execution state behind the iterator protocol.
theorySections.analogy: A ticket dispenser produces the next numbered ticket only when asked instead of printing and storing every future ticket in advance.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Generators can receive values, raise exceptions, delegate, and own cleanup, so they are more capable than a one-way dispenser.
theorySections.concreteExample: sum(line_length(path) for path in paths) can process one file result at a time instead of building an intermediate list.
keyPoints: Iterators are usually single-pass; iterables may create fresh iterators.
yield from delegates values, exceptions, and completion behavior.
Generator cleanup matters when a suspended frame owns files, transactions, or locks.
A list comprehension is eager; a generator expression is lazy.

theorySections.title: Exceptions, context managers, and resource ownership
theorySections.explanation: Exceptions unwind frames until a matching handler is found, executing finally blocks and context-manager exits along the way. raise from records causality between failures. A context manager establishes a resource or state transition in __enter__ and guarantees corresponding __exit__ handling. It may suppress an exception only by deliberately returning true.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Exceptions separate failure propagation from local handling, while context managers guarantee paired setup and cleanup around a scope.
theorySections.analogy: Borrowing a secure room requires signing in and signing out; the attendant records checkout even when the meeting ends unexpectedly.
theorySections.analogyLimit: __exit__ may suppress or transform exceptions, and abrupt process termination can still bypass ordinary cleanup.
theorySections.concreteExample: with open(path) as file closes the descriptor after normal processing or an exception, unlike relying on garbage collection timing.
keyPoints: Catch the narrowest exception where recovery or added meaning is possible.
Use else for work that should run only when try succeeds.
Do not rely on __del__ or reference-count timing for critical resources.
Async context managers pair acquisition and cleanup that require awaiting.

theorySections.title: Imports, packaging, and environments
theorySections.explanation: Import resolves a qualified name along the search path, creates a module object, executes its top-level code once, and caches it in sys.modules. Packages organize import namespaces, while installed distributions provide them and may have different names. Virtual environments isolate interpreter-visible installations, and lock plus metadata policy makes resolution reproducible.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Imports execute and cache modules by qualified name, while environments and lock metadata decide which distributions provide those modules.
theorySections.analogy: A recipe requests an ingredient by pantry label; the environment determines which supplier's package occupies that labelled shelf.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Python modules execute code, can be partially initialized during cycles, and distribution names need not match import names.
theorySections.concreteExample: Running python -m package.module preserves package context, while executing the file path directly can break relative imports.
keyPoints: Circular imports observe partially initialized modules.
Absolute imports and a src layout reduce accidental shadowing.
python -m selects the intended interpreter for pip and module execution.
A lock captures resolution but does not replace compatibility testing.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, async I/O, and the GIL
theorySections.explanation: Threads share memory and suit blocking I/O or native calls that release the GIL. Processes isolate memory and can execute Python CPU work in parallel but pay serialization and startup costs. asyncio schedules cooperative tasks on an event loop; progress depends on awaiting non-blocking operations. Cancellation is control flow that must propagate through finally blocks and cleanup.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Threads, processes, and async tasks solve different scheduling problems; CPython's GIL limits simultaneous Python bytecode but not all useful concurrency.
theorySections.analogy: One interpreter desk serves Python instructions, while tasks hand off the desk during I/O and separate offices can work in parallel processes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Native extensions may release the GIL, alternative interpreters differ, and async tasks still block if code does not yield cooperatively.
theorySections.concreteExample: asyncio can manage thousands of socket waits efficiently, but a CPU-heavy loop blocks the event loop unless moved or divided.
keyPoints: The GIL is not an application thread-safety guarantee.
Async is concurrency, not automatic CPU parallelism.
A blocking call on the event-loop thread stalls unrelated tasks.
Bound task creation, queues, pools, and retries and propagate deadlines.

misconceptions.claim: Python variables store values directly.
misconceptions.correction: Names bind to objects; assignment rebinds a name and mutation changes a referenced mutable object.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Simple immutable examples make rebinding look like copying a value into a box.

misconceptions.claim: Python passes mutable arguments by reference and immutable ones by value.
misconceptions.correction: All arguments pass object references by value under call-by-sharing; mutability only changes what aliases can observe.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: List mutation is visible while rebinding an integer parameter is not.

misconceptions.claim: The GIL makes Python code thread-safe.
misconceptions.correction: The GIL protects interpreter internals in common CPython builds; multi-step application invariants still race and I/O can interleave.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Serialized bytecode is confused with atomic workflows.

misconceptions.claim: async functions automatically run in parallel.
misconceptions.correction: Calling an async function creates a coroutine; tasks make cooperative progress when awaited operations yield.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Concurrent syntax is mistaken for extra CPU resources.

misconceptions.claim: A generator is simply a memory-efficient list.
misconceptions.correction: It is a stateful single-pass computation whose work, failures, and resource use occur during consumption.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Both can be iterated with identical for syntax.

misconceptions.claim: Type hints enforce runtime types.
misconceptions.correction: Annotations are metadata used by tools and frameworks; Python normally does not reject incompatible arguments at function entry.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Static checker diagnostics resemble compiler errors from enforced type systems.

revisionChecklist: Explain name binding, identity, equality, mutability, aliasing, shallow copy, and call-by-sharing.
Trace LEGB lookup, closure cells, late binding, decorators, and nonlocal/global behavior.
Use iteration, context-manager, callable, comparison, hash, and descriptor protocols deliberately.
Distinguish iterable, iterator, generator function, generator object, comprehension, and generator expression.
Explain exception propagation, chaining, finally, context cleanup, and narrow recovery boundaries.
Diagnose imports through package context, sys.path, sys.modules, metadata, and environment selection.
Choose threads, processes, asyncio, vectorization, or native code from the workload and ownership model.
Explain the GIL without claiming application thread safety or universal lack of parallelism.
Use pytest fixtures, property tests, debugger, profiler, tracemalloc, and task/thread dumps for distinct evidence.
Secure serialization, queries, templates, subprocesses, paths, secrets, uploads, and dependencies.
setup: Install a supported Python 3 release and verify python and pip refer to the intended interpreter rather than an operating-system Python.
Create a project-local virtual environment and use python -m pip or a locked project tool so installation targets are unambiguous.
Declare metadata and dependencies in pyproject.toml, separate runtime from development tools, and commit a reproducible lock where supported.
Run modules with python -m package.module to preserve package import semantics and keep executable side effects behind an entry point.
Configure formatting, linting, type checking, unit tests, and coverage as explicit repeatable commands before adding application code.
runtime: Source is parsed and compiled to bytecode that an interpreter executes through frames containing code, global, built-in, and local state.
Names are bound to objects; assignment rebinds a name, while mutation changes an object that several names can reference.
CPython primarily uses reference counting plus cyclic garbage collection, but critical resources need context managers rather than collection timing.
Attribute access follows the data model through instance state, class MRO, and descriptors; special methods implement protocols.
In common CPython builds the GIL serializes Python bytecode per interpreter, while I/O, processes, and releasing native code provide other concurrency paths.
testing: Test pure policy with ordinary values, then integration-test database, filesystem, serialization, network, and framework boundaries realistically.
Use fixtures for explicit setup and cleanup and avoid global monkeypatching that makes dependencies invisible.
Test iterators, context managers, async cancellation, retries, timeouts, partial failures, and cleanup—not only returned values.
Use property-based tests for parsers, transformations, financial invariants, and algorithms with broad input spaces.
debugging: Read a traceback from the final exception through the first relevant application frame and preserve chained causes.
Use breakpoint(), pdb, structured logs, and minimal reproductions to find the first wrong binding or transition.
Use faulthandler and thread/task dumps for hangs; inspect pending tasks, blocking calls, pools, and queues.
Use cProfile or sampling profilers for CPU, tracemalloc for allocation, and database/network traces for external waits.
Inspect sys.path, module.__file__, the environment, and installed metadata when imports differ across machines.
performance: Choose the algorithm and built-in operation first; Python-level loops magnify interpreter overhead while native operations batch work.
Separate CPU, blocking I/O, event-loop delay, serialization, allocation, garbage collection, database queries, and queue waits.
Use generators to bound memory for streams, but measure repeated computation and I/O lifetime introduced by laziness.
Use threads for suitable I/O, processes or native/vectorized code for CPU parallelism, and async only with non-blocking cancellation-aware dependencies.
security: Never eval or exec untrusted input; treat pickle-like object deserialization as code execution and use safe data formats where trust is absent.
Use parameterized queries, safe templates, allow-listed paths and commands, and argument arrays instead of shell-interpolated subprocess strings.
Keep secrets outside source and logs, use least-privilege identities, and validate uploaded size, type, name, and destination.
Pin and review dependencies, verify build sources, minimize transitive packages, and patch supported runtimes promptly.
failureModes: A mutable default argument or late-bound closure shares state or reads a final loop value unexpectedly.
A shallow copy duplicates only the outer container, leaving nested mutable objects shared.
Import cycles expose partially initialized modules or a local file shadows a standard or third-party module.
Blocking CPU or synchronous I/O inside an async task stalls every task on the event loop.
Unbounded tasks, process pools, queues, retries, or response buffering exhaust memory and downstream capacity.
Catching Exception too broadly hides cancellation, context, programmer errors, or a partial external side effect that needs reconciliation.

workedExamples.title: Avoid shared mutable default arguments
workedExamples.code:
def append_tag(tag: str, tags: list[str] | None = None) -> list[str]:
    owned = [] if tags is None else tags
    owned.append(tag)
    return owned

assert append_tag("a") == ["a"]
assert append_tag("b") == ["b"]
workedExamples.explanation: None is an immutable sentinel. A new list is allocated for each omitted argument, while a caller-supplied list is intentionally mutated and returned.

workedExamples.title: Stream records with bounded memory
workedExamples.explanation: The file and generator are consumed inside one context so the resource outlives lazy iteration. Only the current line and tuple need memory.

workedExamples.title: Bound async work and preserve cancellation
workedExamples.code:
async def fetch_all(urls):
    limit = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
    async def one(url):
        async with limit:
            async with asyncio.timeout(2):
                return await client.get_bytes(url)
    async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as group:
        tasks = [group.create_task(one(url)) for url in urls]
    return [task.result() for task in tasks]
workedExamples.explanation: The semaphore bounds downstream concurrency, timeout gives each operation a deadline, and TaskGroup owns child lifetimes so failure cancels siblings and awaits cleanup.

questions.prompt: Is Python pass-by-value or pass-by-reference? Demonstrate the real model.
questions.answer: Python uses call-by-sharing: an object reference is passed by value. The parameter initially names the same object. Mutating that object is visible through aliases, while rebinding the parameter changes only the local name.
questions.whyTricky: Candidates invent separate rules for lists and integers from observed mutability.

questions.prompt: Why is a mutable default argument shared across calls?
questions.answer: Default expressions run once when def executes, and the object is stored with the function. Each omitted argument binds to that object. Use an immutable sentinel such as None and create per-call mutable state inside.
questions.whyTricky: The default appears in the signature and is assumed to run at call time.

questions.prompt: Differentiate __getattr__, __getattribute__, properties, and descriptors.
questions.answer: __getattribute__ participates in every instance lookup; __getattr__ is a fallback. property is a data descriptor. Descriptors define __get__, __set__, or __delete__ and participate in precedence with instance state and MRO; functions are descriptors that bind methods.
questions.whyTricky: Framework magic is memorized without the lookup order.

questions.prompt: What happens when a generator yields, and when is finally run?
questions.answer: yield returns a value and suspends the frame with its position and locals. It resumes on next, send, or throw. finally runs on completion, exception, explicit close, or finalization, but critical resources need explicit owning contexts.
questions.whyTricky: Generators are described as list replacements, hiding suspended frames and cleanup lifetime.

questions.prompt: Why does CPU-heavy work block asyncio, and how should it be handled?
questions.answer: The event loop runs task continuations until they await. CPU-heavy Python code does not yield, so timers and sockets wait. Reduce or chunk work, use processes for Python CPU tasks, or use appropriate vectorized/native code.
questions.whyTricky: async syntax is confused with preemptive scheduling and parallelism.

questions.prompt: Does the GIL remove the need for locks?
questions.answer: No. The GIL is an interpreter mechanism, not an application invariant lock. Workflows span bytecodes, invoke user code, release during I/O/native work, and interleave between check and action. Use locks, queues, immutability, confinement, transactions, or redesign.
questions.whyTricky: Some built-in operations appear atomic in one CPython version and are generalized.

questions.prompt: Why can a circular import expose a missing attribute?
questions.answer: Python inserts a module in sys.modules before finishing its top-level code. In a cycle, the peer receives that partially initialized object, so names defined later are absent. Move shared contracts or reduce import-time coupling.
questions.whyTricky: Import is viewed as textual inclusion rather than cached execution.

questions.prompt: When is shallow copy correct, and why can deepcopy be dangerous?

questions.whyTricky: Copy depth is treated as a more-is-safer setting.

theorySections.title: Values, coercion, equality, and identity
theorySections.explanation: JavaScript has primitive values and objects. Variables hold values, and an object value behaves as a reference to object identity. Strict equality compares primitives according to specified value rules and objects by identity; Object.is differs for NaN and signed zero. Abstract equality runs a coercion algorithm that can cross type boundaries. Truthiness is another conversion and must not be used when zero, empty string, false, null, and undefined carry different domain meanings.
theorySections.plainEnglish: JavaScript variables contain primitive values or object references, and its comparison operators follow different, precisely defined rules rather than one universal idea of equality.
theorySections.analogy: Imagine a form desk that sometimes compares the writing exactly and sometimes converts both answers into a standard form first; an object comparison instead asks whether two tickets point to the same stored file.
theorySections.analogyLimit: The language's coercion steps, NaN, signed zero, Symbols, and reference identity follow formal algorithms that an everyday form desk cannot predict by intuition.
theorySections.concreteExample: 0 == false is true after coercion, 0 === false is false because the types differ, and Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true even though NaN === NaN is false.
keyPoints: Prefer explicit domain normalization over relying on abstract equality.
typeof null is a historical result, not evidence that null is an ordinary object.
NaN is unequal to itself under ===; use Number.isNaN for numeric validation.
Object spread is shallow and invokes specified property enumeration semantics.

theorySections.title: Lexical scope, closures, and execution context
theorySections.explanation: Lexical scope is determined by source nesting. Every function creation captures access to its surrounding lexical environment, not a frozen copy of each value. A closure can therefore preserve private state or retain large object graphs. Function calls create execution contexts, and this is selected by the call expression, explicit binding, construction, or lexical capture in an arrow function. var has function scope and initialization behavior distinct from let and const.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A function keeps access to the live bindings around the place where it was created, while ordinary-function this depends on how that function is called.
theorySections.analogy: A closure carries a backstage pass to labelled storage drawers from its original theatre, even after the original scene has ended.
theorySections.analogyLimit: The pass reaches live bindings rather than frozen photographs, and this, var hoisting, temporal dead zones, and garbage collection have separate language rules.
theorySections.concreteExample: Callbacks created in a loop with let each see their iteration's binding, while callbacks sharing one var binding all observe its final changed value.
keyPoints: Closures capture bindings, so later rebinding can be observed.
let and const are block scoped and inaccessible in the temporal dead zone before initialization.
Arrow functions do not define their own this, arguments, or constructor behavior.
Method extraction can lose its receiver because call-site form determines this.

theorySections.title: Objects, prototypes, classes, and property semantics
theorySections.explanation: An object owns properties with value or accessor descriptors. If an own property is absent, lookup delegates through the object's prototype chain. class syntax defines methods, initialization order, private fields, and inheritance rules but does not replace prototype delegation. Assignment, Object.defineProperty, spread, and Proxy traps have different descriptor and side-effect behavior, so copying syntax is not a universal clone operation.
theorySections.plainEnglish: An object first checks its own properties and then follows a prototype link for missing ones; class syntax organizes this machinery but does not replace it.
theorySections.analogy: A device checks its local instruction card and, if an instruction is absent, consults a linked reference manual belonging to its model.
theorySections.analogyLimit: JavaScript lookup can involve accessors, descriptors, private brands, proxies, mutation, and several prototype levels, so it is not simple document inheritance.
theorySections.concreteExample: An instance can shadow an inherited property with its own value, while deleting that own value reveals the prototype's value again.
keyPoints: Own properties and inherited properties answer different questions.
Object.create chooses a prototype without invoking a class constructor.
Private fields are lexically branded and are not ordinary string-keyed properties.
Enumeration, writability, configurability, getters, and setters are separate property concerns.

theorySections.title: Event loop, jobs, tasks, and asynchronous control flow
theorySections.explanation: A JavaScript job runs to completion before another job runs on the same agent. Promise reactions enqueue microtasks or jobs that run at defined checkpoints, commonly before the host selects another timer or I/O task. async functions return promises, and await suspends the function while scheduling its continuation. Concurrency is created by overlapping host operations, not by await itself. Correct systems bound fan-out and propagate deadlines, cancellation, errors, and cleanup.
theorySections.plainEnglish: One JavaScript job runs until it finishes; promise continuations wait in a high-priority job queue, while the host later selects timers, input, rendering, and I/O work.
theorySections.analogy: A clerk finishes the current customer, empties a tray of promised follow-up notes, and only then calls the next appointment from the building's schedule.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Browsers and Node.js have different host phases, workers use separate agents, and exact fairness or timing is not guaranteed by the clerk picture.
theorySections.concreteExample: A resolved Promise.then callback runs after the current stack but before a zero-delay timer, while a long synchronous loop delays both.
keyPoints: Promise callbacks do not interrupt currently running JavaScript.
A long synchronous callback blocks timers, input, rendering, and other continuations on that agent.
Promise.all fails fast but does not cancel sibling work automatically.
Microtask loops can starve timers or rendering even though each callback is short.

theorySections.title: Modules, packages, and runtime boundaries
theorySections.explanation: ES modules use URL-like identity, static import/export structure, live bindings, and asynchronous loading capabilities. CommonJS loads through runtime require and exports object conventions. Package exports and conditions define public entry points for environments such as import, require, browser, or Node.js. A bundler may transform or replace resolution behavior, so successful bundling does not prove that direct runtime loading follows the same path.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Modules connect named live bindings, while package metadata and the actual loader decide which file and environment those names resolve to.
theorySections.analogy: A switchboard wires a caller to a live extension instead of photocopying every future conversation, and a directory decides which extension a name means.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Cyclic initialization, top-level await, package conditions, URL identity, bundlers, and CommonJS interoperability make the real module graph more complex.
theorySections.concreteExample: An imported counter binding reflects later changes made by its exporting module, but assigning to that imported name is forbidden.
keyPoints: ES module imports are live read-only views of exported bindings.
A module is normally evaluated once per resolved identity, not once per source text.
Circular dependencies expose initialization ordering and temporal-dead-zone behavior.
Browser code and server code have different trust, secrets, filesystem, and API boundaries.

theorySections.title: Memory, performance, and security
theorySections.explanation: Reachability from roots determines whether objects can be collected. Closures, listeners, caches, module state, timers, and DOM references can retain otherwise useless graphs. Engine optimization depends on observed shapes and types and may deoptimize when behavior changes. Security follows data from an untrusted source to a context-sensitive sink; type checks and escaping for one context do not make data safe for another.
theorySections.plainEnglish: The collector removes unreachable objects, engines optimize observed hot behavior, and security depends on keeping untrusted data away from dangerous context-specific operations.
theorySections.analogy: A warehouse keeps every box reachable from an active inventory chain, rearranges frequently used aisles, and requires hazardous deliveries to pass the correct inspection station.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Reachability roots, JIT speculation, deoptimization, DOM retention, and HTML, URL, SQL, or shell contexts each follow technical rules the warehouse cannot model fully.
theorySections.concreteExample: A removed DOM node still leaks when a long-lived listener retains it, and placing a validated string into innerHTML can still create XSS because string type is not HTML safety.
keyPoints: A managed heap can still leak through unintended reachability.
Measure retained size and root paths, not only allocation count.
Stable object shapes can help engines, but architecture and algorithms dominate most application performance.
Use safe APIs and context-aware encoding rather than blacklist filtering.

misconceptions.claim: const makes an object immutable.
misconceptions.correction: const prevents rebinding that variable; the referenced object's properties may still mutate unless an immutability policy is applied.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Variable binding and object state are both casually described as the value.

misconceptions.claim: JavaScript is asynchronous and multi-threaded by default.
misconceptions.correction: A job runs to completion on its agent; hosts overlap I/O and may provide workers with separate agents and communication boundaries.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Many operations complete later, so host concurrency is mistaken for simultaneous execution of one call stack.

misconceptions.claim: await blocks the thread until the promise resolves.
misconceptions.correction: await suspends the async function and returns control; its continuation is scheduled after settlement while other work can run.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: The syntax resembles synchronous blocking code.

misconceptions.claim: Promise.all runs functions in parallel.
misconceptions.correction: It observes promises; operations normally begin when their promises are created, and actual parallelism depends on the host and workload.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: A single combinator appears to be the place where concurrency starts.

misconceptions.claim: Classes replace prototypes.
misconceptions.correction: Class instances still delegate through prototypes; class syntax adds defined construction, private fields, and method semantics.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: The syntax resembles class-based languages.

misconceptions.claim: Garbage collection prevents memory leaks.
misconceptions.correction: Collectors reclaim unreachable values; listeners, caches, closures, timers, and module roots can retain useless graphs.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Leaks are incorrectly defined only as forgotten manual deallocation.

revisionChecklist: Distinguish primitive values, object identity, equality variants, truthiness, nullishness, and explicit coercion.
Explain lexical scope, closure binding capture, temporal dead zones, var hoisting, and this selection.
Trace own property lookup, descriptors, prototypes, class initialization, and method extraction.
Order synchronous code, promise microtasks, timers, rendering, and Node.js host phases without relying on slogans.
Design async work with bounded concurrency, cancellation, timeouts, rejection ownership, and cleanup.
Compare ESM and CommonJS identity, live bindings, cycles, package exports, and runtime/bundler resolution.
Use browser or Node debugging, source maps, CPU profiles, heap snapshots, and event-loop diagnostics appropriately.
Explain engine profiling, shapes, JIT optimization, deoptimization, and why microbenchmarks can mislead.
Prevent XSS, injection, prototype pollution, unsafe redirects, secret exposure, and dependency compromise.
Choose browser, Node.js, worker, stream, and native boundaries from workload and trust constraints.
setup: Install a supported Node.js release and verify node, npm or pnpm, and the lockfile agree with the project's declared engine policy.
Set package type and module entry points explicitly instead of relying on filename or tool defaults that differ between ESM and CommonJS.
Enable strict linting, formatting, a test runner, and source maps; keep browser and Node.js globals distinct in configuration.
Use a project-local package manager through the committed lockfile and inspect lifecycle scripts before installing untrusted dependencies.
Run one module, one test, one debugger session, and one production build before changing application behavior.
runtime: JavaScript executes run-to-completion jobs on an agent; the host event loop schedules later tasks, promise jobs, rendering, and I/O callbacks.
Lexical environments bind names, closures retain reachable environments, and this is chosen by call form rather than lexical location except for arrow functions.
Objects delegate missing property lookup through prototype chains, while classes provide syntax and semantics over constructor/prototype machinery.
Modern engines parse and execute code through interpreter or baseline tiers, collect profiles, optimize hot paths, and deoptimize when assumptions fail.
Browser and Node.js hosts expose different APIs and scheduling phases even though the ECMAScript language core is shared.
testing: Test pure transformations synchronously, async policy with controlled promises or clocks, and host boundaries with realistic browser or server integrations.
Assert rejection, cancellation, timeout, duplicate delivery, partial response, and cleanup behavior rather than only fulfilled promise values.
Use fake timers only when the test owns every relevant clock; they do not automatically control I/O, promise queues, or host scheduling.
Run browser-level tests for DOM, navigation, accessibility, storage, security policy, and rendering behavior that a DOM mock cannot reproduce.
debugging: Read the first relevant stack and preserve Error causes; source maps must match the deployed artifact before line numbers are trusted.
Use breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, watch expressions, and async stack traces to locate the first incorrect state or ordering assumption.
Inspect the browser network waterfall or Node.js diagnostics before attributing waiting time to JavaScript CPU.
Use CPU profiles, allocation/heap snapshots, event-loop-delay metrics, and retained paths for separate performance questions.
For module problems, inspect resolved URLs/files, package exports, package type, conditions, and the actual runtime or bundler resolution trace.
performance: Improve algorithms, round trips, payload size, rendering work, and batching before syntax-level micro-optimization.
Separate JavaScript CPU, event-loop queueing, garbage collection, layout/paint, network, database, and downstream waits.
Bound promise concurrency and stream buffering; Promise.all starts no work itself but can await an already unbounded set of operations.
Measure representative warm and cold paths because JIT state, caches, bundles, and connection reuse change behavior.
security: Treat HTML, URLs, DOM sinks, templates, SQL, shell arguments, object merges, redirects, and deserialization as explicit untrusted boundaries.
Prevent XSS with context-aware encoding, safe DOM APIs, trusted sanitization, and a restrictive Content Security Policy where applicable.
Block prototype-pollution keys and avoid recursively merging attacker-controlled objects into privileged configuration.
Audit package provenance and install scripts, minimize dependencies, pin resolutions, and never ship server secrets into browser bundles.
failureModes: Loose coercion or truthiness collapses distinct states such as zero, empty string, false, null, undefined, and NaN.
A closure, listener, timer, cache, detached DOM tree, or unresolved work retains an object graph indefinitely.
An async callback is launched without awaiting, cancellation, rejection handling, concurrency bounds, or ownership of its lifetime.
Promise microtask ordering is confused with timers or I/O tasks, producing starvation or stale-state races.
ESM/CommonJS, browser/Node.js, or bundler/runtime resolution differences load duplicate, incompatible, or unintended modules.
Untrusted data reaches an HTML, command, query, URL, or object-merge sink and becomes injection or prototype pollution.

workedExamples.title: Preserve zero while defaulting only missing values
workedExamples.explanation: Nullish coalescing defaults only null or undefined. Using input || 25 would incorrectly replace the valid value zero because zero is falsy.

workedExamples.title: Bound asynchronous fan-out
workedExamples.explanation: Only limit workers are active, results preserve input order, and rejection reaches the caller. A production version should also define cancellation, retry, deadline, and partial-result policy.

workedExamples.title: Avoid losing a method receiver
workedExamples.explanation: The arrow field captures the instance this lexically, so extracting the callback keeps the receiver. A prototype method would require binding or a receiver-preserving call site.

questions.prompt: Compare ==, ===, and Object.is with examples that differ.
questions.answer: === avoids cross-type coercion, compares objects by identity, treats NaN as unequal to itself, and treats +0 and -0 as equal. Object.is keeps identity/value comparison but treats NaN as equal to itself and signed zeros as different. == follows an abstract coercion algorithm and should be used only with deliberate knowledge of its cases.
questions.whyTricky: The answer is often reduced to 'always use triple equals' without understanding edge semantics.

questions.prompt: What does a closure capture: values or variables?
questions.answer: A closure retains access to lexical environment bindings. If the binding is later reassigned, the closure observes the new value. Per-iteration let creates a fresh binding, while var in one function scope historically caused loop callbacks to share one changing binding.
questions.whyTricky: A closure is described as a frozen snapshot even though bindings remain live.

questions.prompt: Predict the order of synchronous logs, Promise.then, queueMicrotask, and setTimeout.
questions.answer: Run the current job synchronously. Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks enter the microtask queue in enqueue order and run at the checkpoint after the stack empties. A timer callback is a later host task after its delay threshold and after earlier microtasks. Exact host phases beyond ECMAScript jobs must be identified for browser or Node.js.
questions.whyTricky: Timers are interpreted as exact delays and microtasks as separate threads.
rubric: Orders microtasks before the next timer task.
Separates language guarantees from host phases.

questions.prompt: Why does extracting an object method sometimes make this undefined?
questions.answer: For ordinary functions, this is selected by call form. obj.method() supplies obj as receiver, while const f = obj.method; f() is a plain call and under strict semantics has undefined this. Bind the method, wrap the call, or use a deliberate lexical arrow callback where appropriate.
questions.whyTricky: this is assumed to be captured from the method's definition location.

questions.prompt: Does Promise.all cancel remaining requests after one rejects?
questions.answer: No. The aggregate rejects after the first observed rejection, but sibling operations continue unless they support and receive cancellation. Use AbortController or another cancellation protocol, still observe cleanup and later failures, and define partial-result semantics.
questions.whyTricky: Fail-fast aggregate state is confused with stopping underlying work.
rubric: Mentions cleanup or sibling result ownership.

questions.prompt: Explain an ES module circular dependency without saying imports are copied.
questions.answer: Imports are live read-only bindings to exporter state. Modules are instantiated to connect bindings before evaluation, then evaluated in dependency order. In a cycle, a binding may exist but remain uninitialized, causing a temporal-dead-zone error if read too early. Refactor initialization or shared contracts rather than relying on side-effect order.
questions.whyTricky: Modules are modeled as textual inclusion or object copying.

questions.prompt: How do you diagnose a JavaScript memory leak?
questions.answer: Confirm post-GC retained memory grows under comparable workload, take heap snapshots or allocation profiles, compare dominators and retained sizes, follow paths to roots, then identify the missing lifecycle cleanup. Common roots include listeners, timers, caches, closures, module state, and detached DOM nodes.
questions.whyTricky: High allocation rate or a large heap is treated as proof of a leak.
rubric: Connects a root to lifecycle ownership.

questions.prompt: Why is assigning untrusted input to innerHTML dangerous when JSON parsing succeeded?
questions.answer: JSON parsing establishes data syntax, not HTML safety. innerHTML is an HTML parser sink where attacker-controlled markup and event-capable content may execute. Use textContent for text, safe DOM construction, or a maintained context-appropriate sanitizer plus defense-in-depth CSP.
questions.whyTricky: Successful parsing or type shape is mistaken for output-context encoding.
rubric: Separates data parsing from sink safety.
Names a safe API or sanitizer.

A live read-only binding to an export, connected before module evaluation.
