theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Kotlin adds null-safety, expression-oriented syntax, and coroutines while targeting JVM bytecode and interoperating with Java types and libraries. A rigorous model identifies program, module, function, type, and value, the invariant each unit owns, and the module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with null safety smart casts and type system and data sealed and value classes; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Kotlin operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through null safety smart casts and type system, across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: null safety smart casts and type system
data sealed and value classes
Define invariants for the program, module, function, type, and value.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Kotlin distributes state across values, references, owned resources, and module state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to collections sequences and extension functions; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow collections sequences and extension functions from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: collections sequences and extension functions
Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Kotlin lifecycle is parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. JVM interop and platform types is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for JVM interop and platform types that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: JVM interop and platform types
parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Kotlin involves threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. coroutines suspending functions and structured concurrency must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around coroutines suspending functions and structured concurrency. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: coroutines suspending functions and structured concurrency
threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Kotlin should mirror pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For flows channels and cancellation, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for flows channels and cancellation: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: flows channels and cancellation
pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. For DSLs delegation and inline functions, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving DSLs delegation and inline functions with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: DSLs delegation and inline functions
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Kotlin decomposes algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. Gradle testing and Android boundaries should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for Gradle testing and Android boundaries showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: Gradle testing and Android boundaries
algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Kotlin combines parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Kotlin deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces
source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Kotlin is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the program, module, function, type, and value, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Kotlin build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Kotlin code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Kotlin faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Kotlin defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Kotlin deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Kotlin mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (program, module, function, type, and value) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain null safety smart casts and type system, data sealed and value classes, collections sequences and extension functions, and JVM interop and platform types with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around coroutines suspending functions and structured concurrency.
Design tests across pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose DSLs delegation and inline functions from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Kotlin from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Kotlin adds null-safety, expression-oriented syntax, and coroutines while targeting JVM bytecode and interoperating with Java types and libraries. The principal execution vocabulary is program, module, function, type, and value.
Trace state explicitly across values, references, owned resources, and module state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.
Integration crosses module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Kotlin; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around collections sequences and extension functions creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Kotlin version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For JVM interop and platform types, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Kotlin.
Decompose algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Kotlin behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around null safety smart casts and type system creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.
Incorrect ownership of values, references, owned resources, and module state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to DSLs delegation and inline functions breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Kotlin slice
workedExamples.code: // Kotlin: express the smallest complete program and make ownership explicit.
workedExamples.explanation: Start with the execution model, then introduce abstractions only when they preserve a named invariant. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to null safety smart casts and type system and data sealed and value classes.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Core policy remains testable while Kotlin-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, especially around collections sequences and extension functions.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Kotlin
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates JVM interop and platform types with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with program, module, function, type, and value; trace parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up; identify values, references, owned resources, and module state; cross module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: compare null safety smart casts and type system with data sealed and value classes.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Kotlin, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: build a test strategy for flows channels and cancellation.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around collections sequences and extension functions, one saturation failure around algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, and one integration or compatibility failure at module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: optimize Gradle testing and Android boundaries without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Kotlin only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Kotlin: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Swift is a programming language: a precise way to describe data and the steps a computer should perform.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can write programs, reason about their behavior, and explain why one implementation is safer or faster than another. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Swift like a written language for a very literal teammate: grammar matters, every instruction has a meaning, and missing details become bugs. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: check swift using `swift --version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Swift combines value semantics, reference types, ARC, protocol-oriented design, and structured concurrency for Apple and server runtimes. A rigorous model identifies program, module, function, type, and value, the invariant each unit owns, and the module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with value and reference semantics and optionals enums protocols and generics; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Swift operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through value and reference semantics, across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: value and reference semantics
optionals enums protocols and generics
Define invariants for the program, module, function, type, and value.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Swift distributes state across values, references, owned resources, and module state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to ARC ownership weak and unowned references; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow ARC ownership weak and unowned references from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: ARC ownership weak and unowned references
Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Swift lifecycle is parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. copy-on-write collections is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for copy-on-write collections that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: copy-on-write collections
parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Swift involves threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. errors results and resource lifetime must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around errors results and resource lifetime. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: errors results and resource lifetime
threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Swift should mirror pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For async await actors and Sendable, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for async await actors and Sendable: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: async await actors and Sendable
pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. For Swift Package Manager and modules, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving Swift Package Manager and modules with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: Swift Package Manager and modules
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Swift decomposes algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. ABI resilience and Objective-C interop should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for ABI resilience and Objective-C interop showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: ABI resilience and Objective-C interop
algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Swift combines parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Swift deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces
source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Swift is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the program, module, function, type, and value, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Swift build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Swift code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Swift faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Swift defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Swift deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

Define the core units (program, module, function, type, and value) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain value and reference semantics, optionals enums protocols and generics, ARC ownership weak and unowned references, and copy-on-write collections with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around errors results and resource lifetime.
Design tests across pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose Swift Package Manager and modules from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Swift from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Swift combines value semantics, reference types, ARC, protocol-oriented design, and structured concurrency for Apple and server runtimes. The principal execution vocabulary is program, module, function, type, and value.
Trace state explicitly across values, references, owned resources, and module state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.
Integration crosses module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Swift; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around ARC ownership weak and unowned references creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Swift version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For copy-on-write collections, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Swift.
Decompose algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Swift behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around value and reference semantics creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.
Incorrect ownership of values, references, owned resources, and module state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to Swift Package Manager and modules breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Swift slice
workedExamples.code: // Swift: express the smallest complete program and make ownership explicit.
workedExamples.explanation: Start with the execution model, then introduce abstractions only when they preserve a named invariant. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to value and reference semantics and optionals enums protocols and generics.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Core policy remains testable while Swift-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, especially around ARC ownership weak and unowned references.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Swift
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates copy-on-write collections with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Swift: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with program, module, function, type, and value; trace parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up; identify values, references, owned resources, and module state; cross module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Swift: compare value and reference semantics with optionals enums protocols and generics.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Swift, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Swift: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Swift: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Swift: build a test strategy for async await actors and Sendable.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Swift: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Swift: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around ARC ownership weak and unowned references, one saturation failure around algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, and one integration or compatibility failure at module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Swift: optimize ABI resilience and Objective-C interop without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Swift: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Swift: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Swift: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Swift only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Swift: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: PHP is a programming language: a precise way to describe data and the steps a computer should perform.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can write programs, reason about their behavior, and explain why one implementation is safer or faster than another. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of PHP like a written language for a very literal teammate: grammar matters, every instruction has a meaning, and missing details become bugs. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: check php using `php --version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

the system that executes the program
reusable code that your program can call

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: PHP evaluates request-scoped scripts in a server runtime, combining dynamic values, a broad standard library, and process-managed concurrency. A rigorous model identifies program, module, function, type, and value, the invariant each unit owns, and the module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with request lifecycle and PHP-FPM workers and dynamic types arrays objects and references; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things PHP operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through request lifecycle and PHP-FPM workers, across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: request lifecycle and PHP-FPM workers
dynamic types arrays objects and references
Define invariants for the program, module, function, type, and value.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: PHP distributes state across values, references, owned resources, and module state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to namespaces autoloading and Composer; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow namespaces autoloading and Composer from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: namespaces autoloading and Composer
Classify values, references, owned resources, and module state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The PHP lifecycle is parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. exceptions errors and resource handling is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for exceptions errors and resource handling that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: exceptions errors and resource handling
parse or type-check, compile or interpret, load, execute, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in PHP involves threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. sessions cookies and HTTP boundaries must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around sessions cookies and HTTP boundaries. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: sessions cookies and HTTP boundaries
threads, tasks, event loops, processes, synchronization, cancellation, and memory visibility
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing PHP should mirror pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For PDO parameterization and persistence, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for PDO parameterization and persistence: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: PDO parameterization and persistence
pure policy, module contract, runtime integration, and end-to-end behavior
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across module, function, foreign-function, file, process, and network boundary. For opcache memory and process isolation, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving opcache memory and process isolation with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: opcache memory and process isolation
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on PHP decomposes algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. PSRs testing and deployment should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for PSRs testing and deployment showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: PSRs testing and deployment
algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production PHP combines parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one PHP deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: parsers, deserializers, queries, files, subprocesses, dependencies, and native interfaces
source, dependency lock, binary or package, and debug symbols
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: PHP is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the program, module, function, type, and value, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful PHP build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest PHP code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide algorithmic work, allocation, locality, synchronization, and I/O; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes PHP faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: PHP defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a PHP deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.
