theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: The browser parses HTML into structure, CSS into presentation rules, and JavaScript into behavior while the event loop, rendering pipeline, and security model coordinate the page. A rigorous model identifies document element, style rule, event, request, response, storage entry, and render frame, the invariant each unit owns, and the origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with semantic HTML and accessibility tree and CSS cascade specificity layout and containment; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things HTML, CSS, and Web APIs operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through semantic HTML and accessibility tree, across origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: semantic HTML and accessibility tree
CSS cascade specificity layout and containment
Define invariants for the document element, style rule, event, request, response, storage entry, and render frame.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs distributes state across DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to DOM events and event delegation; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow DOM events and event delegation from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: DOM events and event delegation
Classify DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The HTML, CSS, and Web APIs lifecycle is navigate, parse, style, layout, paint, composite, interact, suspend, restore, and unload. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. browser event loop tasks and microtasks is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for browser event loop tasks and microtasks that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: browser event loop tasks and microtasks
navigate, parse, style, layout, paint, composite, interact, suspend, restore, and unload
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in HTML, CSS, and Web APIs involves tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, workers, streams, cancellation, and browser scheduling. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. rendering pipeline and web performance must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around rendering pipeline and web performance. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: rendering pipeline and web performance
tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, workers, streams, cancellation, and browser scheduling
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing HTML, CSS, and Web APIs should mirror semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For HTTP caching storage and service workers, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for HTTP caching storage and service workers: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: HTTP caching storage and service workers
semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API. For same-origin policy CORS CSP and Trusted Types, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving same-origin policy CORS CSP and Trusted Types with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: same-origin policy CORS CSP and Trusted Types
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on HTML, CSS, and Web APIs decomposes network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. progressive enhancement and responsive design should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for progressive enhancement and responsive design showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: progressive enhancement and responsive design
network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production HTML, CSS, and Web APIs combines origin, URL, DOM sink, message, storage, permission, CSP, CORS, and dependency with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundle, assets, service worker, source maps, and headers; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one HTML, CSS, and Web APIs deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: origin, URL, DOM sink, message, storage, permission, CSP, CORS, and dependency
HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundle, assets, service worker, source maps, and headers
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the document element, style rule, event, request, response, storage entry, and render frame, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful HTML, CSS, and Web APIs build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest HTML, CSS, and Web APIs code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes HTML, CSS, and Web APIs faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a HTML, CSS, and Web APIs deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

Trace navigate, parse, style, layout, paint, composite, interact, suspend, restore, and unload for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain semantic HTML and accessibility tree, CSS cascade specificity layout and containment, DOM events and event delegation, and browser event loop tasks and microtasks with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around rendering pipeline and web performance.
Design tests across semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose same-origin policy CORS CSP and Trusted Types from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model origin, URL, DOM sink, message, storage, permission, CSP, CORS, and dependency with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install HTML, CSS, and Web APIs from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundle, assets, service worker, source maps, and headers, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: The browser parses HTML into structure, CSS into presentation rules, and JavaScript into behavior while the event loop, rendering pipeline, and security model coordinate the page. The principal execution vocabulary is document element, style rule, event, request, response, storage entry, and render frame.
Trace state explicitly across DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is navigate, parse, style, layout, paint, composite, interact, suspend, restore, and unload. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, workers, streams, cancellation, and browser scheduling; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of HTML, CSS, and Web APIs; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.
Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around DOM events and event delegation creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the HTML, CSS, and Web APIs version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For browser event loop tasks and microtasks, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing HTML, CSS, and Web APIs.
Decompose network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model origin, URL, DOM sink, message, storage, permission, CSP, CORS, and dependency; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes HTML, CSS, and Web APIs behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around semantic HTML and accessibility tree creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.
Incorrect ownership of DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, workers, streams, cancellation, and browser scheduling exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to same-origin policy CORS CSP and Trusted Types breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete HTML, CSS, and Web APIs slice
workedExamples.code: // HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: express the smallest complete program and make ownership explicit.
workedExamples.explanation: Start with the execution model, then introduce abstractions only when they preserve a named invariant. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to semantic HTML and accessibility tree and CSS cascade specificity layout and containment.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API. Core policy remains testable while HTML, CSS, and Web APIs-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey, especially around DOM events and event delegation.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for HTML, CSS, and Web APIs
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates browser event loop tasks and microtasks with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundle, assets, service worker, source maps, and headers and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with document element, style rule, event, request, response, storage entry, and render frame; trace navigate, parse, style, layout, paint, composite, interact, suspend, restore, and unload; identify DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache; cross origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: compare semantic HTML and accessibility tree with CSS cascade specificity layout and containment.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in HTML, CSS, and Web APIs, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify DOM, CSSOM, JavaScript heap, browser storage, accessibility tree, and network cache; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, workers, streams, cancellation, and browser scheduling; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: build a test strategy for HTTP caching storage and service workers.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around DOM events and event delegation, one saturation failure around network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code, and one integration or compatibility failure at origin, document, component, event, network request, storage, worker, and browser API. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: optimize progressive enhancement and responsive design without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile network waterfalls, main-thread work, style and layout, paint, memory, and third-party code, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around origin, URL, DOM sink, message, storage, permission, CSP, CORS, and dependency; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundle, assets, service worker, source maps, and headers, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose HTML, CSS, and Web APIs only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: HTML, CSS, and Web APIs: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, semantic markup, pure behavior, component, real browser, accessibility tree, and critical journey, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: React is a framework: a ready-made structure that calls your code at the right points while providing common application features.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can build a working application without recreating routing, lifecycle, configuration, and integration plumbing from scratch. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of React like a furnished workshop: the benches and tools are already placed, but you still need to understand their rules to build safely. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect package using `npm view react version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

technologies.mentalModel: React is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: React is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node, the invariant each unit owns, and the component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with components elements and reconciliation and props state and render purity; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things React operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through components elements and reconciliation, across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: components elements and reconciliation
props state and render purity
Define invariants for the component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: React distributes state across component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to hooks closures and dependency arrays; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow hooks closures and dependency arrays from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: hooks closures and dependency arrays
Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The React lifecycle is create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. controlled forms and event handling is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for controlled forms and event handling that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: controlled forms and event handling
create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in React involves render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. context reducers and external stores must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around context reducers and external stores. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: context reducers and external stores
render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing React should mirror pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For effects synchronization and cleanup, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for effects synchronization and cleanup: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: effects synchronization and cleanup
pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. For server rendering hydration and Suspense, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving server rendering hydration and Suspense with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: server rendering hydration and Suspense
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on React decomposes unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. profiling memoization and error boundaries should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for profiling memoization and error boundaries showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: profiling memoization and error boundaries
unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production React combines untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one React deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data
source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: React is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful React build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest React code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes React faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: React defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a React deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the React mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain components elements and reconciliation, props state and render purity, hooks closures and dependency arrays, and controlled forms and event handling with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around context reducers and external stores.
Design tests across pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose server rendering hydration and Suspense from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install React from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: React is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node.

Trace state explicitly across component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of React; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around hooks closures and dependency arrays creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the React version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For controlled forms and event handling, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing React.

Decompose unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes React behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around components elements and reconciliation creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to server rendering hydration and Suspense breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete React slice
workedExamples.code: // React: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to components elements and reconciliation and props state and render purity.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Core policy remains testable while React-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, especially around hooks closures and dependency arrays.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for React
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates controlled forms and event handling with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: React: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node; trace create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up; identify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; cross component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: React: compare components elements and reconciliation with props state and render purity.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in React, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: React: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: React: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: React: build a test strategy for effects synchronization and cleanup.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: React: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: React: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around hooks closures and dependency arrays, one saturation failure around unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, and one integration or compatibility failure at component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: React: optimize profiling memoization and error boundaries without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: React: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: React: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: React: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose React only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: React: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Next.js is a framework: a ready-made structure that calls your code at the right points while providing common application features.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can build a working application without recreating routing, lifecycle, configuration, and integration plumbing from scratch. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Next.js like a furnished workshop: the benches and tools are already placed, but you still need to understand their rules to build safely. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect package using `npm view next version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Next.js is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function, the invariant each unit owns, and the server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with App Router layouts pages and route segments and server and client component boundaries; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Next.js operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through App Router layouts pages and route segments, across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: App Router layouts pages and route segments
server and client component boundaries
Define invariants for the route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Next.js distributes state across route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to data fetching caching and revalidation; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow data fetching caching and revalidation from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: data fetching caching and revalidation
Classify route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Next.js lifecycle is match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. static dynamic and streaming rendering is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for static dynamic and streaming rendering that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: static dynamic and streaming rendering
match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Next.js involves parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. route handlers middleware and server actions must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around route handlers middleware and server actions. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: route handlers middleware and server actions
parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Next.js should mirror domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For metadata images and asset optimization, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for metadata images and asset optimization: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: metadata images and asset optimization
domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service. For authentication authorization and secret boundaries, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving authentication authorization and secret boundaries with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: authentication authorization and secret boundaries
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Next.js decomposes server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. deployment bundles observability and upgrades should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for deployment bundles observability and upgrades showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
