theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Nuxt is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function, the invariant each unit owns, and the server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with file-based routing layouts and middleware and server routes Nitro and deployment presets; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Nuxt operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through file-based routing layouts and middleware, across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: file-based routing layouts and middleware
server routes Nitro and deployment presets
Define invariants for the route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Nuxt distributes state across route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to universal data fetching and payloads; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow universal data fetching and payloads from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: universal data fetching and payloads
Classify route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Nuxt lifecycle is match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. SSR SSG ISR and hydration is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for SSR SSG ISR and hydration that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: SSR SSG ISR and hydration
match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Nuxt involves parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. composables plugins and runtime config must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around composables plugins and runtime config. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: composables plugins and runtime config
parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Nuxt should mirror domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For caching revalidation and edge behavior, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for caching revalidation and edge behavior: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: caching revalidation and edge behavior
domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service. For authentication and server-only secrets, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving authentication and server-only secrets with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: authentication and server-only secrets
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Nuxt decomposes server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. modules testing and observability should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for modules testing and observability showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: modules testing and observability
server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Nuxt combines route input, server-only secret, action or handler, cache key, rendered markup, authentication session, and deployment runtime with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source graph, dependency lock, server and client bundles, prerendered output, runtime configuration, and deployment image; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Nuxt deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: route input, server-only secret, action or handler, cache key, rendered markup, authentication session, and deployment runtime
source graph, dependency lock, server and client bundles, prerendered output, runtime configuration, and deployment image
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Nuxt is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Nuxt build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Nuxt code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Nuxt faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Nuxt defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Nuxt deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Nuxt mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.

Trace match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain file-based routing layouts and middleware, server routes Nitro and deployment presets, universal data fetching and payloads, and SSR SSG ISR and hydration with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around composables plugins and runtime config.
Design tests across domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose authentication and server-only secrets from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model route input, server-only secret, action or handler, cache key, rendered markup, authentication session, and deployment runtime with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Nuxt from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source graph, dependency lock, server and client bundles, prerendered output, runtime configuration, and deployment image, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Nuxt is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function.

Trace state explicitly across route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Nuxt; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around universal data fetching and payloads creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Nuxt version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For SSR SSG ISR and hydration, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Nuxt.

Decompose server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model route input, server-only secret, action or handler, cache key, rendered markup, authentication session, and deployment runtime; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Nuxt behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around file-based routing layouts and middleware creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to authentication and server-only secrets breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Nuxt slice
workedExamples.code: // Nuxt: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to file-based routing layouts and middleware and server routes Nitro and deployment presets.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service. Core policy remains testable while Nuxt-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation, especially around universal data fetching and payloads.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Nuxt
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates SSR SSG ISR and hydration with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source graph, dependency lock, server and client bundles, prerendered output, runtime configuration, and deployment image and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with route segment, layout, page, server module, client component, request, cache entry, and deployment function; trace match route, execute server work, fetch and cache data, stream or render output, hydrate client boundaries, navigate, revalidate, and deploy; identify route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state; cross server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: compare file-based routing layouts and middleware with server routes Nitro and deployment presets.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Nuxt, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify route parameters, request state, server data, client state, render cache, browser state, and persistent backend state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from parallel route work, streaming, asynchronous data, browser events, cancellation, background revalidation, and deployment capacity; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: build a test strategy for caching revalidation and edge behavior.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around universal data fetching and payloads, one saturation failure around server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts, and one integration or compatibility failure at server and client module, route handler, rendering mode, cache, edge or server runtime, browser, and external data service. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: optimize modules testing and observability without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile server and client waterfalls, cache misses, bundle size, serialization, hydration, database waits, and cold starts, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around route input, server-only secret, action or handler, cache key, rendered markup, authentication session, and deployment runtime; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source graph, dependency lock, server and client bundles, prerendered output, runtime configuration, and deployment image, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Nuxt only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Nuxt: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, domain policy, server module, route contract, rendered page, hydration boundary, and end-to-end navigation, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Svelte is a framework: a ready-made structure that calls your code at the right points while providing common application features.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can build a working application without recreating routing, lifecycle, configuration, and integration plumbing from scratch. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Svelte like a furnished workshop: the benches and tools are already placed, but you still need to understand their rules to build safely. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect package using `npm view svelte version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Svelte is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node, the invariant each unit owns, and the component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with compiled components and generated updates and runes reactivity and derived state; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Svelte operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through compiled components and generated updates, across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: compiled components and generated updates
runes reactivity and derived state
Define invariants for the component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Svelte distributes state across component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to props events bindings and snippets; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow props events bindings and snippets from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: props events bindings and snippets
Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Svelte lifecycle is create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. lifecycle effects and cleanup is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for lifecycle effects and cleanup that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: lifecycle effects and cleanup
create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Svelte involves render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. stores context and shared state must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around stores context and shared state. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: stores context and shared state
render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Svelte should mirror pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For actions transitions and accessibility, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for actions transitions and accessibility: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: actions transitions and accessibility
pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. For SSR hydration and client boundaries, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving SSR hydration and client boundaries with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: SSR hydration and client boundaries
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Svelte decomposes unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. compiler diagnostics profiling and testing should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for compiler diagnostics profiling and testing showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: compiler diagnostics profiling and testing
unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Svelte combines untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Svelte deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data
source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Svelte is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Svelte build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Svelte code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Svelte faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Svelte defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Svelte deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Svelte mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain compiled components and generated updates, runes reactivity and derived state, props events bindings and snippets, and lifecycle effects and cleanup with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around stores context and shared state.
Design tests across pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose SSR hydration and client boundaries from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Svelte from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Svelte is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node.

Trace state explicitly across component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.

The lifecycle is create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Svelte; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around props events bindings and snippets creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Svelte version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For lifecycle effects and cleanup, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Svelte.

Decompose unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Svelte behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around compiled components and generated updates creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to SSR hydration and client boundaries breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Svelte slice
workedExamples.code: // Svelte: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to compiled components and generated updates and runes reactivity and derived state.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Core policy remains testable while Svelte-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, especially around props events bindings and snippets.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Svelte
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates lifecycle effects and cleanup with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Svelte: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with component, element or view, prop or input, state value, event, effect, and rendered node; trace create render description, reconcile changes, commit visible output, run synchronization effects, handle events, and clean up; identify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; cross component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Svelte: compare compiled components and generated updates with runes reactivity and derived state.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Svelte, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Svelte: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify component-local state, derived state, shared client state, server state, URL state, form state, and DOM or native view state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Svelte: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from render scheduling, events, asynchronous data, transitions, cancellation, effects, workers, and main-thread capacity; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Svelte: build a test strategy for actions transitions and accessibility.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Svelte: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Svelte: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around props events bindings and snippets, one saturation failure around unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, and one integration or compatibility failure at component API, event handler, state store, router, browser or native API, data client, and server-rendering boundary. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Svelte: optimize compiler diagnostics profiling and testing without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile unnecessary renders, unstable identity, large trees, layout and paint, bundle loading, data waterfalls, and main-thread work, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Svelte: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around untrusted props and URLs, DOM sinks, rendered HTML, browser storage, navigation, third-party scripts, and server data; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Svelte: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source modules, dependency lock, client and server bundles, assets, source maps, and deployment headers, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Svelte: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Svelte only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Svelte: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, pure state logic, component behavior, accessibility semantics, browser integration, and critical user journey, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: SvelteKit is a framework: a ready-made structure that calls your code at the right points while providing common application features.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can build a working application without recreating routing, lifecycle, configuration, and integration plumbing from scratch. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of SvelteKit like a furnished workshop: the benches and tools are already placed, but you still need to understand their rules to build safely. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect package using `npm view @sveltejs/kit version`, observe the result, and explain what changed.
