theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Tokio is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle, the invariant each unit owns, and the task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with futures polling and wakers and runtime schedulers and task spawning; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Tokio operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through futures polling and wakers, across task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: futures polling and wakers
runtime schedulers and task spawning
Define invariants for the task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Tokio distributes state across task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to async I O reactors and readiness; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow async I O reactors and readiness from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: async I O reactors and readiness
Classify task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Tokio lifecycle is construct runtime, register work, poll or schedule, await readiness, cancel, drain, and shut down. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. ownership Send Sync and task boundaries is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for ownership Send Sync and task boundaries that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: ownership Send Sync and task boundaries
construct runtime, register work, poll or schedule, await readiness, cancel, drain, and shut down
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Tokio involves cooperative tasks, worker threads, work stealing, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. cancellation select and structured task lifetime must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around cancellation select and structured task lifetime. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: cancellation select and structured task lifetime
cooperative tasks, worker threads, work stealing, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Tokio should mirror future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For channels mutexes and backpressure, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for channels mutexes and backpressure: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: channels mutexes and backpressure
future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback. For blocking work and spawn_blocking, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving blocking work and spawn_blocking with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: blocking work and spawn_blocking
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Tokio decomposes blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. tracing testing and runtime tuning should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for tracing testing and runtime tuning showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: tracing testing and runtime tuning
blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Tokio combines network inputs, task-local identity, resource limits, dependencies, and unsafe or native interfaces with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of library crate or package, runtime configuration, executable, trace, and deployment image; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Tokio deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: network inputs, task-local identity, resource limits, dependencies, and unsafe or native interfaces
library crate or package, runtime configuration, executable, trace, and deployment image
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Tokio is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Tokio build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Tokio code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Tokio faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Tokio defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Tokio deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Tokio mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace construct runtime, register work, poll or schedule, await readiness, cancel, drain, and shut down for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain futures polling and wakers, runtime schedulers and task spawning, async I O reactors and readiness, and ownership Send Sync and task boundaries with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around cancellation select and structured task lifetime.
Design tests across future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose blocking work and spawn_blocking from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model network inputs, task-local identity, resource limits, dependencies, and unsafe or native interfaces with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Tokio from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped library crate or package, runtime configuration, executable, trace, and deployment image, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Tokio is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle.
Trace state explicitly across task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is construct runtime, register work, poll or schedule, await readiness, cancel, drain, and shut down. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves cooperative tasks, worker threads, work stealing, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Tokio; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.
Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around async I O reactors and readiness creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Tokio version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For ownership Send Sync and task boundaries, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Tokio.
Decompose blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model network inputs, task-local identity, resource limits, dependencies, and unsafe or native interfaces; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Tokio behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around futures polling and wakers creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.
Incorrect ownership of task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across cooperative tasks, worker threads, work stealing, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to blocking work and spawn_blocking breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test

questions.prompt: Tokio: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with task, future, executor, event source, channel, and resource handle; trace construct runtime, register work, poll or schedule, await readiness, cancel, drain, and shut down; identify task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources; cross task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.

rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Tokio: compare futures polling and wakers with runtime schedulers and task spawning.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Tokio, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Tokio: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify task state, queues, timers, registrations, buffers, and shared resources; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Tokio: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from cooperative tasks, worker threads, work stealing, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Tokio: build a test strategy for channels mutexes and backpressure.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Tokio: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Tokio: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around async I O reactors and readiness, one saturation failure around blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness, and one integration or compatibility failure at task spawn, async I/O, blocking pool, channel, synchronization primitive, and foreign callback. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Tokio: optimize tracing testing and runtime tuning without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile blocking on workers, queue growth, wakeups, contention, allocation, and I/O readiness, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Tokio: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around network inputs, task-local identity, resource limits, dependencies, and unsafe or native interfaces; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Tokio: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, library crate or package, runtime configuration, executable, trace, and deployment image, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Tokio: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Tokio only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Tokio: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, future state machine, scheduler-independent policy, timed integration, and shutdown behavior, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Axum is a framework: a ready-made structure that calls your code at the right points while providing common application features.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can build a working application without recreating routing, lifecycle, configuration, and integration plumbing from scratch. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Axum like a furnished workshop: the benches and tools are already placed, but you still need to understand their rules to build safely. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Axum is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware, the invariant each unit owns, and the router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with routers routes nesting and state and extractors request validation and rejection; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Axum operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through routers routes nesting and state, across router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: routers routes nesting and state
extractors request validation and rejection
Define invariants for the request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Axum distributes state across request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to handlers responses and IntoResponse; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow handlers responses and IntoResponse from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: handlers responses and IntoResponse
Classify request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Axum lifecycle is bootstrap, configure, accept work, invoke hooks, render or respond, and shut down. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. middleware towers and service layers is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for middleware towers and service layers that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: middleware towers and service layers
bootstrap, configure, accept work, invoke hooks, render or respond, and shut down
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Axum involves requests, asynchronous tasks, pools, cancellation, queues, and backpressure. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. async state concurrency and cancellation must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around async state concurrency and cancellation. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: async state concurrency and cancellation
requests, asynchronous tasks, pools, cancellation, queues, and backpressure
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Axum should mirror domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For authentication authorization and headers, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for authentication authorization and headers: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: authentication authorization and headers
domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service. For testing services without sockets, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving testing services without sockets with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: testing services without sockets
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Axum decomposes rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. tracing backpressure and graceful shutdown should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for tracing backpressure and graceful shutdown showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: tracing backpressure and graceful shutdown
rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Axum combines routing, validation, authentication, authorization, templates, persistence, and third-party calls with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source bundle, configuration, dependency lock, server or client build, and deployment image; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Axum deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: routing, validation, authentication, authorization, templates, persistence, and third-party calls
source bundle, configuration, dependency lock, server or client build, and deployment image
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Axum is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Axum build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Axum code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Axum faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Axum defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Axum deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Axum mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace bootstrap, configure, accept work, invoke hooks, render or respond, and shut down for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain routers routes nesting and state, extractors request validation and rejection, handlers responses and IntoResponse, and middleware towers and service layers with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around async state concurrency and cancellation.
Design tests across domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose testing services without sockets from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model routing, validation, authentication, authorization, templates, persistence, and third-party calls with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Axum from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source bundle, configuration, dependency lock, server or client build, and deployment image, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Axum is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware.
Trace state explicitly across request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is bootstrap, configure, accept work, invoke hooks, render or respond, and shut down. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves requests, asynchronous tasks, pools, cancellation, queues, and backpressure; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Axum; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around handlers responses and IntoResponse creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Axum version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For middleware towers and service layers, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Axum.
Decompose rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model routing, validation, authentication, authorization, templates, persistence, and third-party calls; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Axum behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around routers routes nesting and state creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.
Incorrect ownership of request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across requests, asynchronous tasks, pools, cancellation, queues, and backpressure exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to testing services without sockets breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Axum
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates middleware towers and service layers with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback

validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery

questions.prompt: Axum: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with request, component, controller, service, provider, and middleware; trace bootstrap, configure, accept work, invoke hooks, render or respond, and shut down; identify request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes; cross router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.

Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Axum: compare routers routes nesting and state with extractors request validation and rejection.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Axum, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Axum: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify request state, application state, persisted state, caches, and dependency scopes; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Axum: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from requests, asynchronous tasks, pools, cancellation, queues, and backpressure; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Axum: build a test strategy for authentication authorization and headers.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Axum: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Axum: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around handlers responses and IntoResponse, one saturation failure around rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits, and one integration or compatibility failure at router, component API, dependency container, persistence adapter, and external service. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Axum: optimize tracing backpressure and graceful shutdown without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile rendering or request waterfalls, serialization, queries, allocation, and downstream waits, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Axum: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around routing, validation, authentication, authorization, templates, persistence, and third-party calls; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Axum: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source bundle, configuration, dependency lock, server or client build, and deployment image, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Axum: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Axum only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Axum: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, domain policy, framework adapter, real integration, and critical user journey, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.
