theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: MySQL is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, the invariant each unit owns, and the client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes and transactions MVCC and locking reads; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things MySQL operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes, across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes
transactions MVCC and locking reads
Define invariants for the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: MySQL distributes state across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The MySQL lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. redo undo binlog and crash recovery is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for redo undo binlog and crash recovery that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: redo undo binlog and crash recovery
parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in MySQL involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. isolation gap locks and deadlocks must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around isolation gap locks and deadlocks. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: isolation gap locks and deadlocks
transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing MySQL should mirror query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For replication GTIDs and failover, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for replication GTIDs and failover: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: replication GTIDs and failover
query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. For partitioning backups and online DDL, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving partitioning backups and online DDL with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: partitioning backups and online DDL
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on MySQL decomposes cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. users privileges TLS and monitoring should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for users privileges TLS and monitoring showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: users privileges TLS and monitoring
cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production MySQL combines authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one MySQL deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups
schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: MySQL is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful MySQL build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest MySQL code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes MySQL faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: MySQL defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a MySQL deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the MySQL mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes, transactions MVCC and locking reads, optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins, and redo undo binlog and crash recovery with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around isolation gap locks and deadlocks.
Design tests across query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose partitioning backups and online DDL from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install MySQL from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: MySQL is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.

Trace state explicitly across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of MySQL; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the MySQL version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For redo undo binlog and crash recovery, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing MySQL.
Decompose cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes MySQL behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to partitioning backups and online DDL breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.code: // MySQL: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes and transactions MVCC and locking reads.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Core policy remains testable while MySQL-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, especially around optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for MySQL
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates redo undo binlog and crash recovery with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: MySQL: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica; trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover; identify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; cross client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: MySQL: compare InnoDB pages clustered indexes and secondary indexes with transactions MVCC and locking reads.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in MySQL, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: MySQL: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: MySQL: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: MySQL: build a test strategy for replication GTIDs and failover.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: MySQL: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: MySQL: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around optimizer statistics EXPLAIN and joins, one saturation failure around cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, and one integration or compatibility failure at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: MySQL: optimize users privileges TLS and monitoring without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: MySQL: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: MySQL: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: MySQL: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose MySQL only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: MySQL: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: SQLite is a database system: software that stores data, finds it again, and protects correctness when many operations happen together.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can design reliable data models, write efficient queries, and keep important information correct through failures and concurrent updates. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of SQLite like a carefully run library: data has an address, indexes speed up discovery, and borrowing rules prevent conflicting changes. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: SQLite is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, the invariant each unit owns, and the client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with embedded architecture and database files and dynamic typing affinity and constraints; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things SQLite operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through embedded architecture and database files, across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: embedded architecture and database files
dynamic typing affinity and constraints
Define invariants for the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: SQLite distributes state across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to B-tree pages indexes and query planner; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow B-tree pages indexes and query planner from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: B-tree pages indexes and query planner
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The SQLite lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. transactions rollback journal and WAL is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for transactions rollback journal and WAL that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: transactions rollback journal and WAL
parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in SQLite involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. locking concurrency and busy handling must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around locking concurrency and busy handling. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: locking concurrency and busy handling
transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing SQLite should mirror query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For foreign keys migrations and limits, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for foreign keys migrations and limits: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: foreign keys migrations and limits
query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. For backup integrity and corruption handling, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving backup integrity and corruption handling with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: backup integrity and corruption handling
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on SQLite decomposes cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. parameter binding extensions and deployment should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for parameter binding extensions and deployment showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: parameter binding extensions and deployment
cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production SQLite combines authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one SQLite deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups
schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: SQLite is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful SQLite build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest SQLite code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes SQLite faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: SQLite defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a SQLite deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the SQLite mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain embedded architecture and database files, dynamic typing affinity and constraints, B-tree pages indexes and query planner, and transactions rollback journal and WAL with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around locking concurrency and busy handling.
Design tests across query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose backup integrity and corruption handling from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install SQLite from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: SQLite is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.

Trace state explicitly across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of SQLite; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around B-tree pages indexes and query planner creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the SQLite version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For transactions rollback journal and WAL, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing SQLite.
Decompose cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes SQLite behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around embedded architecture and database files creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to backup integrity and corruption handling breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete SQLite slice
workedExamples.code: // SQLite: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to embedded architecture and database files and dynamic typing affinity and constraints.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Core policy remains testable while SQLite-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, especially around B-tree pages indexes and query planner.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for SQLite
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates transactions rollback journal and WAL with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: SQLite: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica; trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover; identify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; cross client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: SQLite: compare embedded architecture and database files with dynamic typing affinity and constraints.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in SQLite, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: SQLite: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: SQLite: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: SQLite: build a test strategy for foreign keys migrations and limits.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: SQLite: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: SQLite: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around B-tree pages indexes and query planner, one saturation failure around cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, and one integration or compatibility failure at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: SQLite: optimize parameter binding extensions and deployment without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: SQLite: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: SQLite: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: SQLite: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose SQLite only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: SQLite: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: SQL Server is a database system: software that stores data, finds it again, and protects correctness when many operations happen together.

theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through databases schemas types and constraints, across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
