theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Apache Cassandra is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, the invariant each unit owns, and the client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with partition keys clustering and query-first modeling and consistent hashing tokens and replicas; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Apache Cassandra operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through partition keys clustering and query-first modeling, across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: partition keys clustering and query-first modeling
consistent hashing tokens and replicas
Define invariants for the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Apache Cassandra distributes state across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to commit log memtables SSTables and compaction; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow commit log memtables SSTables and compaction from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: commit log memtables SSTables and compaction
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Apache Cassandra lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. tunable consistency and quorum math is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for tunable consistency and quorum math that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: tunable consistency and quorum math
parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Apache Cassandra involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. tombstones TTLs and read repair must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around tombstones TTLs and read repair. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: tombstones TTLs and read repair
transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Apache Cassandra should mirror query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For lightweight transactions and counters, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for lightweight transactions and counters: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: lightweight transactions and counters
query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. For repair backup and topology changes, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving repair backup and topology changes with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: repair backup and topology changes
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Apache Cassandra decomposes cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. capacity security and observability should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for capacity security and observability showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: capacity security and observability
cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Apache Cassandra combines authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Apache Cassandra deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups
schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Apache Cassandra is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Apache Cassandra build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Apache Cassandra code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Apache Cassandra faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Apache Cassandra defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Apache Cassandra deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Apache Cassandra mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain partition keys clustering and query-first modeling, consistent hashing tokens and replicas, commit log memtables SSTables and compaction, and tunable consistency and quorum math with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around tombstones TTLs and read repair.
Design tests across query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose repair backup and topology changes from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Apache Cassandra from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Apache Cassandra is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.

Trace state explicitly across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Apache Cassandra; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around commit log memtables SSTables and compaction creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Apache Cassandra version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For tunable consistency and quorum math, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Apache Cassandra.
Decompose cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Apache Cassandra behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around partition keys clustering and query-first modeling creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to repair backup and topology changes breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Apache Cassandra slice
workedExamples.code: // Apache Cassandra: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to partition keys clustering and query-first modeling and consistent hashing tokens and replicas.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Core policy remains testable while Apache Cassandra-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, especially around commit log memtables SSTables and compaction.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Apache Cassandra
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates tunable consistency and quorum math with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica; trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover; identify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; cross client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: compare partition keys clustering and query-first modeling with consistent hashing tokens and replicas.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Apache Cassandra, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: build a test strategy for lightweight transactions and counters.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around commit log memtables SSTables and compaction, one saturation failure around cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, and one integration or compatibility failure at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: optimize capacity security and observability without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Apache Cassandra only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Apache Cassandra: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Amazon DynamoDB is a database system: software that stores data, finds it again, and protects correctness when many operations happen together.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can design reliable data models, write efficient queries, and keep important information correct through failures and concurrent updates. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Amazon DynamoDB like a carefully run library: data has an address, indexes speed up discovery, and borrowing rules prevent conflicting changes. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect image using `docker image inspect amazon/dynamodb-local:latest`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, the invariant each unit owns, and the client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with items keys and access-pattern design and partitions adaptive capacity and hot keys; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Amazon DynamoDB operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through items keys and access-pattern design, across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: items keys and access-pattern design
partitions adaptive capacity and hot keys
Define invariants for the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB distributes state across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to GSIs LSIs and projection; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow GSIs LSIs and projection from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: GSIs LSIs and projection
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Amazon DynamoDB lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. consistency transactions and conditional writes is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for consistency transactions and conditional writes that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: consistency transactions and conditional writes
parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Amazon DynamoDB involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. capacity modes throttling and retries must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around capacity modes throttling and retries. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: capacity modes throttling and retries
transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Amazon DynamoDB should mirror query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For streams TTL global tables and backups, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for streams TTL global tables and backups: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: streams TTL global tables and backups
query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. For single-table design and sparse indexes, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving single-table design and sparse indexes with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: single-table design and sparse indexes
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Amazon DynamoDB decomposes cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. IAM encryption monitoring and cost should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for IAM encryption monitoring and cost showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: IAM encryption monitoring and cost
cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Amazon DynamoDB combines authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Amazon DynamoDB deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups
schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Amazon DynamoDB is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Amazon DynamoDB build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Amazon DynamoDB code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Amazon DynamoDB faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Amazon DynamoDB defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Amazon DynamoDB deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Amazon DynamoDB mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain items keys and access-pattern design, partitions adaptive capacity and hot keys, GSIs LSIs and projection, and consistency transactions and conditional writes with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around capacity modes throttling and retries.
Design tests across query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose single-table design and sparse indexes from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Amazon DynamoDB from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Amazon DynamoDB is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica.

Trace state explicitly across logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Amazon DynamoDB; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.
Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around GSIs LSIs and projection creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Amazon DynamoDB version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For consistency transactions and conditional writes, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Amazon DynamoDB.
Decompose cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Amazon DynamoDB behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around items keys and access-pattern design creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to single-table design and sparse indexes breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Amazon DynamoDB slice
workedExamples.code: // Amazon DynamoDB: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to items keys and access-pattern design and partitions adaptive capacity and hot keys.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Core policy remains testable while Amazon DynamoDB-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, especially around GSIs LSIs and projection.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Amazon DynamoDB
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates consistency transactions and conditional writes with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with record, key, index entry, query, transaction, log record, and replica; trace parse, plan, execute, commit, persist, replicate, compact or vacuum, and recover; identify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; cross client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: compare items keys and access-pattern design with partitions adaptive capacity and hot keys.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Amazon DynamoDB, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify logical data, physical pages or segments, indexes, logs, caches, and replication metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from transactions, locks or versions, latches, queues, consensus or replication, and admission control; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: build a test strategy for streams TTL global tables and backups.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around GSIs LSIs and projection, one saturation failure around cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, and one integration or compatibility failure at client protocol, transaction, schema, storage engine, replication stream, and backup. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: optimize IAM encryption monitoring and cost without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile cardinality error, random I/O, scans, contention, log flush, memory, and network replication, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around authentication, authorization, query parameters, tenant isolation, encryption, auditing, and backups; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, schema, migration, configuration, data files, transaction log, and backup, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Amazon DynamoDB only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Amazon DynamoDB: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, query semantics, transaction invariant, migration compatibility, failover, and restore, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

technologies.title: Neo4j
technologies.summary: Neo4j architecture, setup, lifecycle, testing, debugging, performance, security, deployment, and interview trade-offs.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Neo4j is a database system: software that stores data, finds it again, and protects correctness when many operations happen together.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can design reliable data models, write efficient queries, and keep important information correct through failures and concurrent updates. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Neo4j like a carefully run library: data has an address, indexes speed up discovery, and borrowing rules prevent conflicting changes. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: inspect image using `docker image inspect neo4j:latest`, observe the result, and explain what changed.
