theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: NuGet is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. A rigorous model identifies configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin, the invariant each unit owns, and the configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with package references identities and versions and transitive resolution and central package management; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things NuGet operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through package references identities and versions, across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: package references identities and versions
transitive resolution and central package management
Define invariants for the configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: NuGet distributes state across configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to feeds sources credentials and mapping; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow feeds sources credentials and mapping from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: feeds sources credentials and mapping
Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The NuGet lifecycle is discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. lock files restore and cache is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for lock files restore and cache that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: lock files restore and cache
discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in NuGet involves task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. target frameworks runtime identifiers and assets must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around target frameworks runtime identifiers and assets. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: target frameworks runtime identifiers and assets
task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing NuGet should mirror configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For packing signing and publishing, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for packing signing and publishing: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: packing signing and publishing
configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. For vulnerability audit and provenance, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving vulnerability audit and provenance with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: vulnerability audit and provenance
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on NuGet decomposes dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. troubleshooting conflicts and deterministic CI should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for troubleshooting conflicts and deterministic CI showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: troubleshooting conflicts and deterministic CI
dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production NuGet combines plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one NuGet deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input
configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: NuGet is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful NuGet build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest NuGet code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes NuGet faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: NuGet defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a NuGet deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the NuGet mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain package references identities and versions, transitive resolution and central package management, feeds sources credentials and mapping, and lock files restore and cache with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around target frameworks runtime identifiers and assets.
Design tests across configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose vulnerability audit and provenance from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install NuGet from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: NuGet is best understood as a set of boundaries, lifecycle rules, and failure modes—not a list of APIs. Trace one request or unit of work through those boundaries. The principal execution vocabulary is configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin.

Trace state explicitly across configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of NuGet; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around feeds sources credentials and mapping creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the NuGet version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For lock files restore and cache, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing NuGet.

Decompose dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes NuGet behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around package references identities and versions creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to vulnerability audit and provenance breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete NuGet slice
workedExamples.code: // NuGet: isolate the framework boundary behind a small application-facing interface.
workedExamples.explanation: A thin boundary keeps domain behavior testable and makes lifecycle and failure behavior visible. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to package references identities and versions and transitive resolution and central package management.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Core policy remains testable while NuGet-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, especially around feeds sources credentials and mapping.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for NuGet
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates lock files restore and cache with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: NuGet: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin; trace discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up; identify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; cross configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: NuGet: compare package references identities and versions with transitive resolution and central package management.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in NuGet, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: NuGet: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: NuGet: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: NuGet: build a test strategy for packing signing and publishing.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: NuGet: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: NuGet: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around feeds sources credentials and mapping, one saturation failure around dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, and one integration or compatibility failure at configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: NuGet: optimize troubleshooting conflicts and deterministic CI without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: NuGet: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: NuGet: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: NuGet: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose NuGet only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: NuGet: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

technologies.title: Android
technologies.summary: Android foundations, architecture, setup, command cookbook, testing, debugging, performance, security, production failure modes, and interview practice.

version.policy: Use a supported stable release; verify the project lockfile before an interview exercise.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Android is a mobile development technology: a way to build applications that run within phone and tablet operating-system rules.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can create responsive applications that handle lifecycle changes, limited resources, unreliable networks, local data, and device security. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Android like a shop inside a busy station: it serves users directly but must follow the building's schedules, space limits, permissions, and shutdown rules. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: run the primary health check using `./gradlew assembleDebug`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

keyTerms.meaning: the states an app or screen moves through
the data that determines what the user sees
a capability supplied by the device operating system

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Android is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. A rigorous model identifies screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service, the invariant each unit owns, and the UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with application components intents and manifests and activity fragment and process lifecycle; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Android operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through application components intents and manifests, across UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: application components intents and manifests
activity fragment and process lifecycle
Define invariants for the screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Android distributes state across ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to resources configuration and adaptive UI; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow resources configuration and adaptive UI from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: resources configuration and adaptive UI
Classify ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Android lifecycle is launch, create, appear, interact, background, suspend, restore, terminate, and update. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. ViewModel state flows and saved state is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for ViewModel state flows and saved state that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: ViewModel state flows and saved state
launch, create, appear, interact, background, suspend, restore, terminate, and update
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Android involves main-thread rendering, asynchronous tasks, background work, cancellation, streams, and process death. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. coroutines WorkManager and background limits must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around coroutines WorkManager and background limits. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: coroutines WorkManager and background limits
main-thread rendering, asynchronous tasks, background work, cancellation, streams, and process death
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Android should mirror state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For storage Room networking and offline sync, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for storage Room networking and offline sync: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: storage Room networking and offline sync
state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process. For permissions privacy and app sandbox, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving permissions privacy and app sandbox with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: permissions privacy and app sandbox
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Android decomposes frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. testing profiling packaging and Play delivery should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for testing profiling packaging and Play delivery showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: testing profiling packaging and Play delivery
frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Android combines permissions, intents or URLs, WebViews, local storage, logs, credentials, transport, and platform IPC with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of source, resources, dependency lock, signed application package, symbols, and store metadata; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Android deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: permissions, intents or URLs, WebViews, local storage, logs, credentials, transport, and platform IPC
source, resources, dependency lock, signed application package, symbols, and store metadata
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Android is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Android build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Android code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Android faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Android defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Android deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Android mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace launch, create, appear, interact, background, suspend, restore, terminate, and update for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain application components intents and manifests, activity fragment and process lifecycle, resources configuration and adaptive UI, and ViewModel state flows and saved state with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around coroutines WorkManager and background limits.
Design tests across state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose permissions privacy and app sandbox from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model permissions, intents or URLs, WebViews, local storage, logs, credentials, transport, and platform IPC with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Android from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped source, resources, dependency lock, signed application package, symbols, and store metadata, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Android is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. The principal execution vocabulary is screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service.

Trace state explicitly across ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is launch, create, appear, interact, background, suspend, restore, terminate, and update. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves main-thread rendering, asynchronous tasks, background work, cancellation, streams, and process death; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Android; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around resources configuration and adaptive UI creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Android version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For ViewModel state flows and saved state, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Android.
Decompose frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model permissions, intents or URLs, WebViews, local storage, logs, credentials, transport, and platform IPC; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Android behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around application components intents and manifests creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.

Unbounded work across main-thread rendering, asynchronous tasks, background work, cancellation, streams, and process death exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to permissions privacy and app sandbox breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Android slice
workedExamples.code: # Android: validate inputs, pin versions, run a focused check, and capture observable output.
workedExamples.explanation: The production-shaped example makes configuration and recovery paths explicit before scaling the happy path. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to application components intents and manifests and activity fragment and process lifecycle.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process. Core policy remains testable while Android-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build, especially around resources configuration and adaptive UI.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Android
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates ViewModel state flows and saved state with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats source, resources, dependency lock, signed application package, symbols, and store metadata and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Android: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with screen, component, state holder, navigation route, task, and platform service; trace launch, create, appear, interact, background, suspend, restore, terminate, and update; identify ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state; cross UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Android: compare application components intents and manifests with activity fragment and process lifecycle.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Android, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Android: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify ephemeral UI state, saved state, local data, remote cache, credentials, and lifecycle state; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Android: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from main-thread rendering, asynchronous tasks, background work, cancellation, streams, and process death; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Android: build a test strategy for storage Room networking and offline sync.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Android: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Android: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around resources configuration and adaptive UI, one saturation failure around frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage, and one integration or compatibility failure at UI event, navigation, platform API, network, storage, permission, and application process. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Android: optimize testing profiling packaging and Play delivery without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile frame time, layout, image work, startup, allocation, network, battery, and storage, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Android: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around permissions, intents or URLs, WebViews, local storage, logs, credentials, transport, and platform IPC; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Android: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, source, resources, dependency lock, signed application package, symbols, and store metadata, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Android: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Android only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Android: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, state reducer or view model, component, platform integration, navigation flow, and release build, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Jetpack Compose is a mobile development technology: a way to build applications that run within phone and tablet operating-system rules.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can create responsive applications that handle lifecycle changes, limited resources, unreliable networks, local data, and device security. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Jetpack Compose like a shop inside a busy station: it serves users directly but must follow the building's schedules, space limits, permissions, and shutdown rules. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: run the primary health check using `./gradlew testDebugUnitTest`, observe the result, and explain what changed.
