theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Git is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. A rigorous model identifies configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin, the invariant each unit owns, and the configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with objects blobs trees commits and refs and working tree index and HEAD; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Git operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through objects blobs trees commits and refs, across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: objects blobs trees commits and refs
working tree index and HEAD
Define invariants for the configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Git distributes state across configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to branches merges and three-way reconciliation; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow branches merges and three-way reconciliation from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: branches merges and three-way reconciliation
Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Git lifecycle is discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting
discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Git involves task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. remotes fetch pull push and tracking must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around remotes fetch pull push and tracking. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: remotes fetch pull push and tracking
task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Git should mirror configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For tags signatures and object integrity, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for tags signatures and object integrity: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: tags signatures and object integrity
configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. For reflog recovery bisect and blame, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving reflog recovery bisect and blame with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: reflog recovery bisect and blame
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Git decomposes dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. attributes hooks submodules and secure workflows should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for attributes hooks submodules and secure workflows showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: attributes hooks submodules and secure workflows
dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Git combines plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Git deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input
configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Git is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Git build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Git code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Git faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Git defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Git deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Git mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.
Explain objects blobs trees commits and refs, working tree index and HEAD, branches merges and three-way reconciliation, and rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around remotes fetch pull push and tracking.
Design tests across configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose reflog recovery bisect and blame from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Git from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Git is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. The principal execution vocabulary is configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin.

Trace state explicitly across configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.

Integration crosses configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Git; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around branches merges and three-way reconciliation creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Git version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Git.

Decompose dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Git behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around objects blobs trees commits and refs creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to reflog recovery bisect and blame breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Smallest complete Git slice
workedExamples.code: # Git: validate inputs, pin versions, run a focused check, and capture observable output.
workedExamples.explanation: The production-shaped example makes configuration and recovery paths explicit before scaling the happy path. Name the input, owned state, output, and cleanup path; then relate the slice to objects blobs trees commits and refs and working tree index and HEAD.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Core policy remains testable while Git-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.

workedExamples.title: Invariant-focused contract test
workedExamples.explanation: The test covers observable behavior and the unhappy path rather than private implementation. Add a real integration test for configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, especially around branches merges and three-way reconciliation.

workedExamples.title: Evidence-first production diagnosis
workedExamples.code:
# Evidence-first diagnostic loop for Git
record version-and-config
reproduce smallest-failing-case
capture logs metrics traces and resource state
compare healthy-versus-failing path
change one suspected cause
verify invariant and regression test
workedExamples.explanation: This sequence resists symptom-driven guessing. It correlates rebase cherry-pick and history rewriting with resource and request evidence before proposing a change.

workedExamples.title: Compatible staged rollout and rollback
workedExamples.code:
# Safe-change pseudocode
validate config and compatibility
stage to a small cohort
watch correctness latency saturation and error signals
stop on the declared threshold
promote gradually or roll back
verify data and external side effects after recovery
workedExamples.explanation: A safe release treats configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact and externally visible state as one compatibility problem. Rollback is tested before deployment, not invented after failure.

questions.prompt: Git: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with configuration, task, dependency, input, output, cache entry, and plugin; trace discover, resolve, validate, execute, cache, report, publish, and clean up; identify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; cross configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. Separate documented guarantees from one implementation or deployment.
questions.whyTricky: Fluent API usage often masks a weak model of what actually executes.
rubric: Names the execution unit and lifecycle.
Explains state ownership and a concrete boundary.

questions.prompt: Git: compare objects blobs trees commits and refs with working tree index and HEAD.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Git, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.
questions.whyTricky: Related concepts are often presented together and then treated as synonyms.
rubric: Uses a concrete counterexample or boundary.

questions.prompt: Git: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify configuration graph, dependency graph, workspace, cache, generated output, and remote metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.
questions.whyTricky: In-memory success is frequently mistaken for durable or externally visible completion.
rubric: Names the commit or visibility boundary.

questions.prompt: Git: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from task graph parallelism, workers, locks, remote calls, cancellation, and cache coordination; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Git: build a test strategy for tags signatures and object integrity.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.
rubric: Matches test type to a real boundary.
Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Git: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.
questions.whyTricky: Average latency and temporal correlation routinely point at the wrong cause.
rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Git: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around branches merges and three-way reconciliation, one saturation failure around dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, and one integration or compatibility failure at configuration file, plugin, registry, subprocess, filesystem, network service, and CI runner. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.
questions.whyTricky: Generic lists of possible failures are not actionable without discriminating evidence.
rubric: Pairs each with a useful signal.

questions.prompt: Git: optimize attributes hooks submodules and secure workflows without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile dependency resolution, invalidated work, disk I/O, network fetch, serialization, and worker contention, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.
questions.whyTricky: Local micro-optimizations can move cost, worsen tails, or violate correctness.
rubric: States new trade-offs and verifies end-to-end impact.

questions.prompt: Git: threat-model the most important production boundary.
questions.answer: Inventory assets and actors around plugins, registries, scripts, credentials, generated artifacts, provenance, and untrusted test input; map trust boundaries and abuse cases; authenticate identity; authorize resource and action; validate structure and intent; limit privileges and data; protect secrets and artifacts; and define detection, response, and recovery evidence.
questions.whyTricky: Security is reduced to input sanitization or authentication while authorization and operational recovery are ignored.
rubric: Identifies assets actors and trust boundaries.
Uses least privilege and recovery evidence.

questions.prompt: Git: plan a compatible major-version upgrade.
questions.answer: Inventory APIs, plugins, configuration, lockfile, cache, report, package, signature, and published artifact, stored state and client contracts; pin and read compatibility notes; add dual-read or additive changes where needed; test representative behavior; stage cohorts; monitor declared signals; preserve rollback while compatible; and verify recovery.
questions.whyTricky: A green compile does not prove data, plugin, operational, or behavioral compatibility.
rubric: Explains rollback limits or roll-forward recovery.

questions.prompt: Git: when should you choose an alternative technology?
questions.answer: State the workload, invariant, team and operational constraints. Compare execution model, ecosystem, failure semantics, compatibility, observability, security, cost, and exit strategy. Choose Git only when its strengths align with the dominant constraints.
questions.whyTricky: Preference and ecosystem familiarity are often presented as architecture evidence.
rubric: Names a condition that reverses the decision.

questions.prompt: Git: give a two-minute production readiness review.
questions.answer: Cover pinned versions, configuration validation, configuration semantics, focused task, integration fixture, reproducible build, and isolated CI run, resource bounds, timeout and retry budgets, observability, threat model, secrets and identity, compatible data changes, staged release, rollback or compensation, backup and restore, and an owned incident runbook.
questions.whyTricky: Feature completeness is confused with operability and recoverability.
rubric: Covers correctness performance security and operations.

beginnerGuide.whatItIs: Linux Operations is a platform: a collection of lower-level services and rules on which applications are built or operated.
beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Learn it so you can understand the boundaries underneath an application so you can design, debug, and explain behavior across layers. In interviews, the important part is explaining what happens and why, not reciting names.
beginnerGuide.analogy: Think of Linux Operations like a city's infrastructure: roads, power, rules, and utilities make buildings possible, while failures underneath affect everything above. The analogy is only a starting point; the precise rules come later in this manual.
beginnerGuide.firstStep: Begin with one tiny win: run the primary health check using `uname -a`, observe the result, and explain what changed.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Linux Operations is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. A rigorous model identifies resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy, the invariant each unit owns, and the identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with processes threads scheduling and signals and virtual memory paging and pressure; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Linux Operations operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through processes threads scheduling and signals, across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: processes threads scheduling and signals
virtual memory paging and pressure
Define invariants for the resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Linux Operations distributes state across declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to files inodes permissions and descriptors; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow files inodes permissions and descriptors from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: files inodes permissions and descriptors
Classify declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Linux Operations lifecycle is provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. system calls namespaces and cgroups is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for system calls namespaces and cgroups that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: system calls namespaces and cgroups
provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Linux Operations involves workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. networking sockets routing and firewall must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around networking sockets routing and firewall. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: networking sockets routing and firewall
workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Linux Operations should mirror configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For services boot logs and systemd, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for services boot logs and systemd: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: services boot logs and systemd
configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. For packages storage and filesystems, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving packages storage and filesystems with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: packages storage and filesystems
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Linux Operations decomposes CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. observability performance security and incident response should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for observability performance security and incident response showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: observability performance security and incident response
CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Linux Operations combines identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of declarative configuration, image or binary, policy, state backup, telemetry, and runbook; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Linux Operations deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.

misconceptions.claim: Linux Operations is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Linux Operations build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Linux Operations code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Linux Operations faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Linux Operations defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Linux Operations deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

runtime: Linux Operations is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. The principal execution vocabulary is resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy.

Trace state explicitly across declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.
Integration crosses identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Linux Operations; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around files inodes permissions and descriptors creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Linux Operations version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For system calls namespaces and cgroups, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Linux Operations.
Decompose CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Linux Operations behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around processes threads scheduling and signals creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: explain the execution model from input to cleanup.
questions.answer: Begin with resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy; trace provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire; identify declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata; cross identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator; finish with output, errors, cancellation, and cleanup. questions.prompt: Linux Operations: compare processes threads scheduling and signals with virtual memory paging and pressure.
questions.answer: Define each term, show how they interact in Linux Operations, give one case where either can exist without the other, and choose between designs using the workload, invariant, hidden cost, and failure mode rather than familiarity.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: who owns state and when does it become externally committed?
questions.answer: Classify declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata; identify the owner and mutation authority; distinguish temporary, cached, durable, and external effects; then explain transaction, idempotency, cleanup, and recovery boundaries.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: design cancellation and overload behavior.
questions.answer: Start from workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission; set deadlines and bounded queues or pools; propagate cancellation across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator; stop retries when budgets expire; shed optional work; preserve the core invariant; and expose saturation, drops, and timeout signals.
questions.whyTricky: Concurrency is discussed as throughput while cancellation, queueing, and downstream capacity are omitted.
rubric: Defines overload signals and invariant-preserving degradation.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: build a test strategy for services boot logs and systemd.
questions.answer: Use deterministic unit tests for policy, real integration tests for configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof, and a few critical end-to-end journeys. Add malformed, boundary, duplicate, cancellation, partial-failure, restart, migration, and concurrency cases where the invariant requires them.
questions.whyTricky: A test pyramid label is not a substitute for choosing boundaries that can prove behavior.

Controls nondeterminism and asserts public behavior.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: diagnose a tail-latency regression after a release.
questions.answer: Verify version and workload comparability, split latency across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator, correlate traces with queue, utilization, allocation and downstream waits, inspect CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation, compare healthy and failing cohorts, change one cause, and verify percentiles plus correctness.

rubric: Uses comparable workload and tail percentiles.
Verifies one causal change without sacrificing correctness.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: name three failures and the signal that distinguishes each.
questions.answer: Choose one correctness failure around files inodes permissions and descriptors, one saturation failure around CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation, and one integration or compatibility failure at identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. Pair each with a distinct invariant, log, trace, metric, state inspection, plan, or artifact diff.

questions.prompt: Linux Operations: optimize observability performance security and incident response without premature tuning.
questions.answer: Declare workload and SLO, profile CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation, quantify time and resource cost, improve algorithm or data movement first, introduce bounded batching caching pooling or parallelism only with an invalidation and overload model, then remeasure the full path.

theorySections.title: Core model, vocabulary, and boundaries
theorySections.explanation: Docker is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. A rigorous model identifies resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy, the invariant each unit owns, and the identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator where representation or responsibility changes. Begin with images layers manifests and registries and containers namespaces cgroups and filesystems; distinguish guarantees made by the specification from conveniences supplied by one version or deployment.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Name the things Docker operates on, who owns them, what must remain true, and where control crosses into another subsystem.
theorySections.analogy: Think of a well-labelled workshop: each bench owns particular tools and materials, and a handoff ticket records what crosses to the next bench.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software values may be copied, aliased, retried, scheduled, or persisted invisibly, so the actual contract must come from documented semantics and observed state.
theorySections.concreteExample: Trace one input through images layers manifests and registries, across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator, to an output and cleanup action. Mark every place an error can change ownership.
keyPoints: images layers manifests and registries
containers namespaces cgroups and filesystems
Define invariants for the resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy.
Separate specification guarantees from common implementation behavior.

theorySections.title: Data, state, identity, and lifetime
theorySections.explanation: Docker distributes state across declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata. Correctness requires stable identity, explicit ownership, mutation rules, and a lifetime that covers success, rejection, cancellation, retry, and process failure. Relate those rules to Dockerfiles build context cache and multi-stage builds; do not confuse an in-memory reference, cached representation, durable record, and externally committed effect.
theorySections.plainEnglish: For every piece of state, answer who created it, who may change it, how long it lives, and how another observer knows it is current.
theorySections.analogy: A library catalogue, loan record, and physical book are related but different forms of state with different owners and lifetimes.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital state can be copied instantly, observed concurrently, or survive a process in external storage, so physical custody is only an intuition aid.
theorySections.concreteExample: Follow Dockerfiles build context cache and multi-stage builds from creation through mutation, serialization or persistence, cache interaction, retry, and final cleanup or archival.
keyPoints: Dockerfiles build context cache and multi-stage builds
Classify declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata.
Make identity, mutation, lifetime, and durable effects explicit.
Design idempotency or compensation for repeated external work.

theorySections.title: Execution lifecycle and control flow
theorySections.explanation: The Docker lifecycle is provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire. Framework hooks and convenient APIs often hide several transitions, so a strong explanation names when configuration becomes fixed, when user work begins, what may run lazily, which failures are translated, and what shutdown must drain. networks ports DNS and service discovery is easiest to understand as a state transition rather than a list of calls.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Draw the states from startup to shutdown and explain which code runs at each transition, including the error and cancellation path.
theorySections.analogy: A theatre production has rehearsal, doors-open, performance, scene changes, emergency stops, and closing procedures; skipping a stage causes different failures.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer work may be concurrent, speculative, retried, or restored after a crash, unlike a single linear performance.
theorySections.concreteExample: Write a timeline for networks ports DNS and service discovery that includes initialization, one successful operation, an exception or cancellation, resource release, and graceful termination.
keyPoints: networks ports DNS and service discovery
provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire
Locate lazy work and hidden lifecycle hooks.
Treat shutdown and recovery as normal states, not afterthoughts.

theorySections.title: Concurrency, ordering, cancellation, and backpressure
theorySections.explanation: Concurrency in Docker involves workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission. First state the shared invariant and required ordering; then choose confinement, immutability, messages, locks, atomics, transactions, queues, or single-writer sequencing. volumes bind mounts and data lifetime must include cancellation and bounded demand, because adding workers without capacity control can increase queueing and failure amplification.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Several operations can make progress together, but shared state and limited downstream capacity still need one explicit coordination rule.
theorySections.analogy: A restaurant serves many tables with limited ovens: tickets need ordering, ovens impose capacity, and cancelled orders must stop consuming ingredients.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Schedulers, memory visibility, distributed delivery, and crash recovery have formal rules that human teamwork does not model precisely.
theorySections.concreteExample: Model two competing operations around volumes bind mounts and data lifetime. State which orderings are legal, how cancellation propagates, what is bounded, and how overload is signalled.
keyPoints: volumes bind mounts and data lifetime
workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission
Distinguish concurrency from parallelism.
Bound queues, retries, pools, buffers, and in-flight work.

theorySections.title: Testing and proof of correctness
theorySections.explanation: Testing Docker should mirror configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof. Unit tests prove local policy, integration tests prove real boundary semantics, and a small number of end-to-end tests prove critical journeys. For entrypoints signals health and shutdown, include counterexamples, invalid transitions, repeated work, version compatibility, and resource cleanup; a green happy-path test is not evidence for concurrency or recovery.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Test each rule at the cheapest boundary that can actually prove it, and move outward only when the real runtime or integration defines the behavior.
theorySections.analogy: Inspecting a vehicle includes component tests, subsystem tests, a road test, and a crash simulation; repeating only the road test leaves important claims unproved.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software tests observe selected executions rather than every possible schedule or input, so invariants may also need types, static checks, property tests, or formal reasoning.
theorySections.concreteExample: Create a test matrix for entrypoints signals health and shutdown: ordinary success, malformed input, boundary value, duplicate, timeout, partial dependency failure, restart, and compatible upgrade.
keyPoints: entrypoints signals health and shutdown
configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof
Assert public behavior and invariants rather than private implementation.
Use realistic boundaries for generated, serialized, transactional, or concurrent behavior.

theorySections.title: Diagnostics, observability, and failure isolation
theorySections.explanation: Debugging begins by preserving version, configuration, input, identity, timing, and the first incorrect transition. Correlate logs, metrics, traces, profiles, state inspection, and generated artifacts across identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. For Compose security and supply chain, compare healthy and failing paths, rule out resource saturation and downstream waits, and change one causal variable before declaring success.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Collect evidence that distinguishes competing explanations, then find the earliest state that differs from a healthy run.
theorySections.analogy: A doctor combines symptoms, history, measurements, and controlled tests; one alarming number is not automatically the cause.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Software instrumentation can be incomplete, sampled, delayed, or itself costly, so absence of a signal is not proof that an event did not happen.
theorySections.concreteExample: Diagnose a regression involving Compose security and supply chain with a timeline, correlation ID, resource graph, version diff, smallest reproducer, and a regression test for the first violated invariant.
keyPoints: Compose security and supply chain
Separate symptom, correlation, and cause.
Capture bounded, privacy-aware evidence with stable identities.
Verify the repair under the original workload and failure condition.

theorySections.title: Performance, scaling, and resource economics
theorySections.explanation: Performance work on Docker decomposes CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation. Complexity, data layout, batching, locality, cache behavior, queueing, contention, serialization, and downstream capacity interact. debugging resource limits and production boundaries should be evaluated with a declared workload and tail distribution; faster median latency can coexist with worse overload recovery, cost, fairness, or correctness.
theorySections.plainEnglish: Measure where time and resources are spent, improve the constrained stage, and remeasure the entire path under representative load.
theorySections.analogy: A road widens traffic only until the next junction becomes the bottleneck; unbounded on-ramps merely move the queue.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Computer workloads can change shape abruptly and caches can alter the path, so yesterday's bottleneck may not remain today's constraint.
theorySections.concreteExample: Build a capacity table for debugging resource limits and production boundaries showing arrival rate, service time, concurrency, queue limit, memory per operation, downstream limit, saturation signal, and safe-shedding behavior.
keyPoints: debugging resource limits and production boundaries
CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation
Measure percentiles, utilization, queueing, errors, and cost together.
Prefer algorithm and data-movement improvements before tuning knobs.

theorySections.title: Security, compatibility, operations, and trade-offs
theorySections.explanation: Production Docker combines identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail with version and data compatibility. Validate at each trust boundary, authorize the resource and action, protect credentials and artifacts, and keep an audit trail for sensitive changes. Stage upgrades of declarative configuration, image or binary, policy, state backup, telemetry, and runbook; define rollback triggers, but recognize when external effects or forward-only migrations require roll-forward or compensation instead.
theorySections.plainEnglish: A safe feature must resist hostile input, expose only intended authority, remain diagnosable, and change versions without corrupting data or trapping operators.
theorySections.analogy: A border checkpoint verifies identity and cargo, records entry, limits destinations, and has procedures for policy changes and emergencies.
theorySections.analogyLimit: Digital identities can be delegated, replayed, or automated at scale, while a rollback may not undo messages, money movement, or leaked data.
theorySections.concreteExample: Threat-model one Docker deployment: enumerate assets, actors, trust boundaries, abuse cases, least-privilege controls, audit signals, compatible rollout steps, rollback limits, and recovery verification.
keyPoints: identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail
declarative configuration, image or binary, policy, state backup, telemetry, and runbook
Treat dependencies, plugins, build systems, and generated artifacts as supply-chain boundaries.
Tie rollout and rollback to measurable correctness and safety signals.

misconceptions.claim: Docker is understood once its common API calls are memorized.
misconceptions.correction: API recall is useful only after you can explain the resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy, lifecycle, state ownership, hidden work, and failure contracts.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Tutorials optimize for a quick successful demo, while interviews and incidents test behavior outside the happy path.

misconceptions.claim: A successful Docker build proves the system is correct.
misconceptions.correction: A build checks declared syntax and contracts; runtime inputs, integration semantics, concurrency, resources, permissions, and recovery still require evidence.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Fast deterministic feedback is confused with proof of production behavior.

misconceptions.claim: The shortest Docker code performs the least work.
misconceptions.correction: Convenient abstractions can hide CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation; inspect plans, traces, bundles, generated code, queries, or profiles.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Visible source length is used as a proxy for execution cost.

misconceptions.claim: Adding workers or parallelism always makes Docker faster.
misconceptions.correction: Speedup is bounded by dependencies and capacity; coordination, contention, memory, queues, and downstream saturation can make throughput and latency worse.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Runnable work is mistaken for useful independent work and infinite downstream capacity.

misconceptions.claim: Docker defaults are production guarantees.
misconceptions.correction: Defaults target broad usability and can change by version. Make durability, consistency, timeouts, retries, security, capacity, and lifecycle policy explicit.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Local demos rarely exercise failure, load, multi-tenancy, or upgrade constraints.

misconceptions.claim: Rollback always restores a Docker deployment to the previous state.
misconceptions.correction: Code can roll back while schemas, data, messages, caches, client contracts, credentials, or external effects remain changed; design compatibility and compensation explicitly.
misconceptions.whyItHappens: Deployment artifacts are confused with the entire distributed state of the system.

revisionChecklist: Explain the Docker mental model without product slogans or API lists.
Define the core units (resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy) and one invariant each major abstraction owns.
Trace provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire for success, rejection, cancellation, failure, and shutdown.
Classify declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata by owner, mutation rule, lifetime, and durability.

Explain images layers manifests and registries, containers namespaces cgroups and filesystems, Dockerfiles build context cache and multi-stage builds, and networks ports DNS and service discovery with one concrete example each.
State the ordering, synchronization, cancellation, and backpressure rules around volumes bind mounts and data lifetime.
Design tests across configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof, including a counterexample and recovery case.
Diagnose Compose security and supply chain from evidence and name the first discriminating signal.
Measure CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation under a declared workload before proposing an optimization.
Threat-model identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail with least privilege and auditable decisions.
Plan a compatible version or schema upgrade with staged rollout and realistic rollback limits.
Answer a design comparison by stating workload, invariant, alternatives, trade-off, and failure signal.
setup: Install Docker from an official distribution or ecosystem package source and record the exact runtime, tool, and plugin versions.
Create the smallest isolated project, commit its manifest and lock metadata, and verify one build or execution before adding application code.
Separate local, test, and production configuration; validate required values at startup and keep secrets outside source and generated artifacts.
Enable the formatter, static checks, focused test command, dependency inspection, and diagnostic tooling used by the project.

Build the production-shaped declarative configuration, image or binary, policy, state backup, telemetry, and runbook, run it in a disposable environment, and exercise startup, one successful path, one rejected path, and graceful shutdown.
runtime: Docker is an operational system with inputs, state, lifecycle, resource limits, and observable failure signals. Trace those five things before memorizing APIs. The principal execution vocabulary is resource, process or workload, control-plane object, identity, network endpoint, and policy.

Trace state explicitly across declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata; distinguish durable state, cached state, request-local state, and derived state.
The lifecycle is provision, configure, reconcile, serve, observe, update, drain, recover, and retire. Each transition can allocate resources, expose partial work, or require cleanup.
Integration crosses identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. Every crossing needs a contract for validation, timeouts, cancellation, errors, and observability.

Concurrent behavior involves workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission; correctness comes from a named invariant and ordering rule, not from timing observed in one run.
testing: Test the smallest stable policy without booting all of Docker; include empty, invalid, duplicate, boundary-size, cancelled, and repeated input.

Use real integration tests at configuration validation, isolated workload, integration environment, failure drill, and recovery proof where serialization, lifecycle hooks, generated behavior, transactions, or platform semantics define correctness.

Add property, contract, concurrency, migration, accessibility, or recovery tests when the behavior around Dockerfiles build context cache and multi-stage builds creates a broader invariant than example-based tests cover.
Keep test data deterministic, control clocks and randomness, assert externally visible behavior, and preserve diagnostic artifacts only for failed runs.
debugging: Record the Docker version, resolved dependencies, configuration, input, and first failing boundary before changing code.
Reproduce the smallest failure and compare a healthy path with the failing path using logs, traces, metrics, state inspection, and generated output.
For networks ports DNS and service discovery, locate the first violated invariant rather than the last wrapper error; then test one causal hypothesis at a time.
Inspect queues, pools, locks, resource pressure, network waits, generated plans or bundles, and lifecycle cleanup when the symptom is intermittent or load-dependent.
performance: Define the workload and measure throughput, tail latency, allocation or memory, utilization, queue depth, errors, and cost before optimizing Docker.
Decompose CPU, memory, disk, network, control-plane throughput, quotas, and downstream saturation; improve algorithms and data movement before adding caches, pools, batching, or parallelism.
Bound concurrency and buffers, propagate cancellation and deadlines, and apply backpressure before overload becomes an outage.
Benchmark representative production shapes, include warm-up and cold-start behavior where relevant, and verify that optimization preserves the invariant.
security: Threat-model identity, policy, network path, secret, artifact, host, tenant, and audit trail; validate untrusted structure and intent before invoking privileged behavior.
Authenticate identities, authorize each resource and action, minimize data and permissions, and keep secrets out of source, logs, traces, and client artifacts.
Pin and review dependencies and plugins, verify provenance where available, patch supported versions, and remove unused attack surface.
Use safe APIs for queries, templates, paths, commands, deserialization, and transport; log auditable decisions without exposing sensitive values.
failureModes: Version, plugin, lockfile, runtime, or generated-artifact mismatch makes Docker behave differently across environments.
Hidden work around images layers manifests and registries creates accidental I/O, allocation, queries, rendering, or network calls in a convenient-looking operation.

Incorrect ownership of declared configuration, observed runtime state, logs, metrics, persistent data, and recovery metadata produces stale state, leaks, lost updates, nondeterminism, or unrecoverable partial effects.
Unbounded work across workloads, controllers, queues, leases, failover, retries, and capacity admission exhausts memory, workers, connections, downstream capacity, or retry budgets.
Observability records symptoms without the identity, version, correlation, or state transition needed to isolate the first failure.
A change to Compose security and supply chain breaks compatibility, authorization, stored data, or rollback assumptions even though the build and happy path succeed.

workedExamples.title: Boundary validation without leaking framework concerns
workedExamples.explanation: Validation and error translation stay at identity, API, network, compute, storage, control plane, tenant, and operator. Core policy remains testable while Docker-specific lifecycle and integration behavior remain in adapters.
